docs.title: AI Landing Zones
docs.text:
Build AI applications and agents on a secure, resilient Azure foundation. AI Landing Zones provides workload landing zone reference architectures and deployable implementations. Start with Agent Landing Zone, centralize model access with AI Gateway Landing Zone, or combine both.

Note

Designed and tested for Azure public cloud. Validate government and sovereign deployments separately. Some included services may be in preview.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Agent Landing Zone provides the workload foundation, while AI Gateway Landing Zone centralizes model access.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Bicep and Terraform implementations built on Azure Verified Modules.

docs.title: Workloads
docs.text: A foundation for generative and non-generative AI workloads, focused on AI on Azure Platform.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Build AI applications and agents on a secure Azure foundation for scenarios such as:

Use case Example scenario Knowledge assistants Help employees find answers in organizational policies, procedures, and technical documentation. Document processing Extract, classify, and summarize information from invoices, contracts, and reports. Business process agents Coordinate tasks across business systems, such as handling service requests and approval workflows.

docs.title: Agent Landing Zone
docs.text:
Agent Landing Zone provides an Azure foundation for AI applications and agents, with a default application built on Microsoft Foundry. Deploy the infrastructure, the application, or both using the Agent Landing Zone guide.

These reference architectures show private-network deployment options. Resource selection and reuse depend on the implementation and deployment settings.

docs.title: Standalone
docs.text: The workload owns its networking and supporting services without a shared platform hub.

docs.title: With Platform Hub
docs.text: The workload connects to a platform hub that provides shared connectivity, DNS and egress services.

docs.title: AI Gateway Landing Zone
docs.text:
AI Gateway Landing Zone provides a shared gateway for AI applications and agents, using Azure API Management to centrally manage access to Microsoft Foundry models. Choose a Bicep or Terraform implementation below.

The integrated scenario below combines an Agent Landing Zone, a Platform Hub and a separate AI Gateway Landing Zone. The gateway has its own deployment and connectivity requirements; it is not provisioned automatically by Agent Landing Zone.

docs.title: AI Landing Zone for Azure Container Apps
High-Level Architecture Design: AI Workloads on Azure Container Apps
Executive Summary
docs.text: This article defines a production-ready landing zone architecture for deploying AI workloads on Azure Container Apps. It lists the design considerations and recommendations when using Azure Container Apps for AI workloads.

docs.title: Infrastructure & Compute
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for the infrastructure and compute design area for the landing zone.

docs.title: Environments & Workload Profiles
docs.text:
The Container App Environment serves as the administrative and security boundary. To cater for different workload performance and cost requirements, we utilize multiple workload profiles within a single environment:

  • Consumption Profiles: Best for variable or unpredictable traffic patterns. scale to zero to minimize costs during idle periods.
  • Dedicated Profiles: Best for steady-state workloads or background workers that require reserved compute for consistent latency.
  • Serverless GPUs vs. Dedicated GPUs:
    • Serverless GPUs: Ideal for bursty inference where you only pay for the duration of the request.
    • Dedicated GPUs: Necessary for long-running training, fine-tuning, or supporting larger inferencing models.

The architecture organizes workloads into five distinct workload profiles:

Workload Profile Resource Type GPU Strategy Typical Workloads Latency-sensitive inferencing Container Apps Dedicated GPUs Real-time inference with Ollama, Foundry Models, or similar open-source inference runtimes requiring guaranteed low-latency responses Cost-sensitive inferencing Container Apps Serverless GPUs Bursty inference workloads using Ollama, Foundry Models, or similar open-source inference runtimes where pay-per-request is more economical ML and training Container App Jobs Serverless GPUs Batch training jobs, fine-tuning, embedding generation, and periodic model retraining as run-to-completion tasks. Use dedicated GPUs when latency is critical. Design jobs to be idempotent with checkpointing so that retries or restarts resume safely without reprocessing completed work or corrupting artifacts Apps Container Apps Consumption (CPU) Front-end UIs, MCP servers, and AI agents AI Gateway Container Apps Dedicated (CPU) AI Gateway for routing and load balancing across model endpoints, agents and MCP servers. Runs on a dedicated profile with minimum replicas to avoid cold starts and ensure consistent latency on the critical inference path

docs.title: Networking & Security
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for the networking and security design area for the landing zone.

docs.title: VNet Integration & Egress Control
docs.text:
For enterprise security, we implement "Bring Your Own VNet" to apply custom security controls: - Dedicated Subnet: The Azure Container Apps environment requires a dedicated subnet delegated to Microsoft.App/environments. - Internal vs. External Access: - Internal: The environment is hidden from the public internet; traffic is routed via a Private IP. - External: The environment is reachable via a public load balancer managed by Azure Container Apps. - Egress Control: Route all outbound traffic through an Azure Firewall for inspection and centralized policy enforcement.

Note: Azure NAT Gateway is also supported for egress in workload profile environments with custom VNet integration. Use NAT Gateway when the primary requirement is a static outbound IP without the need for Layer-7 traffic inspection. For scenarios requiring outbound traffic filtering, FQDN-based rules, or threat intelligence, Azure Firewall remains the recommended approach.

docs.title: Private Access & Secret Management
docs.text:
• Private Endpoints: Ensure all communication to back-end services (Cosmos DB, Storage, Key Vault) stays on the Microsoft backbone.
  • Key Vault: All sensitive data (API keys, access tokens, SSL certs) must be stored in Azure Key Vault and referenced as secrets in Azure Container Apps.
  • Managed Identities: Use User-Assigned Managed Identities for all resource-to-resource authentication (e.g., Azure Container Apps pulling from ACR) to eliminate the need for hardcoded credentials.

docs.title: Ingress Security
docs.text:
• HTTPS Enforcement: Set allowInsecure: false on all ingress configurations to enforce TLS and automatically redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
  • IP Restrictions: Configure IP allow/deny rules when relevant to restrict inbound access to known CIDR ranges (e.g., corporate VPN, Azure Front Door backend IPs).
  • Mutual TLS (mTLS): Enable mTLS for service-to-service communication between container apps within the environment to encrypt traffic and verify both client and server identities.
  • CORS: Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing policies for front-end AI chat UIs that call backend inference APIs from browser clients.

docs.title: GenAI Application Dependencies
docs.text:
The architecture relies on a set of Azure services that support the AI workloads:

  • Azure Cosmos DB: Persistent storage for conversation history, agent state, session metadata, and application data.
  • Azure Key Vault: Centralized secret management for API keys, model access tokens, and certificates.
  • Azure Storage Account: Durable storage for model weights (via Azure Files mounts), training datasets, and artifacts.
  • Azure Container Registry (ACR): Private registry for container images. Deploy in the same region as the Azure Container Apps environment for minimal pull latency.
  • Managed Identities: User-Assigned Managed Identities for all service-to-service authentication, eliminating hardcoded credentials.
  • Azure App Configuration: Centrally manage applications' configuration.

docs.title: AI Workload Optimization
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for optimizing the AI workloads to be deployed in the landing zone.

docs.title: Model Serving & Deployment
docs.text:
• Foundry Models: Leverage built-in integrations for turnkey deployment of Microsoft-managed foundry models.
  • Open-Source Model Serving: Deploy open-source model serving runtimes such as Ollama, vLLM, or Hugging Face Text Generation Inference (TGI) as container apps on GPU-enabled workload profiles. These runtimes provide flexible, self-hosted inference for open-weight models (e.g., Llama, Mistral, Phi) and can be paired with either dedicated or serverless GPUs depending on latency and cost requirements.
  • AI Gateway: Deploy an AI Gateway (e.g., Azure API Management, Envoy-based proxies, or custom routing middleware) to centralize traffic management across model endpoints. The gateway enables load balancing, rate limiting, request routing, and failover across multiple backend model deployments, agents and MCP servers.
  • Dynamic Sessions: Provide secure, isolated sandboxes (Hyper-V based) for executing AI-generated code safely.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) Servers: Host MCP servers within Azure Container Apps to allow AI agents to securely query internal databases or execute tools via a standardized interface.

docs.title: Reducing Cold Starts & Storage
docs.text:
Loading multi-gigabyte models (Foundry or open-source) into memory can lead to significant latency.

  • Azure Files Volume Mounts: Download model weights to a persistent Azure File Share once. Mount this share to the container so the model is available instantly on startup without re-downloading.
  • Azure Container Registry (ACR): Deploy Azure Container Registry in the same region as the Azure Container Apps environment to reduce latency.
    • Use the Premium SKU for global distribution and Artifact Streaming to further accelerate container startup times.
  • Optimize Container Image Size: Audit inference container images to remove training-only dependencies, development tools, and unnecessary libraries. Use multi-stage Docker builds to minimize image size.
  • Custom Startup Probes: For AI model containers that take minutes to load large models into GPU memory, configure custom startup probes with extended initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold to prevent premature container kills during initialization.
  • Proactive Wake-Up: Use scheduled Container App Jobs to send warm-up requests to inference endpoints ahead of peak usage (e.g., a daily job at 9 AM) to eliminate cold starts while still benefiting from scale-to-zero during off-hours.

docs.title: AI Agents & Orchestration
docs.text:
Deploy AI agents as individual container apps within the Apps workload profile. Each agent runs as an independent, scalable microservice that can be updated and versioned separately. Use open-source agent orchestration frameworks to build and manage agent workflows, such as Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph, and others.

Agents communicate with model endpoints via the AI Gateway, and leverage MCP servers for tool access and external data retrieval.

docs.title: Autoscaling
docs.text:
• Scaling Rules: Define KEDA-based autoscaling rules tailored to each workload profile:
    • HTTP scaling for front-end UIs and AI Gateway (based on concurrent request count).
    • Custom scaling for event-driven workloads.
  • Min/Max Replicas: Set minimum replicas ≥ 1 for latency-sensitive inference endpoints to avoid cold starts. Set maximum replicas based on GPU availability and cost budget.
  • Session Affinity: Enable sticky sessions for stateful AI chat applications that maintain conversation context in-memory, ensuring subsequent requests from the same user route to the same replica.

docs.title: Deployment & Release Strategy
docs.text:
• Blue-Green Deployment: Use revision labels and traffic weights to implement blue-green deployments. Deploy new model versions or application code to a "green" revision, validate via the labeled FQDN, then shift 100% of traffic. Roll back instantly by re-routing traffic to the "blue" revision.
  • Traffic Splitting: Use percentage-based traffic splitting to gradually roll out new revisions, enabling canary testing of updated inference endpoints.
  • Revision Management: Set maxInactiveRevisions to automatically clean up old revisions and avoid hitting the revision limit (default max of 100 per container app).

docs.title: Resiliency & Global Availability
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for resiliency and availabilitys for the workloads to be deployed in the landing zone.

docs.title: Availability Zones
docs.text:
Enable zone redundancy on the Container App Environment to distribute replicas across multiple physical availability zones within a region. This protects against datacenter-level failures.

  • Environment-Level Setting: Zone redundancy must be enabled at environment creation time — it cannot be added after the fact.
  • Minimum Replicas: Configure a minimum of three replicas for critical workloads to ensure at least one replica runs in each zone.
  • Dependency Alignment: Ensure dependent services (Cosmos DB, Key Vault, Storage) are also configured for zone redundancy to avoid single-zone bottlenecks.

docs.title: Service Resiliency & Health
docs.text:
• Health Probes: Define liveness, readiness, and startup probes to detect unhealthy instances and enable automatic recovery.
  • Resiliency Policies (Preview): Configure retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers for service-to-service communication. Ensure services (inference endpoints, databases, MCP tool,..etc) are idempotent so that retried requests do not cause duplicate side effects.

docs.title: Operational Excellence
docs.text:
• Planned Maintenance Windows: Configure maintenance windows on the Container App Environment to schedule non-critical platform updates during off-peak hours, minimizing disruption to AI inference workloads.
  • Service Discovery: Container apps within the same environment can communicate using their app names as internal DNS hostnames. Use internal ingress for backend services to restrict access to within-environment traffic only.

docs.title: Multi-Region Architecture
docs.text:
For business continuity against full regional outages, deploy across two or more Azure regions:

  • Active-Active: Both regions serve production traffic simultaneously via Azure Front Door. Provides near-instant failover (seconds) but requires globally replicated data stores and synchronized deployments. Best for mission-critical serving workloads (inference endpoints, front-end apps, AI agents, AI Gateway). Training and batch jobs should remain single-region due to data locality requirements and run in the secondary region only during failover.
  • Active-Passive: The secondary region remains on warm standby, activated during failover. Lower cost and complexity, with failover measured in minutes. Suitable for most production workloads. However, cost savings depend on the workload profile types deployed in the standby region. Pre-deploy the environment with consumption-based and serverless GPU profiles in the standby region. Use Infrastructure as Code (Bicep/Terraform) to rapidly provision dedicated GPU profiles only during failover, balancing cost efficiency against recovery time.

Key design considerations:

  • Deploy one Container App Environment per region, each with zone redundancy enabled.
  • Use Azure Front Door for global Layer-7 traffic routing, SSL termination, and automatic health-probe-based failover.
  • Replicate stateful data (conversation history, agent state, model weights) across regions using geo-redundant services (e.g., Cosmos DB multi-region writes, GRS storage accounts).
  • Mirror network topology (VNets, subnets, firewall rules) and identity configuration (Managed Identities, RBAC) consistently across regions.
  • Ensure CI/CD pipelines deploy to all regions in sync to avoid version drift.

docs.title: Observability & Monitoring
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for monitoring, logging, and observability for the workloads deployed in the landing zone.

docs.title: Logging & Diagnostics
docs.text:
• Log Analytics Integration: Configure a Log Analytics workspace as the default log destination for the Container App Environment. Use KQL queries to analyze system logs, container console output, and scaling events.
  • Diagnostic Settings: Configure Azure Monitor diagnostic settings to stream logs and metrics.
  • Azure Monitor Alerts: Set up alerts for critical conditions: failed health probes, high error rates, replica restarts, GPU utilization thresholds, and scaling failures. Use action groups to trigger automated incident response.

docs.title: Distributed Tracing & Metrics
docs.text:
• OpenTelemetry: Configure OpenTelemetry data agents at the environment level to collect distributed traces and metrics from AI agent workflows. This provides end-to-end visibility across multi-agent orchestration chains.
  • Metrics: Monitor platform metrics including CPU/memory utilization, replica count, request count, and response latency. Use these metrics to validate scaling rules and detect performance regressions in model inference endpoints.

docs.title: Agent Landing Zone
docs.text:
Agent Landing Zone provides Azure infrastructure for agents and the Agent Application, a reference application built on Microsoft Foundry. The infrastructure includes the selected networking, identities, AI services and data stores. It can run the Agent Application or your own application.

An agent uses an AI model to answer questions and can call configured tools. The supplied application provides web chat and can retrieve information from connected knowledge sources.

Source code: Azure/agent-landing-zone

docs.title: Infrastructure and application
docs.text:
The deployment template creates Azure resources separately from the application code that runs on them. This supports two deployment runbooks:

Runbook Result Deploy infra only Creates and configures the selected Azure resources without deploying application code. Deploy full stack Creates the infrastructure and deploys the Agent Application, including a Foundry hosted agent.

The default full-stack deployment runs the agent in Foundry Agent Service, the Microsoft Foundry service that hosts and operates agents. A web chat interface connects users to it. Agent Application explains the components, knowledge sources and application behavior.

The planning and Agent Application pages explain concepts and settings. Execution steps stay together in the Runbooks, with prerequisites, commands, validation and rollback.

docs.title: Where do I start?
docs.text:
• What does the template do? How it works introduces the deployment flow and explains where settings belong.
  • What needs planning? Deployment choices covers resources, network integration and deployment tools. The Design checklist supports architecture and security review.
  • How much capacity and budget are needed? Sizing and capacity and Cost planning describe the starting points.
  • Do I only need Azure resources? Deploy infra only provisions the infrastructure without deploying an application.
  • Do I want the supplied application running? Deploy full stack provisions the infrastructure and deploys the Agent Application.

docs.title: Agent tools
docs.text:
Foundry tools let an agent call approved operations. A Toolbox groups configured tools and their connections; an MCP server exposes operations through Model Context Protocol. A Foundry IQ knowledge base instead supplies retrieved grounding. These are different integration boundaries.

This page describes native Foundry integration and the supplied application's limits. Deployment and redeployment follow the Deploy full stack runbook; a custom tool integration requires application development.

docs.title: Tools, Toolbox and knowledge
docs.text:
Need Integration boundary Call a service operation A reviewed Foundry tool or Toolbox connection, consumed by the application. Ground answers in documents A Foundry IQ knowledge source bound to the knowledge base. Change instructions or orchestration Hosted orchestrator source and its configured prompts.

Foundry supports MCP tools and Toolbox connections. Creating either in the portal does not make the default Agent Application consume it.

docs.title: Supplied hosted execution
docs.text:
The default maf_lite orchestrator constructs a Microsoft Agent Framework agent inside the hosted container. It calls the configured model deployment directly and uses a Foundry IQ context provider for knowledge-base retrieval. It does not read a portal-managed prompt agent's tool list or automatically instantiate FoundryToolbox.

Hosted agents run containerized application code. Foundry hosts that code and authenticates invocation, but code defines its model, instructions, tool registration and retrieval behavior. A portal tool attachment alone therefore does not change the running maf_lite orchestration.

docs.title: Authenticated Toolbox contract
docs.text:
Microsoft's hosted Toolbox integration uses an authenticated FoundryToolbox software development kit (SDK) client with platform-provided hosted call context. The application must actually invoke that client, with the appropriate connection, tool authorization and source permissions. An endpoint string or a forwarded call ID without client authentication is not a complete integration.

The supplied hosted entry point initializes user_context={} and does not pass the caller's bearer token into default retrieval. UI OBO to Foundry is not an automatic OBO exchange inside the container. Protected knowledge-base or tool access therefore needs a reviewed authenticated integration, as described in Agent Application access. Caller-supplied group IDs, fabricated platform call IDs and browser bearer forwarding do not satisfy that contract.

Knowledge-base MCP source configuration is separate from callable agent tools. FOUNDRY_IQ_MCP_SOURCES_JSON describes sources consumed by the knowledge-base connector; it does not register a model-callable Toolbox in maf_lite. Foundry IQ describes retrieval configuration.

docs.title: Application extension boundary
docs.text:
A custom integration belongs in the orchestrator's existing strategy and connector modules, with a narrow tool schema, explicit caller authorization, bounded results, timeout/cancellation handling and safe failures. Write actions also need an explicit approval policy. A prompt instruction is not an authorization or approval control.

The runtime principal needs narrowly scoped dependency grants. Secrets remain in Key Vault, not tool definitions or ordinary App Configuration values. The standard bootstrap covers only its declared configuration/model/audit access; extra tool or source access needs separate grants. Agent hosting explains the identities. Private tools also depend on DNS, TLS and authorized egress from the actual hosted network path. Tool destinations receive application data and require data-handling approval.

Bring your own app describes source pins and capability profiles for custom code. New runtime settings are cross-component contracts with the platform that publishes them and every consuming component.

docs.title: Deployment and evidence
docs.text:
Changed orchestrator source requires a new image from the reviewed source pin, an immutable-digest handoff and a new agent version. Runtime settings are cached at startup, so settings-only changes also require a new hosted version, potentially reusing the compatible digest. Deployment settings distinguishes runtime settings from deployment inputs.

Evidence includes an actual tool call and result, denied-user isolation, timeout/outage behavior and no invented result when a required tool fails. Logs and traces can identify calls without retaining credentials, sensitive arguments or full caller-context headers. Portal registration or successful deployment alone does not establish this behavior.

docs.title: Failure boundaries
docs.text: Missing tools can indicate that the code never registered or invoked them, not just a connection failure. Authentication failures concern the client, connection and downstream permissions separately. Stale behavior can indicate a cached process or the wrong deployed version. Recovery retains the authenticated caller boundary and the previous compatible source/image combination rather than bypassing authorization.

docs.title: Agent Application access
docs.text: Agent Application has three independent access boundaries: UI admission, delegated Foundry invocation and document authorization. Signing in does not grant access to every document. This page describes the supplied authentication contract; deployment and redeployment belong to the Deploy full stack runbook.

docs.title: UI sign-in
docs.text:
Single-tenant means sign-in is limited to one Entra directory. A confidential web application keeps its credential on the server, not in browser code. Its registration defines the login callback and exposed API permissions.

The UI uses a confidential, single-tenant Entra web application. Its exposed API scope is api://<client-id>/user_impersonation. The Web redirect URI is the UI's canonical HTTPS origin plus /auth/oauth/azure-ad/callback, including any supported deployment prefix. CHAINLIT_URL identifies that external origin; behind TLS-terminating ingress it prevents an incorrect HTTP callback.

The single-tenant registration and exposed API scope are separate from Azure subscription permissions. Downstream Foundry delegated permissions and consent are also separate from consent to the UI API.

UI runtime key Contract OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_ID, OAUTH_AZURE_AD_TENANT_ID Entra application and directory IDs, not URLs. OAUTH_AZURE_AD_ENABLE_SINGLE_TENANT true for this contract. OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_SECRET Key Vault reference to the credential value, not the secret ID. OAUTH_AZURE_AD_SCOPES UI API scope plus openid, profile, offline_access. Graph scopes such as User.Read are rejected by the callback. CHAINLIT_AUTH_SECRET Persistent, protected session-signing secret. ALLOW_ANONYMOUS false for authenticated access. HOSTED_AGENT_AUTH_MODE user_delegated, the default hosted mode.

Runtime keys normally use App Configuration label agent-lz. The UI identity needs permission to resolve its Key Vault references. Credentials are not plaintext settings or browser code. Deployment settings describes setting ownership and overrides.

docs.title: Application admission
docs.text:
ALLOWED_USER_PRINCIPALS admits individual users by comma-separated tenant-id:object-id values. ALLOWED_USER_NAMES is an alternative list of sign-in names. The lists combine with OR; empty lists admit all successfully authenticated users. The callback does not fetch Graph group membership. These lists restrict UI admission, not Foundry access or document access-control lists (ACLs).

The UI caches configuration at startup. Changes need a UI process reload and a new sign-in. Hosted orchestrator changes need a new agent version. Provisioning can republish template-managed values; deployment inputs and runtime settings are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Hosted retrieval identity boundary
docs.text:
The UI's OBO exchange obtains a token for HOSTED_AGENT_RESOURCE_SCOPE, the deployed Foundry data-plane audience ending in /.default. HOSTED_AGENT_BASE_URL is the endpoint, not that scope. The UI API scope, Foundry consent and Foundry project/agent access all have distinct roles. Microsoft's OBO guidance describes downstream consent.

user_delegated rejects a missing user token without service-identity fallback. service_identity would make Foundry see the UI service rather than the user. Neither mode alone establishes authorization inside the hosted container.

The supplied hosted entry point sets user_context={} and does not supply the user's bearer token to maf_lite retrieval. It performs no automatic retrieval OBO exchange. With ALLOW_ANONYMOUS=false, required-user retrieval fails preflight when that token is unavailable; it does not silently retrieve as a service identity. Removing source permission metadata alone does not repair this missing-token contract.

Protected hosted retrieval requires a developer integration. Foundry's authenticated hosted Toolbox contract uses an authenticated FoundryToolbox client and platform-provided call context. The default maf_lite code does not consume portal Toolbox configuration.

A compatible integration must connect the knowledge base through that contract, retain the platform caller context, and enforce the knowledge source's permissions. Agent tools explains the extension boundary. Browser bearer forwarding or fabricated identity/group headers are not a substitute.

The protected native Blob ingestion default is FOUNDRY_IQ_INGESTION_PERMISSION_OPTIONS=["rbacScope"]. Explicit [] removes permission metadata for the supported intentionally shared Blob corpus. That provides shared-source access, not per-user filtering. Foundry IQ and knowledge-base retrieval permissions describe source-specific requirements.

docs.title: Authorization evidence
docs.text:
Protected retrieval is only established by tests through the deployed integration, using independent signed-in users and nonsensitive documents. An answer without a citation is not sufficient evidence of denial.

Boundary Required observation Sign-in Signed-out callers cannot chat. Admission A user absent from both nonempty admission lists is denied. Foundry invocation An admitted, authorized user can invoke the deployed agent through OBO. Shared document Both authorized users retrieve its content and reference. Restricted document Only its authorized user retrieves it; denied retrieval contains no document ID, excerpt or citation, including exact-title questions. Conversation ownership A different user cannot open the owner's history.

Correlation IDs, effective configuration and agent version provide diagnostic evidence without recording tokens or document contents. Permission changes also depend on propagation and refreshed source metadata.

docs.title: Failure boundaries
docs.text:
Redirect mismatch concerns the exact callback URI. Consent/refresh failures concern UI scopes, tenant and credential lifetime. Invocation denial can instead indicate missing downstream consent or Foundry user/agent access. Tool consent is separate from UI consent, as described in tool authentication.

A denied user retrieving protected content is an authorization failure that blocks exposure of that corpus. Recovery does not replace the delegated caller with a service identity or disable authentication.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Give the Agent Application web UI a controlled public HTTPS entry point while keeping its Container Apps environment private. The optional gateway terminates TLS, applies web application firewall (WAF) rules, and forwards requests over HTTPS to one Container App. The basic routing rule forwards all UI paths, including enabled application routes. Keep application authentication and route authorization enabled.

docs.title: What you'll have after this runbook
docs.text:
Approved users reach the web UI through Application Gateway and its WAF; the UI and Foundry retain their private backend paths.

The UI makes the authenticated Foundry call server-side. This gateway does not publish Foundry project APIs, hosted-agent endpoints, or Foundry IQ knowledge bases. Their private connectivity, authentication, and authorization still apply. Start with a working deployment from the Deploy full stack runbook and application authentication. For hosted runtime/network prerequisites, use Hosted agents and Microsoft's hosted-agent networking and limitations.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Use this runbook when the UI already works privately and approved users need a controlled public entry point. Choose the supported entry point before editing:

docs.title: Choose the entry point
docs.text:
Need Choice Public UI for approved client networks, private backend services Use the template's public gateway below, with explicit public outbound IP address ranges (CIDRs). UI accessible only from your corporate network Leave publicIngress.enabled false and use VPN/peering plus private DNS. See Network isolation. An internal Application Gateway or an existing corporate ingress Integrate it separately with the UI backend. The template option has a public IP only; it has no private-frontend switch.

The gateway requires network isolation. With NETWORK_ISOLATION=false, it stays undeployed even when publicIngress.enabled is true. For an existing public deployment, obtain a separately reviewed private-network design before adding this gateway. Do not change isolation as part of an ingress retry.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A deployed UI in an isolated Container Apps environment, and a deployment host with the private connectivity required by the full-stack runbook.
  • Provisioning permissions from that runbook, including permission to assign the gateway identity's Key Vault role. Certificate import, DNS changes, and Entra app-registration changes may require separate administrators.
  • An approved DNS name, such as chat.contoso.com, and control of its DNS record. Identify allowed users' or proxies' public outbound address ranges in CIDR notation, such as a single approved IPv4 address followed by /32.
  • A valid certificate covering that DNS name, with an exportable private key, stored as an enabled PFX certificate in Key Vault. A PFX file packages the certificate and its private key. Follow Microsoft's Key Vault certificate integration requirements. Use your approved certificate import process; never paste a PFX, password, private key, or client secret into deployment parameters or shell history.
  • A dedicated Application Gateway subnet. The template defaults to AppGatewaySubnet at 192.168.3.0/27; Microsoft recommends /24 for v2 capacity and maintenance headroom. For an existing VNet, have its owner verify the subnet, network security group (NSG) attachment, routing and DNS before provisioning. Do not share the subnet with other workloads.

WAF_v2 and its Standard public IP incur charges even without traffic.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text: Run Steps 1-4 in order. Record the previous publicIngress object, DNS record, UI URL setting and redirect URIs before changing them.

docs.title: 1. Provision a closed staging gateway
docs.text:
In your platform checkout, edit only the publicIngress entry under parameters in main.parameters.json. This is a provisioning input, not a runtime App Configuration setting or an azd env set gateway flag:

"publicIngress": {
  "value": {
    "enabled": true,
    "backendAppIndex": 0,
    "allowedSourceAddressPrefixes": [],
    "wafMode": "Prevention"
  }
}

backendAppIndex is a zero-based position in the composed containerAppsList, not an app name or resource ID. For a new, unmodified hosted deployment, composition removes the orchestrator Container App and the UI (service_name: frontend) becomes index 0. The raw parameter file still lists the orchestrator first. Custom compositions can differ: confirm the selected backend is the UI, never ingestion or an old orchestrator.

Keep the existing hosted deployment inputs. Preview with azd provision --preview and confirm only approved resources and roles change. Apply from the connected host:

azd provision

This applies foundation changes and runs provisioning hooks; it is not a gateway-only deployment. Follow the full-stack procedure if application deployment is incomplete. Keep the reviewed parameter file on every runner to preserve ingress settings on later provisions.

Read the resulting identifiers. CONTAINER_APP_INTERNAL_FQDN is the backend's fully qualified DNS hostname:

azd env get-value PUBLIC_INGRESS_ENABLED
azd env get-value PUBLIC_INGRESS_GATEWAY_RESOURCE_ID
azd env get-value PUBLIC_INGRESS_IDENTITY_PRINCIPAL_ID
azd env get-value PUBLIC_INGRESS_PUBLIC_IP
azd env get-value CONTAINER_APP_INTERNAL_FQDN

Expected: enabled is true; the backend FQDN belongs to the UI Container App. With no hostname or certificate configured there is no HTTPS listener. The empty source list and subnet Internet deny rule prevent public browser access to this staging configuration. VNet-origin traffic remains subject to separate private-network controls. Test application health after configuring the listener and UI sign-in URL.

docs.title: 2. Prepare certificate access and DNS
docs.text:
1. Record the certificate's versionless secret URI, for example https://<vault-name>.vault.azure.net/secrets/<certificate-secret-name>/. This is neither an ARM resource ID nor a /certificates/ URI. Do not append a secret version: the versionless reference enables certificate rotation.
  2. Verify the gateway's user-assigned identity, using PUBLIC_INGRESS_IDENTITY_PRINCIPAL_ID. The template assigns Key Vault Secrets User on its deployed landing-zone vault. For an external RBAC vault, have its owner grant that role to this identity at the vault scope; for an access-policy vault, follow the documented secret-read policy. Allow role propagation before continuing.
  3. Verify network access from the gateway subnet to Key Vault. For a private vault, its private endpoint and privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net DNS zone must resolve correctly from the gateway VNet. A role assignment alone does not provide network access. Do not make the vault public as a workaround.
  4. Create the public DNS A record for your chosen hostname pointing to PUBLIC_INGRESS_PUBLIC_IP. Provisioning does not create this public DNS record. Confirm that the gateway can also resolve the UI's backend FQDN to the internal Container Apps environment.

The client-facing certificate covers your public hostname. The backend uses the Container App's own hostname for the HTTP Host header, TLS server name indication (SNI) and certificate validation. Do not replace the backend with the public gateway hostname. Microsoft's Container Apps gateway guidance explains this backend routing pattern.

docs.title: 3. Configure the UI's external sign-in URL
docs.text:
Before user testing, set the UI's CHAINLIT_URL to https://<your-hostname> using the runtime-setting change procedure, with App Configuration label agent-lz. An explicit UI environment variable overrides App Configuration; remove or update a conflicting override.

In the UI's Entra app registration, add this Web redirect URI:

https://<your-hostname>/auth/oauth/azure-ad/callback

Apply the URL change by restarting/redeploying the UI Container App: the UI loads this setting at process startup. This does not require a hosted agent restart. Do not rewrite the provisioning-managed FRONTEND_APP_ENDPOINT to the public hostname; it describes the deployed Container App endpoint. Keep delegated authentication/OBO and source authorization unchanged. Document permissions are enforced by the application and its data sources, separately from the gateway's WAF controls.

docs.title: 4. Admit HTTPS clients
docs.text:
Update the same publicIngress.value object, replacing the placeholders:

{
  "enabled": true,
  "backendAppIndex": 0,
  "frontendHostName": "<your-hostname>",
  "sslCertSecretId": "https://<vault-name>.vault.azure.net/secrets/<certificate-secret-name>/",
  "allowedSourceAddressPrefixes": ["<approved-client-egress-CIDR>"],
  "wafMode": "Prevention"
}

Run azd provision again from the connected host. Both hostname and certificate are required for the HTTPS listener; a nonempty source list admits TCP/443 from those CIDRs. Do not substitute 0.0.0.0/0 without an explicit public exposure decision.

The gateway also configures an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, but the shipped subnet NSG does not open Internet port 80, so HTTP connections time out. Distribute the https:// URL directly.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
1. Check azd env get-value PUBLIC_INGRESS_LIVE: true confirms that the hostname and certificate inputs are present. The following checks validate TLS, reachability and chat.
  2. In the Azure portal, open the deployed Application Gateway → Backend health. Confirm that the backend pool contains the UI FQDN and is healthy. The shipped HTTPS probe checks / and accepts 200–499, so a login denial or even a missing page can pass. Then test the UI.
  3. From an allowed client network, run nslookup <your-hostname> and open https://<your-hostname> in a browser. Expect the public gateway IP, a trusted certificate for that hostname, the UI, and a successful sign-in returning to the same hostname. Do not bypass certificate validation.
  4. Send a chat request and confirm the streamed response completes. Test a representative long response and any enabled uploads. The gateway backend timeout is 30 seconds, with separate WAF request/upload limits. Validate transport with completed chat responses.
  5. Repeat the connection test from an unapproved public network: TCP/443 should be blocked. With test accounts and known restricted documents, verify permitted retrieval and denial for an unauthorized user through Foundry IQ after the protected-retrieval integration gate in the Deploy full stack runbook is resolved. The gateway does not implement that missing runtime identity integration.

The shipped WAF uses the Open Worldwide Application Security Project Core Rule Set (OWASP CRS) 3.2 in Prevention mode. Check its logs for blocked legitimate requests before widening access. Use narrowly scoped, reviewed rules rather than disabling the WAF.

Detection mode logs without blocking; if temporarily approved for tuning, retain the source allowlist and return to Prevention. See WAF modes and policy behavior. Application Gateway supports WebSockets, but WAF does not inspect frames after the upgrade.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check and recovery No gateway created Check PUBLIC_INGRESS_ENABLED, isolation, and that Container Apps/environment deployment is enabled with a nonempty app list. There is no PUBLIC_INGRESS environment toggle; edit the parameter object. HTTPS timeout Verify client egress CIDR, DNS A record, HTTPS listener, and subnet NSG attachment. Test HTTPS, not port 80. Preserve required GatewayManager and AzureLoadBalancer rules. Certificate/listener failure Check secret URI, certificate expiry/enabled status, identity permissions, private DNS and vault reachability. Check gateway Resource Health and Azure Advisor for Key Vault errors. Versionless references poll for renewal about every four hours; keep renewal monitoring in place. 502 or unhealthy backend Confirm the selected app is the UI, the image is deployed, and private DNS/routing, Host/SNI and HTTPS work. Use Microsoft's backend-health troubleshooting. Do not disable backend TLS validation. Sign-in redirects to an internal hostname Recheck CHAINLIT_URL, environment overrides, exact Web redirect URI, and UI process reload. Do not change Foundry endpoints to the gateway URL. UI loads but chat fails or disconnects Inspect UI/Foundry errors separately from WAF logs and gateway timeouts. Repair delegated auth or private connectivity rather than switching to service identity. Timeout/transport changes beyond the exposed parameter contract require a reviewed infrastructure extension.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
1. To withdraw newly introduced public client access, set allowedSourceAddressPrefixes: [] in the reviewed root parameter object. Run azd provision from the connected platform root while ingress remains enabled. If reverting an existing gateway update, review and restore its recorded backend, hostname, certificate reference and approved source list only when the previous certificate and route are still usable. Preview those changes before provisioning. If they are not usable, keep public access closed.
  2. From the withdrawn public client network, verify TCP/443 is blocked. This removes the shipped client allow rule, but does not remove separately added rules or revoke application sessions. Review those separately.
  3. Restore any changed DNS record with its owner. If reverting the UI URL change, first verify the previous approved private or gateway route is usable. Restore its recorded CHAINLIT_URL and any changed environment override, retain its Web redirect URI, and reload the UI. Test sign-in on that route before removing the newly added redirect URI.
  4. Remove the new DNS record if no approved route uses it. Keep certificates and Key Vault access needed by other consumers.

Setting publicIngress.enabled to false does not delete previously created resources in incremental deployments, and is not an access-revocation procedure.

After closing access and checking remaining references with their owners, arrange explicit deletion of only the dedicated ingress resources (gateway, public IP, WAF policy, subnet NSG and gateway identity), clean up their role assignments, DNS record and obsolete redirect URI, and remove any subnet NSG reference before deleting that NSG.

Coordinate with the network owner. Do not delete the shared subnet, vault or UI, or tear down the environment to undo a gateway change.

docs.title: Agent Application
docs.text:
Agent Application is the customizable reference app supplied by Agent Landing Zone. The supplied app-definition.json identifies its UI, orchestrator and optional ingestion components. Deployment composition applies the selected topology to that definition. A fresh environment uses hosted-no-panel: Agent App UI runs in Azure Container Apps and Agent App Orchestrator runs as a container in Foundry Agent Service. Its default strategy is maf_lite.

These pages explain the components and their integration boundaries. The Deploy full stack runbook contains the deployment procedure. Bring your own app covers customer-owned applications.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
An Entra tenant is an organization's identity directory. An API access token is a credential: its audience identifies the receiving API, and a delegated scope identifies a permitted operation on behalf of a user. It is a bearer token because possession lets a caller present it, so it must stay protected.

A delegated call acts for the signed-in user; on-behalf-of (OBO) exchanges that user's token for a downstream API token.

Agent App UI supplies chat, sign-in and the delegated call to the hosted agent. Its optional embedding and feedback surfaces have separate integration limits.

Concept Reference UI admission, Foundry invocation and document authorization Sign-in and document access Chat inside an existing portal Embed chat Ratings and comments User feedback

docs.title: Agent hosting
docs.text: Agent hosting explains the hosted container, immutable image handoff and runtime identities. Hosting the container in Foundry does not turn its code into a portal-managed prompt agent.

docs.title: Model, tools and knowledge base
docs.text:
Grounding supplies retrieved information so the model can answer from connected sources.

The default maf_lite code calls the configured model deployment directly. Its configured grounding path is the Foundry IQ knowledge-base connector, with RETRIEVAL_BACKEND=foundry_iq as the fresh default. A knowledge base binds sources and returns retrieved content; it is not the model or the hosted container.

Foundry offers native tools and Toolbox connections. A Toolbox groups tools and their connections, including tools exposed through Model Context Protocol (MCP), a protocol for making operations callable by agents. These are the service integration path for additional operations. The supplied maf_lite code does not automatically consume a Toolbox added in the portal. An authenticated Toolbox integration requires application development. Agent tools describes that contract.

flowchart LR
    User <--> UI["Agent App UI"]
    UI <-->|Delegated Foundry invocation| Agent["Hosted orchestrator"]
    Agent <--> Model["Model deployment"]
    Agent <--> KB["Foundry IQ knowledge base"]
    Agent -.->|Custom authenticated integration| Tools["Foundry tools / Toolbox"]

The flow shows request dependencies, not proof of document authorization. The hosted entry point supplies neither authenticated user context nor a user bearer to default retrieval. Required-user retrieval fails without that token. Protected retrieval needs the integration and allow/deny validation described in Agent Application access.

docs.title: Ingestion
docs.text: Fresh environments use native Foundry IQ ingestion for the configured Blob source, without Agent App Ingestion. The optional ingestion Container App provides application-managed processing and eligible conversation PDF uploads. Native source ingestion alone does not enable chat attachments. Ingestion and conversation uploads explains these boundaries.

docs.title: Grounding
docs.text: Knowledge Reference Documents and knowledge-base retrieval Foundry IQ Microsoft 365 knowledge Work IQ Fabric data and data agents Fabric IQ SharePoint content SharePoint

docs.title: Capabilities and extensions
docs.text: Multimodality distinguishes document image extraction from direct image or voice input. NL2SQL explains structured-data grounding and the boundary for custom SQL tools.

docs.title: Know what you are changing
docs.text:
Deployment inputs select Azure resources and application components. Runtime settings control the supplied application's behavior, typically in Azure App Configuration with label agent-lz. Other applications can have different runtime settings. Deployment settings identifies the owner and location of each value.

Runtime configuration is cached in process. A changed hosted runtime setting requires a new agent version; affected UI or ingestion processes also need to reload their settings. The Deploy full stack runbook covers deployment and redeployment.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Promote one reviewed application revision through DEV → TEST → PROD with protected approvals. This optional continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) flow automates the platform's application and foundation lifecycle; Azure DevOps is not required for an interactive deployment.

docs.title: What you'll have after this runbook
docs.text:
One reviewed source revision promoted through DEV, TEST and PROD, with protected approvals and a private deployment path for each environment.

Each environment builds its own images from the reviewed source. The pipeline does not promote one identical image between environments.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
Use this runbook when your team needs repeatable source promotion with separate deployment identities and approval gates for each environment.

For interactive execution, use the Deploy infra only or Deploy full stack runbook. For component changes, see Custom applications.

Choose the right pipeline

The downloadable example below verifies the same source commit in every job and enforces successful prior stages. Images are built per environment. Keep the platform's incorporated infra/ and lifecycle hooks in that same revision. Do not substitute pipelines from a separate foundation checkout.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A reviewed platform revision and stage-specific deployment inputs.
  • An Azure DevOps project with administrators authorized to manage agent pools, service connections, variable groups and protected Environments.
  • Azure administrators who can approve the scoped deployment/runtime role plan, and an Entra administrator for application sign-in and consent.
  • A connected Linux runner path to each private environment. Bootstrap that connectivity before running a pipeline that depends on it.

Steps 1-3 detail the toolchain, identity and input preparation. Do not queue a deployment until they and the protected checks in Step 4 are complete.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the repository and runners
docs.text:
Use your reviewed platform revision. Keep manifest.json, app-definition.json, main.parameters.json, azure.yaml, infra/, config/, contracts/ and scripts/ together at its root. Infrastructure is incorporated under infra/; do not deploy it from a second foundation checkout. Commit your configuration and compatible component pins before queuing a pipeline. Do not commit credentials or local azd environments.

The downloadable example initially deploys the Agent Application with hosted-no-panel, native Blob ingestion and private endpoints. Set the same reviewed topology and ingestion selection across the three environments. The table lists deployment inputs placed in each stage's YAML settings map in Step 3; the task applies them to its selected azd environment. How it works explains how the hooks process these inputs.

Input Choices and effect DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGY Keep hosted-no-panel for this default deployment. HOSTED_AGENT_RESOURCE_SCOPE Required before first provision for hosted modes: the deployed Foundry delegated-user audience followed by /.default. It has no implicit runtime default. DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP Keep 'false' for native Foundry IQ source ingestion. Additional ingestion and upload capabilities require their own acceptance checks. Preserve existing selections during recovery. NETWORK_ISOLATION Explicit 'true'. Do not change it merely to make a pipeline pass. BUILD_MODE acr-task; private image builds use the foundation's ACR Tasks pool. Local Docker is not required.

See Deployment settings, Hosted agents and ingestion compatibility. Preserve an existing environment's recorded layout. This example is not a procedure for changing runtime layouts.

Automation does not close runtime capability gaps

Keep maf_lite and Foundry IQ as the default runtime choices. The protected-retrieval gate in the Deploy full stack runbook applies to CI/CD. Do not promote until the developer-owned identity integration and real-user allow/deny tests pass. Pipeline settings, weaker source permissions and successful greetings are not substitutes.

docs.title: Runner requirements
docs.text:
Create authorized Linux self-hosted Azure Pipelines agent pools, with a runner able to reach each environment's private endpoints through its VNet or a peered hub/VPN. Bootstrap the deployment network before this full-stack pipeline: an agent cannot depend on the VNet it is about to create to become reachable. Use Network isolation for DNS, routing and egress checks. The CI-only pool need not reach Azure data-plane endpoints.

Every runner needs Bash, PowerShell 7 (pwsh), jq, Git, curl, Azure CLI with Bicep, Azure Developer CLI (azd), and Python 3.12+ with pip and venv. Hosted deployment also needs an azd version supporting the pinned hosted-agent/azure.yaml service.

Install and pin approved tool versions in your agent image; record them in your release evidence. Populate the self-hosted agent's Python tool cache for UsePythonVersion@0 (3.12) before queuing a job. Allow package, source and container-build dependency egress. Hooks themselves bootstrap a temporary pip environment during post-provision.

From the agent's Bash shell, verify:

python3 --version
pwsh --version
jq --version
git --version
az version
az bicep version
azd version

The YAML uses pool.name, not pool.vmImage. A private ACR Tasks agent pool is a different resource from an Azure Pipelines agent pool: it builds images, but does not run azd, topology discovery or post-provision hooks. A Microsoft-hosted public agent is not the default private deployment runner. For an intentionally public deployment, review network inputs and runner policy separately.

Use dedicated, preferably ephemeral agents. workspace.clean isolates jobs; the final cleanup removes only explicitly listed runtime state directories and temporary tool configuration, leaving source checkouts intact. Do not place unrelated files in the agent workspace or run untrusted pull requests on deployment agents.

docs.title: 2. Establish identities and permissions
docs.text:
Create an Azure Resource Manager workload identity federation (WIF) service connection per environment, following the foundation setup. Restrict each connection to this pipeline and its target subscription/scopes. The AzureCLI@2 task authenticates noninteractively; all azd and hook commands run inside it, with azd config set auth.useAzCliAuth true. Do not add interactive az login, azd auth login, client secrets or exported federation tokens.

Set AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID to the connection identity's enterprise application / service principal object ID, not its application/client ID or app-registration object ID. Set AZURE_PRINCIPAL_TYPE=ServicePrincipal; the default parameter type is User. Review deployment and data-plane permissions separately from subscription read access.

Have an administrator approve these minimum roles:

Identity Required access to review Deployment service principal Contributor for resource deployment plus scoped role-assignment authority (for example User Access Administrator) wherever Bicep and hooks create grants. Subscription-scope deployments, provider registration and hub/shared resources can require additional scope; use the foundation guide's scope review. Do not solve data-plane denials by adding Owner. Deployment service principal, configuration/build operations App Configuration Data Owner for publishing settings; required Key Vault secret access when resolving references; Search service/index configuration permissions and the Foundry configuration/model/deployment actions used by the enabled hooks. ACR Tasks build/run and registry/Container Apps update permissions must also be authorized. These are separate from ARM Contributor. Check the effective grants from Bicep for the explicit principal and add only missing scoped roles. Deployment service principal, hosted authoring Foundry User on the exact project, plus account read access; authority to create the scoped runtime assignments in the hosted access plan. Cognitive Services Contributor/OpenAI User alone do not grant hosted-agent data-plane authoring. Runtime managed identities Capability-profile roles and separate hosted project/image-pull/runtime grants. Do not substitute the pipeline identity for the runtime identity. Delegated application users Application consent, Foundry caller/agent access where applicable, and the intended source/document permissions. Pipeline success grants none of these to users.

Also confirm service/model availability, quota, provider registration and Responsible AI acceptance in each target subscription. Do not set preflight bypass flags to work around an unattended failure. Allow RBAC propagation before retrying.

docs.title: Complete the application sign-in setup separately
docs.text:
The pipeline service connection authenticates deployment jobs. The UI uses a separate Entra application registration and tenant consent, which must be configured outside the deployment scripts. Arrange this with an Entra administrator for each isolated application environment:

  1. Create the confidential application registration; expose its api://<client-id>/user_impersonation scope and request version-2 access tokens.
  2. Register the final HTTPS UI URL with /auth/oauth/azure-ad/callback. Set CHAINLIT_URL to that canonical HTTPS origin without a trailing slash. For a first deployment, discover the assigned frontend URL, finish this setup, and restart the UI before accepting DEV.
  3. Create/rotate its client credential under tenant policy. Store it in Key Vault, publish a Key Vault reference as OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_SECRET, and publish OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_ID, OAUTH_AZURE_AD_TENANT_ID and OAUTH_AZURE_AD_SCOPES under App Configuration label agent-lz. Protect CHAINLIT_AUTH_SECRET and keep it stable.
  4. Configure and consent the downstream delegated permissions for the deployed audience, including Foundry OBO for hosted mode. Graph scopes are not a replacement for the UI's single-token API scope. Grant intended caller access.
  5. Review conflicting unlabelled/service settings and restart affected components. Then test actual user sign-in and document allow/deny behavior.

Follow delegated authentication for the exact keys and consent boundaries, and runtime settings for publishing/restart behavior. Complete tenant consent and sign-in configuration through a separately reviewed administrative procedure or automation before accepting the deployment. Keep these tasks separate from the deployment connection's Azure permissions; do not grant it broad Microsoft Graph permissions for onboarding.

docs.title: 3. Fill the pipeline inputs
docs.text:
Download both files, then place them beside each other in .pipelines/ in your platform repository, not in its infra/ folder:

  • azure-pipelines.yml
  • deploy-stage.yml
  • Optional local check: validate.py

Replace these values before authorization. DEV, TEST and PROD must have separate resource groups, azd environments, connection identities, configuration stores, secrets and data. Apply the environment boundaries for runtime identities, sign-in, network isolation and test data.

New Agent environments use three groups. The example's AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP selects Foundry/root; application and network names default to that name plus -app and -network. Grant the deployment identity the required permissions for every target, including group creation when enabled, not just the root group's refresh. See resource group destinations for pre-created groups or an explicit one/two-group layout. Existing environments keep their mapping.

Never copy DEV's .azure state into TEST or PROD. Initialize or securely restore the intended environment on each runner, refresh its outputs when needed and reapply approved inputs. Keep .azure and sibling child state private.

Exact example input Required replacement / source REPLACE_CI_LINUX_POOL Authorized Linux validation pool with the toolchain above. REPLACE_DEV_VNET_LINUX_POOL, REPLACE_TEST_VNET_LINUX_POOL, REPLACE_PROD_VNET_LINUX_POOL Authorized, connected Linux deployment pool for each target. May be the same pool only if its connectivity and isolation policy cover all targets. REPLACE_DEV_WIF_SERVICE_CONNECTION, REPLACE_TEST_WIF_SERVICE_CONNECTION, REPLACE_PROD_WIF_SERVICE_CONNECTION Exact Azure DevOps WIF service connection names, authorized for this pipeline only. REPLACE_DEV_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, REPLACE_TEST_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, REPLACE_PROD_SUBSCRIPTION_ID Target subscription GUIDs matching those connections' allowed scopes. REPLACE_DEV_RESOURCE_GROUP, REPLACE_TEST_RESOURCE_GROUP, REPLACE_PROD_RESOURCE_GROUP New target names for first provision, or the exact previously azd-provisioned groups for redeployment. REPLACE_DEV_REGION, REPLACE_TEST_REGION, REPLACE_PROD_REGION Supported foundation locations (AZURE_LOCATION). REPLACE_DEV_FOUNDRY_REGION, REPLACE_TEST_FOUNDRY_REGION, REPLACE_PROD_FOUNDRY_REGION Foundry/model locations with quota (AZURE_AI_FOUNDRY_LOCATION). REPLACE_DEV_COSMOS_REGION, REPLACE_TEST_COSMOS_REGION, REPLACE_PROD_COSMOS_REGION Cosmos locations supported by the selected topology/foundation (AZURE_COSMOS_LOCATION). REPLACE_DEV_SERVICE_PRINCIPAL_OBJECT_ID, REPLACE_TEST_SERVICE_PRINCIPAL_OBJECT_ID, REPLACE_PROD_SERVICE_PRINCIPAL_OBJECT_ID Connection service principal object IDs; keep AZURE_PRINCIPAL_TYPE: ServicePrincipal. REPLACE_DEV_HOSTED_RESOURCE_SCOPE, REPLACE_TEST_HOSTED_RESOURCE_SCOPE, REPLACE_PROD_HOSTED_RESOURCE_SCOPE Explicit delegated-user Foundry scope ending in /.default, matched to the deployed audience and consent (for example https://ai.azure.com/.default where that is the target audience). Required before provisioning; not the UI's api://<client-id>/user_impersonation scope. environment: agentlz-dev, agentlz-test, agentlz-prod Precreated Azure DevOps Environment resource names. Rename consistently if required; these are approval resources, not azd environments. AZURE_ENV_NAME: agentlz-dev, agentlz-test, agentlz-prod Unique azd names, retained exactly for subsequent refresh/deploy runs. variableGroup: agentlz-dev-secrets, agentlz-test-secrets, agentlz-prod-secrets Create these Library variable groups and authorize only this pipeline. Each must contain the secret variable AGENTLZ_SECRET_SETTINGS_JSON, initially the string {}. AGENTLZ_SECRET_SETTINGS_JSON in each group JSON object of additional documented azd/hook inputs, with string values. It cannot override the inline deployment controls. Empty {} is valid for the Agent Application example. This is not automatic publication of OAuth/runtime settings or a private Git credential mechanism. Inline settings in each stage Review topology, ingestion, isolation and regional settings. Add required Deployment settings inputs for your approved network, source, models or reused resources. Keep nonsecret configuration reviewable here; never put secret values in YAML.

The inline settings maps keep deployment inputs visible for review. Values are reapplied after environment refresh on every job. RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX=true requires the connected-host check; it does not create connectivity. The example leaves AZURE_SKIP_NETWORK_ISOLATION_WARNING=false.

The inspected POSIX preProvision hook's interactive warning checks the separate AZURE_NETWORK_ISOLATION variable, not the example's NETWORK_ISOLATION input. Do not inherit that alias in the runner or environment. If an existing workflow must retain a truthy alias, explicitly review setting the warning flag to true for unattended execution while retaining RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX=true.

The warning flag alone can defer configuration when RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX is not truthy; never use that combination as a private deployment shortcut.

Protect variable-group edits as well as YAML changes. Secret masking is not a data-loss prevention system; keep pipeline debug and shell tracing off. Use Key Vault references for runtime secrets instead of literal secret JSON wherever the contract supports them.

docs.title: Private component repositories and custom definitions
docs.text:
The platform connection authenticates Azure, not GitHub or Azure Repos Git. See Private Git authentication for repository access.

The root deploy hook clones selected Agent Application components as sibling checkouts using manifest repository/tag pins, then verifies the expected commit. Use approved read-only Git credentials for those private repositories separately.

The example does not install a private-Git credential: before adopting private component pins, add your organization's reviewed, job-scoped credential-helper or SSH-agent/known-host setup inside the authenticated task, with guaranteed cleanup. Test the exact repository/tag access without printing tokens. Source checkout authorization alone does not authorize the hook's new clones.

Never put tokens in manifest URLs, command-line URLs, url.insteadOf global configuration, .azure, or downloadable artifacts. Keep persistCredentials: false; the example uses a temporary GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL because hooks can write safe-directory entries. Do not rely on an agent owner's persistent Git credentials.

If using an Azure Repos job token, separately grant the build identity read access to the required repositories and review job-token scope before explicitly mapping it into the credential mechanism. It is not a GitHub credential.

For a custom application, adapt CI validation to the selected definition and add AGENTLZ_APP_DEFINITION to each stage before first provision. Keep the application ID stable. Custom definitions accept local sources or immutable image digests, not remote Git URLs.

Materialize local source in every job with a clean Git checkout at its declared source.commit, preserving .git metadata and the definition's relative layout. Explicitly check out pinned component repositories or pinned submodules if needed, using the separate Git credentials above.

Do not feed these hooks a git archive tree without Git metadata: they check the component's actual git rev-parse HEAD. Source commit checks do not reject uncommitted edits; validate clean trees.

Add the custom definition folder's explicit .azure and .logs paths to the fixed cleanup list. Never include source or workspace roots.

Custom hosted services follow their own definition/image contract. The downloaded template's preparation branch is for the Agent Application; replace that branch with the documented custom hosted workflow before using it for a custom hosted definition.

docs.title: 4. Protect and register the pipeline
docs.text:
1. In Pipelines → Environments, create the three exact Environment names. On agentlz-test and agentlz-prod, configure Approvals and checks outside YAML, with accountable reviewers, no self-approval where policy requires it, and restricted administrator/pipeline permissions. Approval for TEST accepts DEV evidence; approval for PROD accepts TEST evidence. Configure branch control and an exclusive lock where appropriate. Do not overlap release runs.
  2. Authorize this pipeline, not all pipelines, to use the environments, pools, WIF connections and variable groups. Protect the release branch and require pipeline/template review.
  3. In Pipelines → New pipeline, select your platform repository and Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file, then .pipelines/azure-pipelines.yml. Save it. Do not start production until all inputs and checks are ready.
  4. Queue a run from a reviewed branch/commit. This sample has no automatic trigger. Leave all stages selected; never use stage selection as a promotion bypass.

CI validates the application definition and manifest JSON, installs hook dependencies and compiles Bicep without deploying. Before promotion, require security scanning, Bicep what-if, Azure readiness checks, real-user acceptance and your existing unit/contract tests.

Each deployment stage requires succeeded() and an explicit result equal to Succeeded for every prerequisite. Failed, Canceled, Skipped and SucceededWithIssues cannot promote. Do not replace these conditions with always(), succeededOrFailed() or independent stage-selection parameters. Azure DevOps Environment approvals are external protected-resource checks. Verify they are configured in Azure DevOps before queuing a run.

docs.title: 5. Run and inspect the deployment
docs.text:
Open the queued run, select each stage and inspect the authenticated task's logs. Confirm the target and command order below. Stop promotion on an unexpected target, deferred configuration or failed capability check.

The template checks out Build.SourceVersion again and fails if HEAD differs. It activates Python 3.12 and installs config/requirements.txt in that job; a CI virtual environment is not available on a later agent.

Inside AzureCLI@2, it initializes a local azd environment (or explicitly selects one already present), sets the intended resource group, and checks group existence:

  • New group: no refresh is attempted before the first provision.
  • Existing group: azd env refresh --environment <name> --no-prompt must reload the previous azd deployment outputs. Access, discovery or refresh errors fail the job; there is no || true. An existing empty/unrelated resource group is not a prior azd deployment. Use a fresh target for this example or explicitly review and onboard the existing foundation first.

The same azd name and subscription must locate the previous deployment. Review the refreshed target and outputs for an existing environment; do not create a second deployment by renaming the environment.

For split-group deployments, retain .azure/<environment-name>/resource-groups.json after first provision and securely restore that same environment's file on subsequent runners. azd env refresh restores outputs, not this immutable destination binding.

The example does not archive or restore the binding for you; integrate your organization's protected state handling before redeployment. Never reuse another stage's binding or publish .env files as pipeline artifacts. Review deployed state and application binding before adopting an existing environment into CI.

After refresh, reviewed environment settings are applied, then the template runs:

Topology Ordered commands from the platform root Hosted Agent Application azd hooks run preup --no-prompt → azd provision --no-prompt → azd deploy --no-prompt

Preup validates/checks binding before standalone provisioning. Preprovision resolves topology using python -m config.deployment.topology and composes infra/main.parameters.json; subsequent hooks use --describe to read its JSON. Post-provision configures application services and roles. Provision prepares the hosted foundation prerequisites. Deploy automatically builds or reuses the immutable image, materializes its application handoff and creates the hosted version plus the other selected components, without another provision.

This full workflow is deliberately repeatable on fresh agents. A hosted deployment may reuse a compatible digest when its provenance is available, but disposable local state and different environment registries can cause rebuilding. Agent Application Container App scripts build per environment.

This is immutable source promotion, not build-once immutable-image promotion: mutable base images, package feeds, tool versions, generated configuration and credentials can affect results. Pin dependencies/base images and record actual image digests per environment.

If identical images are mandatory, design and validate a separate digest-based application contract with cross-registry availability and permissions before adopting that promotion model.

No build artifacts are published or downloaded. Do not add a whole-workspace publish step: hooks copy .azure to sibling components and create .logs. Exclude .azure, .env/environment files, logs, secret files, credential/config caches, .git credentials and Python dependency environments from any future artifact. If changing to CI artifacts, deploy from the downloaded validated tree and explicitly solve the Git metadata requirement for local custom sources.

Cleanup runs even after failure. Its fixed path list removes .azure and .logs from the platform root, hosted-agent/, and the three manifest component sibling checkouts (agent-app-ui, agent-app-orchestrator, agent-app-ingestion). It leaves their source files intact and removes the job-specific temporary Python environment, azd config and Git config.

Update the explicit state-directory list when changing component names or adding a custom definition folder; do not replace it with recursive deletion of source/workspace roots.

AzureCLI@2 owns its isolated Azure CLI authentication context. Abrupt agent loss can prevent cleanup: reimage ephemeral agents or securely clean their disks before reuse.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Expected pipeline results are a green CI job, successful DEV deployment, TEST waiting for its protected Environment check, then PROD waiting after successful TEST. Match the recorded Build.SourceVersion and reviewed manifest pins to the run being approved.

Before promotion, record release evidence for the preceding environment:

  1. azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP identifies the Foundry/root target. AZURE_APP_RESOURCE_GROUP identifies the application target and AZURE_NETWORK_RESOURCE_GROUP the local network target; omitted overrides use the Foundry/root group. App Configuration has the expected platform outputs and effective settings under label agent-lz; the selected apps have real, healthy image revisions, not just provisioned placeholders. Record image digests and hosted routed version.
  2. Complete Entra setup above. Verify HTTPS login/callback, authenticated API access and (for hosted mode) real-user OBO invocation. The hook's managed-identity greeting checks basic runtime response; use the UI for these real-user tests.
  3. Ingest a controlled document through the selected configured source. With an authorized user, retrieve its expected content/citations. With a user lacking that document's permission, verify the content is not returned. Also verify unauthenticated requests are rejected where required. Check that logs do not contain tokens or protected document bodies.
  4. Exercise selected ingestion/upload, history, panel and continuity features; check disabled surfaces are unavailable. Conversation uploads require Agent App Ingestion and upload eligibility; native Blob ingestion handles the configured source separately.
  5. Inspect service health, RBAC and private endpoint resolution, and attach sanitized evidence to the run/change record. See application health and diagnostics and document authorization guidance.

Do not approve TEST or PROD until the preceding environment meets these checks. Some post-provision setup sections currently log a configuration failure and continue, so review the logs as well as the hook exit status. Require your organization's acceptance checks to pass.

docs.title: Local example validation
docs.text:
With Python and PyYAML installed, run from the downloaded example directory:

python -m pip install PyYAML==6.0.3
python validate.py

Expect the local checks to pass. They exercise stage conditions for prerequisite result combinations, embedded script syntax and exact cleanup targets with rm intercepted, without deleting anything or calling Azure. They cannot validate live service connections, approvals, RBAC, private networking or tenant consent. Perform those acceptance checks separately.

docs.title: Troubleshoot, redeploy and recover
docs.text:
Symptom Action Connection login fails, or azd asks for sign-in Verify WIF issuer/subject/audience, pipeline authorization and connection scope. Keep azd CLI-auth configuration and commands inside the authenticated task. Do not add interactive login. ARM succeeds but App Configuration/Search/Foundry returns 403 Check the deployment principal's scoped data-plane roles and propagation. For hosted authoring, check exact project access. Do not substitute subscription Owner or disable authorization. Private DNS/connectivity check fails Verify the Azure Pipelines runner's network/DNS/firewall path. An ACR Tasks pool does not connect the pipeline agent. Keep post-provision nondeferred. Refresh fails Check the azd environment name, subscription, prior deployment and read permission. Stop; do not swallow the error or silently provision another group. Stale sibling checkout / source mismatch Use the clean workspace and exact manifest/local source commits. Do not remove commit validation or update pins only in PROD. Hosted image preparation fails Verify the provisioned foundation, manifest pin, ACR build/pull access and private build pool, then retry azd deploy; see hosted redeployment. No separate preparation or second provision is required. Green deploy but UI login/retrieval fails Complete registration/consent/runtime settings, inspect sanitized hook/service logs and run the real-user positive/negative checks. See Troubleshooting. TEST or PROD starts without the expected approval Stop the run and fix Environment checks/permissions outside YAML before restarting.

For an application-only redeployment with unchanged compatible foundation/binding and hosted handoff, use the same initialization/authentication procedure and azd deploy, following Redeploy applications only. Do not replace full provisioning with deploy-only for infrastructure, RBAC, topology or ingestion-selection changes.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
