Runtime settings control an application's behavior and vary by application. Here they describe Agent Application, the supplied reference app. Its settings are usually stored in Azure App Configuration.

docs.title: Repository boundaries
docs.text:
The platform repository coordinates infrastructure and application deployment. The Agent Application's runtime code lives in separate component repositories.

Area Responsibility Infrastructure: platform infra/ Repository-owned Bicep source for Azure resources, identities and access. manifest.json → infra.source records the upstream AI Landing Zone source it incorporates. Platform integration: root files, scripts/ and config/ Selects the application, composes deployment parameters, configures provisioned services and coordinates deployment. Runtime component repositories Own Agent App UI, Agent App Orchestrator (strategies and tools), and optional Agent App Ingestion. The manifest identifies their repositories and source pins.

The infra.source entry records the upstream version incorporated into this repository. Deployment uses the platform's own infra/ tree, which includes Agent Landing Zone changes.

docs.title: The manifest records a validated combination
docs.text:
manifest.json records the platform release and each Agent Application component's repository, release tag and exact Git commit. A Git commit identifies an exact source revision; a tag is a readable label for a version. These identify the code versions validated together.

The hooks fetch selected Container App components into sibling directories and verify their commits. Hosted image preparation fetches the pinned orchestrator separately. Deploying the reference app needs no repository forks.

The Agent Application's app-definition.json also records component commits and is validated against the manifest. A modified combination needs its own integration validation. See Custom applications for repository customization and pinning rules.

docs.title: Parameters describe the environment
docs.text:
The checked-in root main.parameters.json maps deployment inputs to infrastructure parameters. Values can be literals or references to the selected azd environment's variables. Inline defaults apply where declared; other unset inputs can use Bicep defaults.

Before provisioning, the hooks resolve the application and hosting topology, apply environment inputs and generate infra/main.parameters.json for Bicep.

Edit the source, not the generated output

Use documented deployment inputs and the root parameter file. Do not edit infra/main.parameters.json; the next composition can overwrite it. See Deployment settings for inputs and defaults.

An application definition describes the selected application's components and capabilities. The environment records that definition's id on first provision and rejects a different one later. This identifies the deployed application; it is not a Microsoft Entra ID application registration ID.

Microsoft Entra ID handles sign-in and service identities in an organization's directory, called a tenant. An application registration describes a sign-in application to that service. Custom application selection therefore happens before the first provision.

Hosting, orchestration strategy and ingestion selection are separate decisions. For example, choosing a hosted orchestrator does not select an ingestion path. The configuration and application definition must form a supported combination. The hosted runtime rejects unsupported strategies rather than silently switching strategy or host. The multimodal and nl2sql strategies are not supported by this host.

docs.title: azure.yaml connects azd to the lifecycle
docs.text:
The root azure.yaml points azd at infra/ and registers PowerShell and shell lifecycle hooks. The hooks configure Azure services and coordinate application deployment.

Stage What the platform does Before azd up (preup) Validates the application definition and checks that it matches the environment's recorded application. Before provisioning (preprovision) Resolves application selection and topology, composes infrastructure parameters and runs preflight checks. After provisioning (postprovision) Configures Azure services, reconciles application access and publishes runtime settings and outputs. Before deployment (predeploy) Checks infrastructure readiness and the recorded application, validates topology and required connectivity, then coordinates the selected application deployments.

azd provision includes service configuration through its post-provision hook. Some Container Apps initially contain placeholder images; azd deploy replaces them with the selected application code.

Container App deployment builds verified component code through each component's azure.yaml. Hosted orchestration uses the prepared image described below. Custom applications supply their own definitions and projects for deployment.

docs.title: App Configuration carries runtime settings
docs.text:
Deployment inputs describe what to create. Runtime settings describe how applications use the resulting services.

Provisioning and configuration publish settings to Azure App Configuration under the agent-lz label. The Agent Application loaders also select other labels, which can affect which setting takes precedence. Bootstrap values such as the store endpoint must be available before remote configuration can load. Secrets belong in Key Vault and are referenced rather than copied into checked-in settings.

The same label is used across environments, so separation depends on distinct configuration, identities and data, as described in Environment boundaries. Local .azure/ state is private deployment state, not a source-controlled input file. Child workspaces receive copies and need the same protection.

See Deployment settings for setting names, sources and reload requirements.

docs.title: Why hosted agents need image preparation
docs.text:
A Foundry hosted agent needs an immutable image before its agent version can be deployed. That creates a bootstrap dependency on the registry and Foundry resources.

An image digest identifies the built container image by its content. It is not a source commit or a mutable image tag.

  1. Infrastructure prerequisites. Initial provisioning creates and configures the required Azure services and access rules.
  2. Automatic image preparation during deploy. The deployment hook builds the pinned orchestrator and its hosted entrypoint image when needed, recording the digest and build details.
  3. Application handoff during deploy. The hook binds the image to the provisioned project, registry and network metadata without another provision.
  4. Application publication. Deployment creates the hosted agent version and deploys the other selected application components.

Image preparation does not start the agent, and provisioning does not create the running data-plane agent version. Deploy-only reuses a compatible generated image, or rebuilds when generated source/startup provenance changes. Operators use azd provision followed by azd deploy, or azd up; there is no required standalone preparation command.

The same source pins do not guarantee the same image digest when images are built independently. If a promotion process requires the identical image, its digest and registry availability need separate preservation and verification.

The Deploy full stack runbook provides execution steps. For strategy eligibility and image behavior, see Agent hosting.

docs.title: From understanding to deployment
docs.text: The planning references explain deployment design, sizing and cost. For execution, the named runbooks are Deploy infra only or Deploy full stack. Those runbooks contain the prerequisites, topology-specific sequence and validation steps.

docs.title: Ingestion and conversation uploads
docs.text:
Foundry IQ provides the standard source-ingestion path. Conversation attachments and custom processing are separate capabilities that can require optional Agent App Ingestion.

This page explains those boundaries. Deployment steps are in the Deploy full stack runbook; source and index inputs are described in Deployment settings.

docs.title: 1. Standard ingestion with Foundry IQ
docs.text:
The default source is Azure Blob Storage, with FOUNDRY_IQ_PATTERN=azureBlob and container documents. Azure AI Search, which powers Foundry IQ, creates and manages the indexing pipeline for this knowledge source. It extracts content, splits it into smaller passages (chunks), generates embeddings (vectors used for similarity search) and populates an index used by the knowledge base.

Agent App Ingestion is not required for this path. New Agent Application environments default to DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP=false.

Source documents belong in the configured Blob container and optional folder, not in a chat attachment. Search's ingestion identity needs access to storage and the configured extraction and embedding services. The default permission metadata is ["rbacScope"]; ingestion permissions and the querying user's authorization remain separate requirements. Microsoft's Blob knowledge-source guide describes the managed pipeline and service requirements.

Successful ingestion does not establish protected retrieval in the hosted application. The shipped hosted entrypoint supplies empty user context to the retrieval strategy, so the connector cannot forward an on-behalf-of (OBO) token. This limitation affects protected Blob retrieval as well as the sources below.

Foundry also supports native SharePoint options, including previews:

Native option What happens to the content Foundry IQ indexedSharePoint source A service-managed pipeline copies and processes SharePoint content into a Search index. No Agent App Ingestion is required by the service. Foundry IQ remoteSharePoint source The knowledge base queries Microsoft 365 at retrieval time. It does not copy the SharePoint corpus into a landing-zone index. Retrieved text still reaches the agent and model. Foundry Agent Service SharePoint tool The agent calls a native tool backed by Microsoft 365 retrieval, outside the knowledge-base source list. It does not require the custom ingestion application.

These product options are not all wired into Agent Application. The indexed SharePoint template needs a source-contract update; remote retrieval and native tools need their own connection, consent and trusted delegated-user integration. Native tool calls require the user's identity, not application-only access. SharePoint explains the options and current integration gaps. Preview status is a governance consideration, not a reason to assume custom ingestion is required.

The accelerator's ingestion-free validation accepts native Blob or an explicitly bound, independently populated Search index. A SharePoint-only replacement needs source-specific integration and authorization validation; a product-supported source is not automatically a supported deployment selection.

docs.title: 2. Conversation file uploads
docs.text:
A chat attachment is processed for one conversation, not added to the shared native Blob corpus. This path requires Agent App Ingestion, its reachable endpoint and a compatible Search index. Alongside the default native Blob source, the additional conversation searchIndex source needs FOUNDRY_IQ_CONVERSATION_UPLOAD_ENABLED=true. The flag is invalid without the ingestion app.

With DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP=false, Agent App UI hides attachment controls and rejects server uploads and client preflight before resolving an ingestion endpoint or Dapr fallback. Setting it to true permits the upload path, but does not make authenticated retrieval work automatically.

The UI's attachment controls require authenticated access. Anonymous Copilot sessions cannot upload. The chat handler accepts PDFs, up to five files, 15 MiB per file and 25 MiB total. Hosted uploads require the UI's existing hosted conversation identifier. A text turn establishes it in the non-continuity hosted path; continuity-enabled chat does not populate that upload identifier.

The upload payload can carry the uploader's object ID as permission metadata. That is not sufficient by itself: the index must enforce those permissions and retrieval must preserve conversation scope and trusted user authorization.

Conversation scope uses the hosted backend's conversation namespace, not the local UI thread ID. The same identifier must reach the indexed upload and retrieval filter. Retrieval must match both conversationId and the trusted uploader in metadata_security_user_ids; the identifier alone grants no access.

The default hosted entrypoint supplies no authenticated owner, so the native Blob conversation-upload source is skipped. The delegated-token gap described above also affects protected conversation retrieval. Enabling ingestion does not resolve it. The conversation PDF reference describes source bindings. Hosted use still needs the reviewed Foundry IQ identity integration.

docs.title: 3. Custom ingestion only when needed
docs.text:
Agent App Ingestion is useful when the managed source does not meet processing requirements, or when conversation uploads or the application's custom SharePoint jobs are required. Its format-specific processing performs chunking and embedding generation and writes content to Search. An independent pipeline can instead populate a compatible index exposed through a Foundry IQ searchIndex source.

The optional application's SharePoint connector uses Microsoft Graph application credentials and indexing/purge jobs. It copies content and permission metadata into Search; permission synchronization and query-time enforcement still need validation.

Every selected item's supported ACLs are reconciled on each SharePoint index run, even when content is unchanged, without re-downloading or embedding that content. Grants and revocations replace stored permissions on all affected documents and chunks. See SharePoint permission synchronization for scheduling, filter boundaries, inherited-permission support and recovery.

It is separate from native SharePoint knowledge sources and the native Foundry tool. Its SHAREPOINT_* credentials are not the SHAREPOINT_REMOTE_* retrieval settings. Secrets belong in Key Vault.

For the bundled Agent Application, DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP selects the optional component through the Deploy full stack runbook, not a runtime-only edit. Existing environments retain their recorded selection; custom application definitions retain their declared components. Selection does not change retrieval bindings or document authorization. Omitting the application does not delete deployed resources, indexed documents or identity grants; retirement needs separate authorization.

For every path, acceptance includes a document that an allowed user can retrieve with its citation and that a denied user cannot retrieve. Source permissions, query-time enforcement and private-network connectivity require separate validation. Private Blob ingestion is covered in Network isolation.

docs.title: Images and voice
docs.text: Agent Application can ground text answers in image descriptions extracted from documents. This differs from passing an image or audio directly to a model. The default hosted maf_lite path uses text input and retrieved text. This page explains capability boundaries; the Deploy full stack runbook contains deployment procedures.

docs.title: Supported content
docs.text: Content Hosted application behavior Diagrams in a shared collection Native Foundry IQ Blob ingestion can produce image descriptions when its model and extraction requirements are met. Conversation PDF Optional Agent App Ingestion processes uploads; hosted retrieval also needs the owner/identity integration described below. Screenshot or standalone image Not accepted by the supplied hosted input adapter or PDF upload handler. Voice No supplied capture, transcription, realtime audio or playback integration.

docs.title: Document image grounding
docs.text:
Native Blob ingestion can verbalize images during document processing. The knowledge base then returns extracted content to the orchestrator; the model receives text, not the original image.

This path uses RETRIEVAL_BACKEND=foundry_iq, FOUNDRY_IQ_PATTERN=azureBlob, FOUNDRY_IQ_KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_KIND=azureBlob and FOUNDRY_IQ_CONTENT_EXTRACTION_MODE=standard. Agent App Ingestion is not required.

The provisioning template sets disableImageVerbalization=false, but only supplies chatCompletionModel for its supported Content Understanding model names. gpt-4.1 is supported; the default gpt-5-nano is not in that allowlist. The flag alone therefore does not establish working image verbalization in a fresh deployment. Standard extraction also requires a compatible region, Foundry AI Services endpoint and embedding deployment. Blob source prerequisites describe service requirements.

In main.parameters.json, the chat entry of modelDeploymentList uses canonical_name: CHAT_DEPLOYMENT_NAME; model.name identifies the family and name identifies the deployment. A model change affects availability, quota and extraction compatibility. Deployment settings identifies the configuration inputs. The rendered source's model binding and extracted diagram content are the evidence of successful processing, not the model name alone.

The ingestion identity's source/model access is independent of the user's retrieval permissions. Private connectivity follows Network isolation. Protected hosted retrieval still requires the identity integration and allow/deny evidence; image extraction does not provide it.

docs.title: Conversation PDFs
docs.text:
DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP defaults to false, so fresh deployments hide and reject uploads. Optional Agent App Ingestion is required for eligible PDF attachments, as described in Ingestion and conversation uploads.

With a native Blob primary source, conversation retrieval requires FOUNDRY_IQ_CONVERSATION_UPLOAD_ENABLED=true and provisioned FOUNDRY_IQ_CONVERSATION_KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_NAME. The name identifies a Search knowledge source, not a URL or conversation ID. Its upload filter requires the pinned 2026-05-01-preview API. Missing or failed upload sources can be skipped; shared-corpus retrieval can continue.

The UI needs an established hosted conversation ID and an eligible signed-in session. It accepts at most five PDFs, 15 MiB each and 25 MiB combined. Anonymous embedded sessions cannot upload.

Processing confirmation does not prove retrieval isolation: the hosted entry point supplies no authenticated owner context to the default connector, so the native Blob conversation-upload source is skipped. Working protected conversation retrieval requires a reviewed owner-identity integration, delegated retrieval authorization and cross-user validation.

Agent App Ingestion's separate MULTIMODAL setting controls figure extraction and captioning in its custom pipeline. It does not enable direct screenshot input. Scanned or diagram-only PDFs depend on the extracted content.

docs.title: Evidence and configuration lifecycle
docs.text:
Grounded image answers depend on completed ingestion, extracted content, a compatible model binding and the intended source reference. A processed PDF can still be absent from retrieval; shared-source answers alone do not prove conversation-upload retrieval works.

Runtime configuration is cached. A changed hosted setting needs a new agent version; affected UI and ingestion processes also need to reload. Source/model changes follow the Deploy full stack runbook. The pinned API remains part of the application contract rather than an independent setting to change without compatibility validation.

docs.title: Direct image and voice extensions
docs.text:
Screenshot input requires caller and adapter development to validate and forward image content to a compatible model. Microsoft's vision input guide describes model APIs, not an enabled Agent Application feature.

Voice requires client/service integration for capture, transcription or realtime audio, and playback. The Realtime audio guide describes those APIs. Bring your own app covers the application boundary. Both extensions need authentication, input limits and source authorization when connected to retrieval.

docs.title: Network isolation
docs.text:
Use private networking for production and workloads with sensitive data. Set NETWORK_ISOLATION=true explicitly before provisioning. The template's current default is false; that default is not the recommended production configuration.

Reserve public service endpoints for organization-approved, short-lived evaluations or demonstrations with synthetic or non-sensitive data. Public endpoints still require authentication and authorization, but those checks do not make them private. Do not disable isolation to work around connectivity or deployment failures.

This page explains connectivity, DNS and build requirements rather than deployment steps. How it works introduces the input formats and deployment lifecycle.

A private endpoint gives a service a private IP address in a VNet. Private DNS directs its normal hostname to that address. A virtual private network (VPN) connects an authorized remote computer or network to the VNet.

A jumpbox is a virtual machine (VM) used for administration; Azure Bastion provides remote access to it. A NAT gateway provides outbound address translation. None of these connections grants permission to read service data.

With NETWORK_ISOLATION=true, Agent Landing Zone uses private endpoints and private DNS for the deployed workload services. With the default empty allowedIpRanges, public access to those service endpoints is disabled. Azure Resource Manager remains public; telemetry and optional public ingress have separate settings.

An explicit, nonempty allowedIpRanges in main.parameters.json enables IP-restricted public access on services that support those rules, even with isolation enabled. Those public paths and any reused network or DNS resources remain part of the connectivity design.

The Deploy infra only and Deploy full stack runbooks contain the procedures. The Azure DevOps runbook covers optional pipeline automation. Deployment choices explains standalone and hub integration. An AI Gateway governs model requests, not workload networking or user access. Private endpoints, DNS, routes, firewall rules and authorization remain necessary.

With the resource group destinations, locally owned private endpoints default to the resolved network group, which can differ from their services' groups. The explicit AZURE_PE_RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME override and existing-VNet/SIDE_BY_SIDE precedence in Deployment settings still apply.

Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot publication

Publish to Teams and M365 adds a manual, source-IP-filtered public exception for the Foundry Activity route while Foundry and Bot Service public network access stays disabled. Microsoft calls this a source IP-filtered Activity Protocol public endpoint.

Channel messages use public HTTPS, not Private Link, so this path is not private end to end. If public agent ingress is prohibited, do not use that publication path. Other Foundry APIs remain private, and the template does not enable this exception.

The Connect Copilot Studio runbook describes an authenticated agent flow and Power Platform VNet delegation to reach the Foundry private endpoint; it does not require the Activity-route public exception.

docs.title: What changes with isolation
docs.text:
Area NETWORK_ISOLATION=false NETWORK_ISOLATION=true Workload service access Public endpoints, with service authentication and authorization Private endpoints by default DNS Public DNS Private DNS zones linked to the VNet Jumpbox, Azure Bastion, NAT gateway Not deployed by default Deployed by default Container image builds Local Docker or regular ACR Tasks ACR Task agent pool inside the VNet by default Post-provision and deploy Run from an authorized host that can reach the endpoints Run from an authorized host connected to the VNet

Note

The ACR Task agent pool is created only for isolated deployments. When isolation is off, supported components can build with local Docker or regular ACR Tasks. No pool is created, even if DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL is true.

docs.title: Isolation and provisioning
docs.text: NETWORK_ISOLATION=true is resolved before provisioning. All twelve subnets are created by default. Choose who manages them before first provision.

docs.title: Choose subnet ownership
docs.text:
These choices apply with network isolation enabled. Hub connectivity and DNS remain separate decisions.

Network choice USE_EXISTING_VNET DEPLOY_SUBNETS Responsibility New VNet and subnets false true The template creates the VNet and selected subnets. Existing VNet, template-managed subnets true true Supply EXISTING_VNET_RESOURCE_ID; the template creates/updates selected subnets. Existing VNet, externally managed subnets true false Supply the VNet ID; its owner prepares every subnet required by enabled consumers.

Using an existing VNet does not make deployment read-only. Individual creation flags can exclude subnets from template management. See the network selection examples.

docs.title: Default subnets
docs.text:
The new VNet's default address space is 192.168.0.0/21. Names and ranges can be overridden using the subnet inputs.

Purpose Default name Default CIDR Delegation Foundry Agent Service agent-subnet 192.168.0.0/24 Microsoft.App/environments Container Apps environment aca-environment-subnet 192.168.1.0/24 Microsoft.App/environments Foundry/grounding private endpoints pe-subnet 192.168.2.0/26 None Bastion AzureBastionSubnet 192.168.2.64/26 None Firewall AzureFirewallSubnet 192.168.2.128/26 None VPN/ExpressRoute reservation GatewaySubnet 192.168.2.192/26 None Application Gateway AppGatewaySubnet 192.168.3.0/27 None Jumpbox jumpbox-subnet 192.168.3.64/27 None Build agents devops-build-agents-subnet 192.168.3.96/27 None Application private endpoints application-pe-subnet 192.168.3.128/26 None Power Platform powerplatform-subnet 192.168.4.0/24 Microsoft.PowerPlatform/enterprisePolicies AI Gateway ai-gateway-subnet 192.168.5.0/24 Microsoft.Web/serverFarms

Creation is not service selection. A false subnet creation flag does not disable its consumers: any enabled consumer still needs a valid subnet. With isolation off, no VNet or subnets are provisioned.

Prepared subnets are not deployed services. These reservations do not deploy APIM or VPN/ExpressRoute gateways, create a Power Platform enterprise policy, or associate a Power Platform environment. Those integrations need separate setup.

Enabled application Cosmos DB, Key Vault, App Configuration, Container Apps, ACR and Azure Monitor Private Link Scope endpoints use the application private endpoint subnet. Foundry/grounding endpoints use pe-subnet by default. Application endpoints never fall back to the Foundry subnet, including when application subnet creation is disabled. This separation is independent of resource group count.

Keep the reserved name GatewaySubnet; do not attach an NSG, default-route UDR or delegation to it. AI Gateway uses APIM Standard v2/Premium v2 outbound VNet integration, with a subnet of /27 or larger, delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms and associated with an NSG. Preserve an outbound HTTPS path to Azure Key Vault. No reserved subnet name is required for APIM; do not place APIM private endpoints in its delegated integration subnet.

The Power Platform /24 is a capacity default, not a platform minimum. Size for environment demand: approximately 25–30 IPs per production environment or 6–10 per nonproduction environment, plus five subnet-reserved IPs. See Power Platform subnet sizing.

Azure Resource Manager (ARM) creates and manages Azure resources through a public control plane, but azd provision also runs lifecycle hooks. An existing environment can need private App Configuration access before ARM deployment to resolve its topology. Post-provision also needs private connectivity, so an unconnected host cannot complete every stage.

The matching deployment runbook therefore requires a connected host. The default Foundry hosted deployment automatically prepares its image and application handoff during azd deploy, as described in Deploy full stack.

docs.title: Private network access
docs.text:
Private services can be reached through:

  • Point-to-site or site-to-site VPN into the landing zone VNet or a peered hub.
  • A VM or build agent in the VNet or a peered VNet, with private DNS zone access.
  • The jumpbox VM deployed by the landing zone, reached through Azure Bastion.

docs.title: Jumpbox access
docs.text:
The default jumpbox is a Windows VM. Unless overridden, its administrator user is testvmuser. The password is supplied through the secure vmAdminPassword provisioning input, not a documented Key Vault secret. Unavailable credentials require an authorized administrator's approved reset procedure, without exposing passwords in shell history or logs.

Azure Bastion provides portal access to the VM. It still needs the deployment prerequisites. Docker is not installed by default and is unnecessary for ACR Task agent-pool builds.

docs.title: Connected-host requirements
docs.text:
The connected host needs the same reviewed platform Git commit or release tag and approved inputs as the original workspace. Its local azd environment also needs current provisioning outputs. The Deploy infra only runbook explains environment selection, output refresh and separate provisioning/configuration steps.

The jumpbox's managed identity, an Azure-managed service identity that does not need a stored password, needs the selected application's configuration and build roles.

For hosted-agent authoring, the runner needs Foundry User on the exact Foundry project, plus read access to the Foundry account. Cognitive Services Contributor and OpenAI User alone do not grant the agent data-plane actions.

Subscription or resource-group Owner is not an appropriate fix for this denial. See Foundry RBAC for the current role catalog and scopes. New grants need time to propagate.

An infrastructure-only deployment stops after provisioning and post-provision configuration. It can contain placeholder Container Apps without running the selected applications. The Deploy full stack runbook also deploys application code.

docs.title: Post-provision can be deferred
docs.text:
When isolation is enabled, post-provision can be deferred instead of failing. RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX=false (or 0, no, skip) requests deferral, as does AZURE_SKIP_NETWORK_ISOLATION_WARNING=true while RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX is not truthy. A truthy RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX, such as true, requests the connectivity check even if the warning flag is set. Deferral produces:

Post-provision configuration explicitly deferred; application setup is incomplete.

If the other provisioning stages succeed, azd provision reports success, but the application is not configured. Deferral does not bypass earlier topology or provisioning checks. Configuration remains incomplete until deferral is cleared and configuration succeeds from a connected host. The Deploy infra only runbook provides those steps.

When the deferral settings are not set and the private endpoints cannot be reached, post-provision fails with:

Private post-provision prerequisites failed. Connect through VPN/VNet and rerun postProvision; configuration has not started.

Warning

RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX only controls whether post-provision is deferred. It does not provide connectivity. azd deploy always checks private reachability, and fails with "Private deployment prerequisites failed" when the host cannot reach the endpoints.

docs.title: Image builds in isolated deployments
docs.text:
Public build agents cannot reach the default private registry. Remote builds use an ACR Task agent pool inside the VNet (DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL=true). Hosted topology composition selects this pool when network isolation is enabled.

If the pool is missing, azd deploy stops before building. Pool creation uses DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL=true through the matching deployment runbook. Where a component supports local builds, BUILD_MODE=local instead needs a VNet-connected host with working Docker.

The local alternative applies to component scripts that support BUILD_MODE=local. Automatic hosted orchestrator image preparation and isolated custom source builds still require the private pool. Supplying an already-built immutable digest can skip those builds. To deploy without a pool, the root pre-deploy check also requires BUILD_MODE=local. Each remaining service must support local builds for that exception to work.

docs.title: Application-specific package feeds
docs.text:
The root deployment defaults include dependency-verified package feed destinations alongside common language and OS package registries, through the scoped infrastructure build-egress configuration. This is a build-only allowlist, not a runtime or general Internet exception. It does not allow every mirror recorded in a custom application's lockfile. The exact component commit's resolved URLs and download redirects determine its build needs.

Additional dependencies are declared in parameters.additionalAcrTaskBuildFqdns.value in the root main.parameters.json. This is an explicit array, not an azd environment variable. Provisioning applies it; the connected runner needs the same reviewed parameter file to preserve the setting on later provisions.

The Agent Application orchestrator frontend lockfile uses ms-feed-2.pkgs.visualstudio.com, ms-feed-12.pkgs.visualstudio.com, ms-feed-17.pkgs.visualstudio.com, and ms-feed-25.pkgs.visualstudio.com. Their public package downloads redirect to *.vsblob.vsassets.io. These four exact feeds and the redirect content delivery network (CDN) are included in the Agent Landing Zone default build allowlist. packages.microsoft.com is already included in the OS-package rule and does not need an additional entry.

With extendFirewallForAcrTaskBuilds=true (the default) and an effective ACR Task agent pool, the feeds, redirect CDN, and additional hosts are allowed only from the build-agent subnet over HTTPS on port 443. They are not added to jumpbox, application, or agent-subnet rules. The additional-host array defaults to empty.

Disabling the build-egress extension removes these package rules. Re-enabling it restores them. This egress rule has no DNS-proxy dependency and does not change client DNS.

Do not enable public registry access, allow all Internet egress, disable TLS verification, or change dependency integrity hashes to work around a failed build.

See Package installation fails inside the build pool for diagnosis.

docs.title: Component runtime egress
docs.text:
Application components declare additional runtime destinations in components[].egress. The plan follows actual enabled workloads: optional ingestion, hosted or preserved Container App orchestration, and additive custom applications. The bundled UI needs no additional fixed destination. Both orchestrator and ingestion initialize tiktoken, whose empty-cache startup downloads encoding assets from openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net over HTTPS/443.

These are runtime rules, not build-feed rules or replacements for private endpoints, authentication, DNS or routing. Configured SharePoint, SQL, MCP and other custom destinations require their own dependency review.

docs.title: Review before provisioning
docs.text:
From the platform root with the prepared Python environment, set the intended topology, ingestion selection and application definition in the selected azd environment, then run:

python -m config.deployment.egress --plan --environment <environment-name>

This reads the named local azd environment and validates declarations without Azure access. Review policyMode, selected components, destinations and purposes. The preprovision hook repeats this calculation, prints it and saves .azure/<environment-name>/component-egress-plan.json before foundation deployment. Approval of provisioning includes these declared requirements.

After infrastructure exists and local provisioning outputs are current, use:

python -m config.deployment.egress --review --environment <environment-name>

This is read-only. It resolves actual workload subnet prefixes and, for a deployment-managed policy, reports additions, updates and removals. A fresh deployment cannot resolve subnet prefixes until its infrastructure exists. Postprovision and predeploy print this resolved plan before managed reconciliation. If postprovision is explicitly deferred, reconciliation is also deferred; predeploy still enforces the connectivity and plan checks.

docs.title: Policy ownership
docs.text:
Deployment Behavior NETWORK_ISOLATION=false No component firewall reads or writes; declarations do not create a firewall Isolated with a deployment-managed firewall Reconciles only marked application rules in AgentLzComponentEgress, priority 400 Isolated with an external firewall Reports required rules and legacy components; never reads or mutates the external policy

For managed policies, the runner needs management-plane subnet reads and Microsoft.Network/firewallPolicies/ruleCollectionGroups/read and write on the deployment policy. The reconciler does not write the parent policy. For external policies, the network owner compares the report with their own policy and applies approved changes. Reporting does not prove that egress is allowed.

Shared destination/protocol/port tuples produce one rule, with sources and ownership combined across components. Removing one owner narrows sources where possible; the rule remains until its final declared owner disappears.

Enabled legacy components with absent declarations retain their earlier owned requirements. Other rules and collections, including unmarked entries inside the component group, are preserved. Ownership collisions, malformed marked rules, conflicting priorities or concurrent changes fail rather than being silently adopted or overwritten.

docs.title: Source scope and recovery
docs.text:
Rules use the actual provisioned Container Apps or Foundry agent subnet prefixes, including existing-VNet selections, not the whole VNet or *. Subnet scope is not component isolation: every workload sharing a source subnet can use its union of allowed destinations. Existing platform rules can also allow traffic. Use dedicated subnets or environments and an approved network design when workloads need distinct egress boundaries.

After changing declarations or selections, review the new local plan and run the normal provisioning sequence before deploying. A missing or stale saved plan stops apply before Azure access. Do not copy a plan or provisioning outputs from another environment.

For rollback, first review explicit empty declarations for the components whose additional rules should be removed, then reconcile using the current hooks. Keep declarations for any remaining consumers. Only afterward roll back hooks or metadata: reverting code alone does not remove existing rules. Never delete shared foundation groups or externally managed policy content.

docs.title: Private connectivity checks
docs.text:
The runbooks check service hostnames from the deployment runner, including the host in APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT:

Check Expected result Meaning DNS Only private IPv4 addresses (10.x, 172.16 through 31.x or 192.168.x) The runner resolves the private endpoint rather than the public endpoint. Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) Connection succeeds on port 443 Routing and firewall policy allow the endpoint connection. TLS Handshake succeeds with the original hostname and normal certificate validation The connection reaches the expected service securely.

Public DNS answers usually indicate a missing private-zone link or an incorrect VPN/hub forwarding path.

On Windows, nslookup can differ from the operating system resolver used by the Python prerequisite check, especially with VPN Name Resolution Policy Table (NRPT) rules. That check requires private IPv4 answers and rejects mixed public/private, IPv6, loopback and link-local answers.

It then verifies TCP 443 and TLS without sending an HTTP request or credentials. Connectivity is not authorization: API access and document permissions still need tests with the intended user identities.

docs.title: Opt-in firewall DNS proxy
docs.text:
ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY defaults to false and maps to the Bicep boolean enableFirewallDnsProxy (also default false), which sets dnsSettings.enableProxy. It applies only when the existing deployAzureFirewall and networkIsolation gates enable firewall deployment. It is intended for a topology that deliberately uses the firewall as its DNS forwarding path. The matching deployment runbook applies the selection through normal provisioning.

Enabling the proxy does not redirect VNet or VPN clients to the firewall or rewrite their DNS configuration. It is independent of the build-feed egress allowlist.

Client DNS routing and private-zone resolution remain separate requirements. A proxy cannot repair missing zone links, VPN routes or application authentication. Disabling it requires confirmation that the deployed DNS path does not depend on it before reprovisioning.

docs.title: Private native Blob ingestion
docs.text:
For the default native Blob path, Search reads and processes Blob documents for Foundry IQ retrieval. A searchIndex source instead exposes an index populated by another pipeline. Their private-network setup differs.

Native azureBlob ingestion uses outbound shared private links managed by Search. Configuration verifies deployment-owned links, targets and groups before dependent cleanup/mutation and again before knowledge source creation. It does not automatically approve target connections. Pending links require approval by an authorized target administrator for each connection.

The gate is limited to NETWORK_ISOLATION=true, RETRIEVAL_BACKEND=foundry_iq and rendered native azureBlob sources, excluding the searchIndex pattern. It checks the Agent Application Search link to deployment Blob storage (blob) and the links to the deployment Foundry account (openai_account, foundry_account, cognitiveservices_account). It does not configure the separate Foundry Search service or unrelated services.

Exact names come from the template's SEARCH_SHARED_PRIVATE_LINKS manifest, including bounded Foundry names. The exact Search shared-link GET must return the expected name, target and group. If its body includes a resource ID, that must match too.

The target service receives a private endpoint connection (PEC) request. Because its name, message and endpoint ID may not identify the originating Search link, an administrator must verify and approve the correct request. The configuration script reads the deployment's Search links and leaves target-side approval to that administrator. See Microsoft's approval and shared-link status procedure, sections 2 and 3.

A Pending source link stops immediately with its exact Search ID, target ID, group and link name for administrator investigation and approval. After approval, configuration needs another run. Each source link must report connection status Approved and provisioning state Succeeded before configuration continues. Read timeouts or denials require restored connectivity or Search read permissions, not public access. See Search shared private links are not ready.

Polling has a 600-second total readiness budget, a 10-second interval and ARM request timeouts of at most 30 seconds (limited by the remaining budget). Each exact Search shared link must be Approved and Succeeded, the documented source-side readiness signal. Approved links whose provisioning is still propagating use bounded polling. Pending approval does not spend this budget waiting for an unprovable target match.

Administrator-approved links are usable even when target PECs are paginated, opaque or unreadable by the runner. The existing Azure CLI/managed-identity credential is reused. The runner needs Search shared-link read permission, with no new secret, target PEC read/write requirement or automatic RBAC grant.

Native ingestion supports configured Foundry IQ source kinds and is not feature-equivalent to Agent App Ingestion. Choosing it does not remove Entra ID authentication, on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange, RBAC or document-level authorization. OBO exchanges a user's token for another API's token while retaining that user's delegated identity.

Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2 uses Blob storage with a hierarchical directory namespace. In particular, FOUNDRY_IQ_INGESTION_PERMISSION_OPTIONS=[] is a deliberate shared-source metadata choice for active, supported non-ADLS native Blob ingestion, not a workaround for a private connection failure.

Infrastructure-published [] for ai_search (any pattern) or foundry_iq / searchIndex is accepted as unused metadata, not a shared-source opt-in: no native Blob source is rendered. See Explicit shared-source permission options.

docs.title: Integrate with an existing hub
docs.text:
Hub integration uses DEPLOYMENT_MODE=ailz-integrated with explicit settings:

Setting Purpose DEPLOYMENT_MODE=ailz-integrated Declares integration intent; does not attach a hub or override component flags by itself HUB_INTEGRATION_HUB_VNET_RESOURCE_ID Hub VNet to peer with HUB_INTEGRATION_CREATE_HUB_PEERING Create spoke-to-hub peering for a new spoke VNet (default true); hub owner supplies reverse peering. Existing VNet peerings are externally managed HUB_INTEGRATION_PEERING_ALLOW_GATEWAY_TRANSIT Allow gateway transit (default false) HUB_INTEGRATION_PEERING_USE_REMOTE_GATEWAYS Use the hub gateway (default false) HUB_INTEGRATION_EGRESS_NEXT_HOP_IP Next hop for egress, for example the hub firewall HUB_INTEGRATION_EXISTING_ROUTE_TABLE_RESOURCE_ID Existing route table to attach AZURE_PE_RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME, AZURE_PE_LOCATION Where to place private endpoints EXISTING_* Reuse the existing VNet, private DNS zones, jumpbox, Bastion, NAT gateway or monitoring resources

Deployment settings lists the inputs; hub-and-spoke design explains their network effects. Execution steps belong to the Deploy infra only runbook.

docs.title: Ask questions about SQL data
docs.text:
Structured Query Language (SQL) queries and changes database tables. This integration permits only read-only queries.

Structured-data grounding can connect a Fabric data agent to a Foundry IQ knowledge base. Agent Application supplies connector code, not a complete hosted SQL integration. Delegated identity and response compatibility require additional validation before protected data can be exposed. This is a concept page; deployment follows the Deploy full stack runbook.

docs.title: Structured-data grounding
docs.text:
Fabric warehouses and lakehouses store analytical data. A Fabric data agent generates and executes read-only SQL over their tables. A Power BI semantic model uses Data Analysis Expressions (DAX). Fabric owns schema context and query execution; the hosted orchestrator consumes results from the knowledge base.

The default hosted application does not execute a direct natural-language-to-SQL (NL2SQL) plugin. A direct SQL tool is a custom application extension described under Agent tools, not a runtime switch that supplies this feature.

docs.title: Fabric source contract
docs.text:
The Fabric data agent must be published and shared with the intended users, who also need permission to its underlying data. The Search service and Fabric workspace use the same Entra tenant. Supported capacity, tenant settings and network reachability are source requirements. Fabric data agent requirements and the knowledge-source contract describe service limits.

The Foundry IQ Fabric Data Agent source is a preview integration. Its binding is a fabricDataAgent knowledge source with workspace and data-agent item IDs. FABRIC_DATA_AGENT_ENABLED and FABRIC_DATA_AGENT_KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_NAME identify this route. FABRIC_IQ_ENABLED identifies the separate ontology route. The source supports low or medium retrieval reasoning effort, not minimal. Fabric integration describes the bindings and Deployment settings identifies setting ownership.

docs.title: Identity and API boundaries
docs.text:
The connector needs service authentication and a separate Search-audience delegated user token for remote-source authorization. The supplied hosted entry point provides neither a user bearer nor authenticated user context to default retrieval.

Required-user retrieval can fail before the source is called; the remote-source connector itself skips this source when its delegated token is absent. UI sign-in and Foundry invocation do not close that gap. Agent Application access explains the required authenticated integration.

The supplied parser expects dataAgentAnswer and dataAgentRawData. The platform and orchestrator pin 2026-05-01-preview. The service contract also documents fabricAnswer and fabricEmbeddedResources with 2026-08-01-preview. The parser's separate ontology branch can read fabricAnswer, but does not handle fabricEmbeddedResources and classifies that answer as ontology content. Compatibility requires a validated API, parser and response combination, including table/chart handling. Changing the API setting alone does not implement that compatibility.

docs.title: Validation boundary
docs.text:
A meaningful pilot compares a fixed, known aggregate from an approved table with the same question in Fabric and in the hosted application. The published agent's selected tables, business definition, date boundaries and permissions all affect the result. Creating a Fabric data agent is a separate service procedure, not evidence that hosted integration works.

Required evidence includes activity from the intended knowledge source, correctly parsed results and denial for a user without source access. That validation depends on resolving the identity and API boundaries first. Read-only execution prevents writes; it does not itself authorize a caller or guarantee a correct answer.

docs.title: Failure boundaries
docs.text: A Fabric answer missing from chat can indicate skipped delegated retrieval, an incorrect binding or incompatible response fields. An incorrect aggregate can instead reflect source schema or business definitions. Knowledge-base source references and provisioning inputs share a lifecycle; removing a pilot binding does not require deleting tables or other knowledge sources.

docs.title: Need a direct SQL connection?
docs.text: A custom Foundry tool needs a service that enforces caller authorization, read-only database permissions, allowlisted data access, bounded execution time/result size and audit logging. Native Foundry tools or a Toolbox connection do not automatically add that service to the hosted maf_lite code. This path requires implementation and end-to-end security validation.

docs.title: Deployment choices
docs.text:
Deployment design covers network ownership, deployment tooling and resource selection. It is separate from whether a runbook stops at infrastructure or also deploys application code.

How it works introduces the concepts and input formats. This page explains design choices, not their execution order. Deploy infra only and Deploy full stack are the deployment runbooks; Sizing and capacity and Cost planning cover capacity and spending.

docs.title: Network and gateway design
docs.text:
An Azure virtual network (VNet) contains private address ranges and subnets, smaller ranges assigned to services. Domain Name System (DNS) resolution turns a service hostname into an IP address. A hub is a shared network; a spoke is a workload network connected to it. Peering connects VNets, while routes determine where traffic goes. Egress means outbound traffic. A NAT gateway translates private outbound addresses to a public address.

For production and workloads with sensitive data, choose a private network, whether standalone or connected to an existing hub. Set NETWORK_ISOLATION=true explicitly: the template currently defaults to false. Standalone describes who manages the network; it does not mean the services should be public.

Use public service endpoints only for approved, short-lived evaluations or demonstrations without sensitive data. Authentication remains required, but does not provide private network access.

Choice Purpose Configuration and dependencies Standalone (default network ownership) The workload team owns its network, DNS and operations, without a platform hub dependency. DEPLOYMENT_MODE=standalone and NETWORK_ISOLATION=true for private networking. Plan outbound access, private DNS and a connected deployment host. Hub integration A platform team owns shared connectivity, firewall, DNS or monitoring. DEPLOYMENT_MODE=ailz-integrated plus explicit isolation, peering, routing, DNS and reuse inputs. Spoke resources can be omitted where the hub supplies them. AI Gateway Multiple workloads need centrally governed model access, such as routing, authentication or token policies. The separate AI Gateway implementation has its own endpoint, authentication, supported APIs, policies and network requirements. Agent Bicep does not deploy or connect it automatically.

AI Gateway governs model access and can accompany either network topology. Workload connectivity and user/document authorization remain separate requirements. Application Gateway serves a different purpose: optional web application firewall (WAF) protection for access to the web UI.

Hub integration needs agreement with the platform team on:

  • Routes and peering: owners for both directions and a hub ID in HUB_INTEGRATION_HUB_VNET_RESOURCE_ID. Egress uses either HUB_INTEGRATION_EGRESS_NEXT_HOP_IP or HUB_INTEGRATION_EXISTING_ROUTE_TABLE_RESOURCE_ID, not both, with matching return routes and gateway-transit settings.
  • Spoke resources: DEPLOY_AZURE_FIREWALL, DEPLOY_BASTION and DEPLOY_NAT_GATEWAY can be disabled where the hub supplies those services under agreed ownership.
  • DNS: template-owned zones, supported EXISTING_PRIVATE_DNS_ZONE_*_RESOURCE_ID inputs, or POLICY_MANAGED_PRIVATE_DNS=true. Policy-managed DNS and bring-your-own (BYO) zone IDs are alternative modes. Zone owners must supply the required links/forwarding; peering alone does not propagate DNS.
  • Runner: the host that executes deployment commands needs private connectivity and service DNS resolution. This connection is required separately from the private Azure Container Registry (ACR) pool used for image builds. The registry stores those images.

See Network isolation for connectivity requirements and hub-and-spoke design for supported network settings.

docs.title: Deployment tooling
docs.text:
Azure role-based access control (RBAC) grants an identity a role at a resource scope. Deployment roles can differ from application data-access roles.

Tool Available path Boundary to understand Bicep with azd (default) Deploy infra only or Deploy full stack. The Agent Application workflow includes parameter composition, service configuration, RBAC and hosted image preparation. Deployment uses the platform's own infra/, not a separate upstream checkout. Terraform Terraform overview. Infrastructure building blocks, not parity with the Agent platform lifecycle. terraform apply does not deploy/configure the Agent Application. Security settings and state need separate review and protection. Azure portal Portal overview. ARM-based infrastructure with its own defaults and platform-integration behavior. It can create placeholder application resources; it does not execute Agent platform hooks or the hosted image/version workflow.

The Deploy infra only runbook provisions the platform's foundation without building or deploying application images. Different implementations are not interchangeable owners of the same environment; resource reuse needs explicit state and dependency ownership.

docs.title: Resource group ownership
docs.text:
New Agent environments default to three workload resource groups. The resource group destinations separate application, Foundry/grounding and workload networking ownership, with one, two or three distinct groups in the same subscription. This is an Agent Bicep/azd contract, not a Terraform or portal parity claim. Existing environments retain their destination mapping. Network isolation and hub/BYO integration remain separate decisions.

Agree names, owners, scoped deployment/RBAC/data permissions and retention before a new deployment. Prefer pre-created groups when the deploying identity must not create groups at subscription scope, and set CREATE_RESOURCE_GROUPS=false. New environments otherwise create missing additional groups by default. One root provisioning workflow coordinates the groups; three independent manual deployments are not required. Existing-environment migration and automatic deletion of shared groups are outside this feature.

docs.title: Resource selection and reuse
docs.text:
The selected application's definition and generated infra/main.parameters.json describe the resolved resources. The default is hosted-no-panel, with maf_lite orchestration and native Foundry IQ Blob ingestion.

Resource family Selection or reuse decision Agent Application hosts and stores Fresh environments use DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGY=hosted-no-panel: hosted orchestrator, frontend, no panel and no Agent Application Cosmos DB. Agent hosting explains this layout's capabilities and limits. Existing selections are retained unless explicitly changed. Agent App Ingestion DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP=false is the fresh default for native Blob ingestion. The optional component supports custom processing and conversation uploads; Ingestion describes those requirements and independently populated indexes. Omitting the component leaves existing resources and grants in place. Search, Storage and Foundry agent backing services Agent Application Search/Storage and Agent Service backing resources are separate. Where enabled and not reused, Agent Service can add another Search, Storage and Cosmos DB. Native parameters aiSearchResourceId, aiFoundryStorageAccountResourceId and aiFoundryCosmosDBAccountResourceId reuse a dedicated backing trio for the same Foundry instance, not arbitrary shared workload stores. Network and access infrastructure USE_EXISTING_VNET=true requires EXISTING_VNET_RESOURCE_ID and agreed subnet/delegation ownership for DEPLOY_SUBNETS. Supported jumpbox, Bastion and NAT reuse have their own EXISTING_* inputs. Existing VNet peerings are externally managed. Monitoring Supported existing Log Analytics/Application Insights inputs require workspace compatibility, owner agreement and the intended private monitoring path. Mixing sources is not a substitute for those requirements. Optional add-ons Speech, Bing grounding and public ingress require explicit selection. Disabling a service is not a reuse mechanism and can break its consumers.

The Foundry backing IDs above are native root main.parameters.json parameters, not automatically mapped azd environment variables. See Deployment settings for mapped inputs and the shared inventory for broader resource detail. DEPLOY_AAF_AGENT_SVC is required by the default Foundry hosting path, not an optional resource-count reduction.

docs.title: Deployment readiness
docs.text:
A deployment plan identifies the platform Git commit or release tag, selected application, topology, enabled/reused services, regions and naming inputs. A Git commit identifies the exact code; the manifest records the compatible component code. The environment also records the selected application definition, as explained in How it works.

Readiness includes regional service/model quota, supported host capabilities and resource-creation permissions. Role assignment needs additional scoped permissions; Contributor alone is insufficient. Hosted authoring needs project data-plane access. Hub and DNS access requires approval from the resource owners.

Private deployments additionally require working runner DNS and routes. Transport Layer Security (TLS) encrypts connections and verifies service certificates. Native Blob shared links need administrator approval. Sign-in and retrieval validation includes both allowed and denied users, not only endpoint access. The runbooks include these checks, the deployment preview and the execution sequence for the reviewed capacity and cost plan.

docs.title: Deploy via portal
docs.text:
The AI Landing Zone portal wizard creates Azure infrastructure. It does not run the Agent Landing Zone application lifecycle or deploy the supplied Agent Application.

The portal deployment guide describes that separate infrastructure workflow. Its options and defaults are specific to the portal templates, not to the Agent Landing Zone runbooks.

For the Agent Application, the Deploy full stack runbook contains the complete procedure, including service configuration, hosted agent image preparation and application deployment.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Connect a deployment host or developer workstation to an isolated Agent Landing Zone using a point-to-site (P2S) VPN. The result is private DNS resolution and HTTPS access to the workload services from that computer. Once connected, you can run deployment hooks or development tools directly; Bastion and a jumpbox are not required for this path.

docs.title: What you'll have after this runbook
docs.text:
Your computer connected to the private VNet through a VPN, without Bastion or a jumpbox.

The figure shows a standalone gateway. An approved hub VPN can provide the same access with the appropriate peering, gateway transit, client routes and DNS.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
Use this runbook when a workstation must reach private workload endpoints without using a jumpbox. Reuse an approved corporate VPN when available; create a new gateway only with the network owner's approval.

The foundation creates private endpoints and DNS zones when isolation is enabled. It does not create a VPN gateway, configure P2S authentication, issue certificates, distribute client profiles or create a DNS Private Resolver. These tasks need network administration outside azd.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Use the reviewed platform checkout, intended azd environment and approved inputs from the Deploy full stack runbook. This procedure does not change the hosted orchestrator topology or Foundry IQ configuration.
  • Arrange network permissions at the gateway, VNet, peering and DNS scopes. The network administrator needs permission to create or update those resources; a developer connecting an approved VPN does not need those deployment permissions.
  • Agree on nonoverlapping address ranges for the VNet, peered networks, P2S client pool and workstation's local network.
  • Have a supported VPN client and either an approved client certificate or an authorized Microsoft Entra account. VPN authentication is separate from Azure CLI, azd and application authentication.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text: Run azd commands from the reviewed platform root with the intended environment selected. Record any existing gateway, peering, route and DNS settings before changing them, and identify which changes affect other users.

docs.title: 1. Select the private network
docs.text:
The following deployment inputs control workload isolation and hub connectivity. Set them in the selected azd environment with azd env set; see How it works for input processing. For a new isolated environment, enable isolation before provisioning:

azd env set NETWORK_ISOLATION true

Keep parameters.allowedIpRanges.value empty in main.parameters.json for the default private-only workload service posture. Do not enable public access to make the VPN work. See Network isolation for the separate control-plane, telemetry and optional ingress boundaries.

Choose one network path:

Path Foundation inputs and network work Standalone VNet Keep DEPLOYMENT_MODE=standalone. The administrator adds a route-based Azure VPN Gateway and P2S configuration to the target VNet separately. Existing hub VPN Set DEPLOYMENT_MODE=ailz-integrated and HUB_INTEGRATION_HUB_VNET_RESOURCE_ID to the hub's full ARM resource ID. Reuse its approved gateway, P2S policy and DNS path, and configure gateway transit and client routes as described below.

For a newly created spoke using a hub-owned gateway, the shipped inputs are:

azd env set DEPLOYMENT_MODE ailz-integrated
azd env set HUB_INTEGRATION_HUB_VNET_RESOURCE_ID <hub-vnet-resource-id>
azd env set HUB_INTEGRATION_CREATE_HUB_PEERING true
azd env set HUB_INTEGRATION_PEERING_USE_REMOTE_GATEWAYS true
azd env set HUB_INTEGRATION_PEERING_ALLOW_GATEWAY_TRANSIT false

These flags configure the spoke-to-hub peering. The hub administrator must create/configure the reverse hub-to-spoke peering with gateway transit allowed, and confirm the hub gateway exists before applying the spoke inputs. The template does not configure that reverse peering.

Do not set the spoke's ALLOW_GATEWAY_TRANSIT flag to true to share a hub-owned gateway. For an existing VNet (USE_EXISTING_VNET=true with EXISTING_VNET_RESOURCE_ID), have the network owner configure both peering directions separately.

Preserve approved egress routing through HUB_INTEGRATION_EGRESS_NEXT_HOP_IP or HUB_INTEGRATION_EXISTING_ROUTE_TABLE_RESOURCE_ID where required. These do not configure P2S client routes or authentication. Use the network reference for other reuse inputs.

For a fresh VPN-only deployment, you may explicitly set DEPLOY_JUMPBOX=false and DEPLOY_BASTION=false before provisioning. They otherwise default on for isolation. Verify the VPN before removing an existing access path.

Provision using the Deploy infra only runbook. If the VPN cannot exist until the VNet is provisioned, use that runbook's deferred post-provision procedure, then return here. Deferral leaves application setup incomplete and does not bypass earlier private-access checks.

docs.title: 2. Configure the gateway and authentication
docs.text:
For an existing hub VPN, ask its administrator for an approved client profile and continue to step 3. For a new gateway, follow Microsoft's P2S certificate setup or P2S Microsoft Entra setup:

  1. Identify the target VNet from the provisioned environment: azd env get-value VNET_RESOURCE_ID. This is a resource ID, not a VPN server address. Create a route-based VPN gateway with a supported SKU and a subnet named exactly GatewaySubnet. The foundation reserves 192.168.2.192/26 by default; verify the selected range against the sizing in the Microsoft procedure. Do not attach an NSG, default-route UDR or delegation to GatewaySubnet. Record ownership of the gateway and subnet with the network team before subsequent foundation provisioning.
  2. In the gateway's Settings > Point-to-site configuration, select Configure now for a new configuration and enter the approved client address pool. Choose the tunnel/authentication combination for your clients:
    • Certificate: upload the public root certificate data; generate and install a client certificate signed by that root on each authorized computer. Use a unique certificate per device so one device can be revoked without replacing every client's certificate. Protect private keys and PFX passwords; do not put them in source control, command history or the root-certificate upload field.
    • Microsoft Entra ID: use OpenVPN (SSL) and Azure VPN Client. Enter the tenant, audience and issuer values from the current Microsoft procedure for your Azure cloud. Prefer its Microsoft-registered audience and follow its registration and consent requirements. Use a currently supported Windows or macOS client. For Linux, select a supported certificate/client combination from the Microsoft procedure.
  3. Save the configuration, then select Download VPN client. This generates a configuration package, not the client application. Install the supported client and import the profile using the matching Microsoft instructions.

The gateway administrator controls admission to the VPN. Confirm the approved certificate or Entra access policy before distributing client profiles.

docs.title: 3. Connect DNS and routes
docs.text:
The VPN client needs routes to the workload's private endpoint addresses and a DNS server that can resolve its private zones.

  1. Provide a reachable DNS path: an existing hub DNS forwarder, or a separately deployed Azure DNS Private Resolver inbound endpoint. Ensure the private zones are linked to the resolver/forwarder's VNet, or reachable through its approved forwarding design. A spoke zone link alone does not make a hub resolver aware of the zone. See private endpoint DNS integration for the zone-link and forwarding pattern.
  2. Configure the VPN client DNS settings, or the corporate DNS conditional forwarders used by that client, to use that path. Permit UDP and TCP 53 to the resolver. Do not point remote clients directly at Azure's 168.63.129.16 virtual DNS address or use hosts-file entries as the solution. Use Microsoft's Azure VPN Client DNS configuration when distributing custom DNS settings in its profile.
  3. Confirm the VPN profile includes the destination VNet/spoke routes and the resolver's network. Check the return path to the P2S pool and any intervening firewall, NSGs and route tables. For a hub VPN, verify traffic can return from the workload to the client through the approved hub route. Follow Microsoft's P2S routing guidance for your OS and peering topology; peering is not generally transitive.
  4. Connect the VPN. On Windows, inspect route print and, for Azure VPN Client, its connection details. For Entra connections, inspect Get-DnsClientNrptPolicy rather than relying on ipconfig /all to show the VPN DNS servers. After peering, route or DNS changes, regenerate and reimport the client profile as required and reconnect.

ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY=true only enables the proxy on a deployed isolated spoke firewall. It does not configure VPN client DNS, link missing zones or create a resolver. Leave it unchanged unless the approved DNS design uses it.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Run these checks on each deployment host and developer workstation, not only on a VM in Azure. Select the intended environment and refresh outputs if needed; refresh does not provision or complete configuration.

The shipped outputs include APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT, KEY_VAULT_URI, AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT, AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_ENDPOINT and, for the selected Foundry IQ/Search deployment, KNOWLEDGE_BASE_ENDPOINT. Use each nonempty value's hostname, not the resource ID or a private IP. The registry output is a login-server hostname; URL outputs include https:// and can include a path.

For example, in PowerShell:

$endpoint = azd env get-value APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT
$serviceHost = ([uri]$endpoint).DnsSafeHost
nslookup $serviceHost
[System.Net.Dns]::GetHostAddresses($serviceHost)
Test-NetConnection $serviceHost -Port 443
curl.exe --verbose --output NUL "https://$serviceHost/"

Expected results:

  • The operating system resolver returns only the intended private IPv4 addresses. Windows Name Resolution Policy Table (NRPT) rules can make nslookup differ. If it does, inspect Get-DnsClientNrptPolicy and query the VPN's intended DNS server directly with nslookup <hostname> <dns-server-ip>. Resolve the difference before accepting the host's DNS path.
  • TcpTestSucceeded is True, and TLS completes with normal certificate validation. A service HTTP 401 or 403 response confirms reachability; test service operations with the authorized identity separately. Do not use --insecure.

Repeat for the required service hosts. For the registry, assign its AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_ENDPOINT value directly to $serviceHost rather than parsing it as a URL. Keep their original hostnames for TLS; do not replace application endpoints with IP addresses or privatelink aliases.

The lifecycle prerequisite check rejects public or mixed DNS answers and checks TCP/TLS reachability: App Configuration before post-provision and deployment, the Foundry project additionally before hosted deployment, and ACR before hosted image builds. Test the remaining service hosts individually.

docs.title: After validation: deploy or develop
docs.text:
• Deployment host: authenticate Azure CLI and azd with the approved deployment identity. Complete deferred post-provision using the Deploy infra only runbook, then continue the Deploy full stack runbook for hosted image preparation and application deployment. RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX=true requests connectivity checks; despite its name, it works from a VPN-connected host and does not require a jumpbox. Keep the private ACR Task pool for hosted image preparation; the pool is not a VPN endpoint or deployment workstation.
  • Developer workstation: keep the VPN connected while using private Azure endpoints. Authenticate development tools separately and use the approved project and service roles. Local application development guidance belongs in Custom applications. Hosted agents continue to run in Foundry.

Configure service RBAC and document permissions separately from network access. Preserve application authentication, OBO and source access-control lists. For hosted-agent authoring, verify the runner's Foundry User role on the exact project and account read access as described in Network isolation. Do not grant Owner to solve a data-plane denial.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check first Tunnel will not connect Client/tunnel compatibility, certificate validity or Entra policy, and the gateway's current profile. Tunnel connects; names resolve publicly Client DNS/NRPT, conditional forwarders and private-zone links to the resolver VNet. Do not enable public service access. Private DNS works; TCP 443 fails Overlapping local ranges, missing spoke routes, reverse peering/transit, return route to the P2S pool, NSGs and firewalls. TLS fails Original hostname, client trust and any approved inspection path. Do not disable certificate validation. HTTP 401/403 after successful TLS Correct tenant, token audience and scoped service roles. Check authorization separately from connectivity.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
1. Disconnect the VPN on the affected workstation. Restore its previous approved DNS and route/profile configuration if changed, then confirm normal corporate connectivity. Keep an existing administrative access path available.
  2. To revoke newly granted access, have the gateway administrator use the approved certificate-revocation or Entra access policy process. Deleting a local profile does not revoke credentials. Remove pilot profiles and device certificates only after recording which credential was revoked.
  3. Have the network owner review the recorded changes and restore only the pilot-specific peering, route or DNS settings that are no longer needed. Verify existing consumers still resolve and reach their services.
  4. If a dedicated gateway was created only for this pilot, authorize its itemized retirement with the network owner after checking dependencies. Do not delete a shared hub gateway, resolver, private DNS zone or workload private endpoint. Keep workload isolation and application authentication unchanged.

docs.title: Publish to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot
Objective
docs.text:
Publish an agent already hosted in Microsoft Foundry to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Start with a tested agent in a private-network Foundry project, then use its endpoint, identity and version throughout this runbook. The agent can be part of your own application.

You will create a Bot Service resource, enable channel access and publish the agent's app listing. These are manual post-deployment tasks; the landing zone template does not perform them.

docs.title: What you'll have after this runbook
docs.text:
Your existing Foundry agent available in Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, with authenticated messages delivered through Azure Bot Service.

This channel path is not private end to end

Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot deliver messages to a public HTTPS Activity endpoint, restricted to Microsoft channel source IPs and requiring authentication. They do not use the Foundry private endpoint.

If your organization requires no public agent ingress, do not use this publication path.

The dashed path is for publication setup and later changes, not for Teams conversations.

The Bot Service box represents Microsoft's managed channel service, not a bot hosted inside your VNet. Its resource uses publicNetworkAccess: Disabled, as Microsoft's Foundry publishing procedure prescribes. That resource setting does not make Teams/M365 delivery private: the channel service calls the public Foundry Activity route shown above.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
Use this runbook after the hosted agent works and you need Teams or Microsoft 365 Copilot distribution while Foundry public network access remains disabled. For a Copilot Studio private relay instead, use Connect Copilot Studio.

Microsoft calls this a source IP-filtered Activity Protocol public endpoint: a public endpoint for the messaging route, restricted by the source IP addresses of Microsoft's channel services. See the Foundry REST publishing flow.

Step 3 sets activity.enable_m365_public_endpoint=true to enable that specific exception. Foundry and Bot Service keep public network access (PNA) disabled; management APIs and other agent protocols remain private.

Path Network access Bot Service to the Activity endpoint Public HTTPS, with Microsoft-managed source IP filtering and authentication. Not Private Link. Connected workstation to the Foundry project API Private endpoint, for publication setup and later changes.

Microsoft manages the allowed source ranges. You do not open public ingress on your VNet. An allowed source IP still needs valid authentication and authorization; public does not mean anonymous.

During setup, your connected workstation calls the Foundry project API through the private endpoint to read the agent configuration, enable Activity and select the tested version. The private endpoint carries those requests; it is not the resource you are configuring.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Agent: Have a working hosted agent in a Foundry project, with its own agent identity, a stable endpoint and a version you have tested. If you still need to deploy an application, start with the Deploy full stack runbook or Custom applications, then return here.
  • Network access: Run the commands from a VNet-connected host that resolves and reaches the Foundry project's private endpoint. This procedure requires Foundry PNA to be disabled. For a project with public access enabled, use the Foundry portal publishing procedure.
  • Tools: Install Azure CLI, Bicep CLI and PowerShell 7.4 or later. Run Steps 1-4 in the same PowerShell session; later blocks use variables set by earlier ones.
  • Azure permissions: You need Foundry User on the project, plus Azure Bot Service Contributor Role and permission to create deployments in the target resource group. Resource-group Contributor covers both bot creation and deployment. A subscription administrator must register Microsoft.BotService if it is not already registered.
  • Microsoft 365 access: Use member accounts in the same tenant as Foundry, with access to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot and app policies that allow the agent. Guest accounts cannot call these agents. Tenant-wide publication needs approval from a Microsoft 365 administrator.

Licensing and costs
