To use the agent in Microsoft Copilot Chat, users need an eligible Microsoft 365 subscription. The Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on is optional:

  • With the add-on: No additional Microsoft 365 usage charge for using this agent.
  • Without the add-on: Access to shared tenant data, such as SharePoint or Copilot connectors, can incur usage-based charges in Copilot Credits.

In both cases, Azure costs are separate: the license does not cover Foundry model usage, agent hosting or other Azure services. See licensing and costs for custom engine agents.

Approve the data flow first

Obtain your organization's approval before sending data through this channel. Microsoft 365 processes publishing metadata and conversations under its own compliance and data-residency commitments. Validate how the agent authenticates users and enforces data permissions in both Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot before rollout.

The Agent Application's default hosted runtime has a protected-retrieval integration gap described in the Deploy full stack runbook. Channel publication does not resolve it or prove per-user document authorization.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text: Complete Steps 1-4 in order, then run all client and configuration checks under Validation. Keep the backup and publication results for rollback.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the agent and save its configuration
docs.text:
In the Azure portal, collect the subscription ID, resource group name, Foundry resource name and project name. Then open the agent in Foundry and record its name and tested version. Use these values for the agent you want to publish.

Expand the block below, replace every placeholder and run it on the connected host. The commands check the agent's identity and save its configuration before you change it. Keep Shared for the initial pilot. Tenant-wide access requires the separate approval described below before enabling it.

PowerShell: select the target and save a backup 
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true

$subscriptionId = "<subscription-id>"
$resourceGroup = "<foundry-resource-group>"
$foundryName = "<foundry-resource-name>"
$projectName = "<foundry-project-name>"
$agentName = "<agent-name>"
$agentVersion = "<tested-agent-version>"
$botName = "<globally-unique-bot-name>"
$publishScope = "Shared"

az login
az account set --subscription $subscriptionId
$tenantId = az account show --query tenantId --output tsv
az account show --query "{subscription:id,tenant:tenantId}" --output table

$pna = az cognitiveservices account show --name $foundryName `
    --resource-group $resourceGroup --query properties.publicNetworkAccess --output tsv
if ($pna -ne "Disabled") { throw "This runbook requires Foundry PNA Disabled." }

$work = Join-Path $HOME ("teams-publication-" + (Get-Date -Format "yyyyMMdd-HHmmss"))
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $work | Out-Null
Set-Location $work

$projectEndpoint = "https://$foundryName.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/$projectName"
$agentUri = "$projectEndpoint/agents/$([uri]::EscapeDataString($agentName))"
$token = az account get-access-token --resource https://ai.azure.com `
    --query accessToken --output tsv
$headers = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $token" }
Remove-Variable token

$agent = (Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers).Content | ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable
if (-not $agent.instance_identity.client_id -or -not $agent.agent_endpoint) {
    throw "The agent needs a unique identity and stable endpoint. Stop before publishing."
}
$agent | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 100 | Set-Content agent-before.json
@{
    subscriptionId = $subscriptionId
    tenantId = $tenantId
    resourceGroup = $resourceGroup
    foundryName = $foundryName
    agentUri = $agentUri
    botName = $botName
} | ConvertTo-Json | Set-Content target.json
$agent.agent_endpoint | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 100
"Working folder: $work"

Expected result: The commands complete without errors and display the intended tenant and subscription, the endpoint configuration and a working-folder path. Record that path. Keep target.json and agent-before.json in that folder, outside source control; neither file contains the bearer token.

Before continuing, choose who can use the agent. The block starts with $publishScope = "Shared", which is the recommended pilot scope. Your choice controls both catalog visibility and permission to call the agent:

$publishScope Who can call the agent Store visibility Shared Only identities with the required Foundry permissions can invoke it, through BotServiceRbac. The publisher finds it under Your agents and can share the link with authorized testers. Publishing approval is not required. Tenant Everyone in the Foundry tenant can invoke it, through BotServiceTenant. It appears under Built by your org after Microsoft 365 admin approval.

For tenant-wide distribution, set $publishScope = "Tenant" in the same session before Step 3, and only after your organization approves that access. For a Shared pilot, ask an administrator to grant selected testers Foundry Agent Consumer at the agent scope. Grant this access before sharing the app link.

If the agent identity check fails

Stop and have the agent owner supply a supported agent identity and stable endpoint before retrying this runbook. Bot Service needs the agent identity's client ID (instance_identity.client_id), not the project's managed identity or an application registration belonging to another client.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the bot and Teams channel
docs.text:
Complete the three sections below in order. This creates a separate Bot Service resource and its Teams channel; the same channel also serves Microsoft 365 Copilot. You do not need to add a bot runtime or modify the landing zone template.

1. Check Bot Service provider registration

Run this command in the PowerShell session from Step 1:

az provider show --namespace Microsoft.BotService --query registrationState --output tsv

Expected result: The provider state is Registered. If it is not, ask a subscription administrator to run az provider register --namespace Microsoft.BotService --wait, then check again. Do not deploy the bot until registration is complete.

2. Save bot-service.bicep in the working folder

Create a file named bot-service.bicep in the $work folder created in Step 1, and paste the following template into it:

param botName string
param displayName string
param msaAppId string
param tenantId string
param endpoint string

resource bot 'Microsoft.BotService/botServices@2022-09-15' = {
  name: botName
  kind: 'azurebot'
  location: 'global'
  sku: {
    name: 'F0'
  }
  properties: {
    displayName: displayName
    endpoint: endpoint
    msaAppId: msaAppId
    msaAppTenantId: tenantId
    msaAppType: 'SingleTenant'
    publicNetworkAccess: 'Disabled'
  }
}

resource teams 'Microsoft.BotService/botServices/channels@2021-03-01' = {
  parent: bot
  name: 'MsTeamsChannel'
  location: 'global'
  properties: {
    channelName: 'MsTeamsChannel'
  }
}
3. Deploy the bot and verify its network setting

Replace <agent-display-name> with the name users should see. Run the commands from $work to deploy the saved template into the Foundry resource group.

$displayName = "<agent-display-name>"
$activityEndpoint = "$agentUri/endpoint/protocols/activityProtocol"

az deployment group create --resource-group $resourceGroup `
    --name "teams-bot" --template-file bot-service.bicep `
    --parameters botName=$botName displayName="$displayName" `
        msaAppId=$($agent.instance_identity.client_id) tenantId=$tenantId `
        endpoint=$activityEndpoint --output none

$botServiceId = az bot show --name $botName --resource-group $resourceGroup `
    --query id --output tsv
az resource show --ids $botServiceId --api-version 2022-09-15 `
    --query "properties.{endpoint:endpoint,pna:publicNetworkAccess}" --output json

Expected result: The bot's endpoint matches the agent's activityProtocol URL, and its network setting is "pna": "Disabled". The bot uses the agent's identity; you do not need a client secret, public VNet ingress or a custom connector.

docs.title: Step 3: Enable the source-IP-filtered public Activity route
docs.text:
Run the block below to enable the public HTTPS Activity exception, apply the Bot Service authorization scheme for your chosen audience and send traffic to the tested agent version. The block reads the current configuration so it can preserve the existing protocols and non-Bot authorization schemes. It also checks for Foundry's default Entra authorization. If you changed that configuration, review the endpoint authorization settings before proceeding.

Preserve access for existing consumers

The API replaces the submitted protocol configuration and authorization array. Keep the protocols and authorization schemes your agent already uses, such as responses, invocations and Entra. Removing them can break other clients. Pinning the version also affects all consumers of the stable endpoint, not just Teams and Copilot. Avoid concurrent agent configuration changes.

PowerShell: enable Activity and pin the tested version 
if ($publishScope -notin @("Shared", "Tenant")) { throw "Choose Shared or Tenant." }
$agent = (Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers).Content | ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable
$protocols = $agent.agent_endpoint.protocol_configuration
if (-not $protocols) { throw "Review the agent's existing protocols before continuing." }
$activity = $protocols.activity
if (-not $activity) { $activity = @{} }
$activity.enable_m365_public_endpoint = $true
$protocols.activity = $activity

$botScheme = if ($publishScope -eq "Tenant") { "BotServiceTenant" } else { "BotServiceRbac" }
$schemes = @($agent.agent_endpoint.authorization_schemes |
    Where-Object { $_.type -notin @("BotServiceRbac", "BotServiceTenant") })
$schemes += @{ type = $botScheme }
if ("Entra" -notin $schemes.type) { throw "Review missing Entra authorization before continuing." }

$patch = @{
    agent_endpoint = @{
        protocol_configuration = $protocols
        authorization_schemes = $schemes
        version_selector = @{
            version_selection_rules = @(
                @{ type = "FixedRatio"; agent_version = $agentVersion; traffic_percentage = 100 }
            )
        }
    }
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 100

Invoke-RestMethod -Method Patch -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/merge-patch+json" -Body $patch |
    Out-Null

Expected result: The update completes without errors and prints no output. You will check the final configuration under Validation.

docs.title: Step 4: Publish the app
docs.text:
This step submits the listing directly to the catalogs. If your organization requires package review before submission, use the REST package-download procedure rather than publishing directly.

Replace the placeholders below with approved listing details, including your organization's HTTPS website, privacy statement and terms of use. These details are visible to users; do not include secrets or sensitive information.

PowerShell: publish to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot 
$publishRequest = @{
    agentDisplayName = $displayName
    botServiceArmId = $botServiceId
    publishScope = $publishScope
    publishAsAutopilot = $false
    appVersion = "1.0.0"
    shortDescription = "<short-description>"
    fullDescription = "<full-description>"
    developerName = "<organization-name>"
    developerWebsiteUrl = "https://<organization-domain>"
    privacyUrl = "https://<organization-domain>/privacy"
    termsOfUseUrl = "https://<organization-domain>/terms"
}
$body = $publishRequest | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10
$body | Set-Content publish-request.json
$result = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
    -Uri "${agentUri}/microsoft365/publish?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
$result | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Set-Content publish-result.json
$result

Expected result: The response contains titleId. If you selected Tenant, ask a Microsoft 365 administrator to approve the request in Microsoft 365 admin center > Agents > Requests. Approval is required before tenant-wide discovery, and app policies can still restrict availability.

App version versus agent version

appVersion is the version of the store listing. Increase it when you republish metadata or change publication scope. $agentVersion selects the running agent version; changing that version does not require republishing the listing.

Optional: inspect a copy of the published app package

To inspect or retain the package after direct publication, run this block in the same session. It reuses the publication request:

Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "${agentUri}/microsoft365/zip?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -OutFile appPackage.zip

Extract the ZIP and review its manifest and icons with the package inspection checklist. Keep the generated IDs and agent sections unchanged.

The download call does not submit the app to the catalogs, but it can update the agent's publishing configuration and requires agent write permission. Downloading this copy does not require uploading it again.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Returning later or using a new PowerShell session?

Use this block only to resume verification or maintenance after the bot has been created. Run it on the connected host, replacing <saved-working-folder> with the path recorded in Step 1. It restores the connection variables and gets a fresh token without recreating the bot or republishing the app.

$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true
Set-Location "<saved-working-folder>"
$target = Get-Content target.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable
$resourceGroup = $target.resourceGroup
$foundryName = $target.foundryName
$agentUri = $target.agentUri

az login --tenant $target.tenantId
az account set --subscription $target.subscriptionId
$token = az account get-access-token --resource https://ai.azure.com `
    --query accessToken --output tsv
$headers = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $token" }
Remove-Variable token
$botServiceId = az bot show --name $target.botName --resource-group $resourceGroup `
    --query id --output tsv

After publication, open the agent in both clients. For Shared, sign in with the publishing account. For Tenant, wait for admin approval and find the agent under Built by your org.

Client Open the agent Teams Open Apps, find the agent, add it and open its chat. Microsoft 365 Copilot Open the Agents area, find the agent in the agent store and add it. For Shared, look under Your agents.

Complete these checks in each client before making the agent available to users:

  1. Complete any sign-in prompt. Send a greeting, a representative workload question and a follow-up. Confirm that the answers use the expected tools and knowledge sources.
  2. For a Shared pilot, test with an authorized user and a tenant member who lacks agent permission. The second user must be denied. Use member accounts, not guests. With Tenant, all tenant members are authorized to call the agent; test protected-data restrictions separately as described next.
  3. If the agent handles protected data, test with identities that should and should not access that data. Confirm the intended restrictions in both clients, regardless of publication scope.

Then return to the connected host and run the final configuration check:

PowerShell: verify the endpoint and both PNA settings 
$after = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" -Headers $headers
$after.agent_endpoint | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 30
az cognitiveservices account show --name $foundryName --resource-group $resourceGroup `
    --query properties.publicNetworkAccess --output tsv
az resource show --ids $botServiceId --api-version 2022-09-15 `
    --query properties.publicNetworkAccess --output tsv

Expected result: The tested version receives 100% of traffic. The original protocols and Entra authorization are preserved, activity.enable_m365_public_endpoint is true, and the Bot Service scheme matches your publication scope. Both PNA values must remain Disabled.

Channel limitations

Published agents do not support streaming responses or citations. File uploads and image generation are not supported in Microsoft 365 Copilot, although they are available in Teams. Test the capabilities your agent uses in each client and review the Foundry publishing limitations before rollout.

Channel support does not add upload or image-generation handlers to the supplied Agent Application. Its images and voice contract and protected-retrieval integration gate still apply.

docs.title: Update or stop publication
docs.text:
Use the following actions to maintain the published agent. If your PowerShell session ended or its token expired, resume the session before running the maintenance commands.

Task Action Release a new runtime version Test the version, then follow the REST API tab in the active-version instructions from the connected host. Keep the existing bot and listing. Roll back agent behavior Use the same REST instructions to select the previous tested version. This changes the version for every consumer of the stable endpoint. Change the listing name, descriptions or URLs Edit publish-request.json, increase appVersion and run Update listing metadata below. Keep botServiceArmId and publishScope unchanged for a metadata-only update. Check publication after redeployment Recheck the active version, Activity exception and authorization, then repeat Validation. The landing zone template does not manage this manual configuration. Update listing metadata

Open publish-request.json in the saved working folder. Update the listing details, increase appVersion and review the entire request before running the block below. A Tenant update can require renewed admin approval.

$body = Get-Content publish-request.json -Raw
$result = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
    -Uri "${agentUri}/microsoft365/publish?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
$result | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Set-Content publish-result.json
$result

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom What to check or do A project GET or PATCH fails or times out. Check private DNS and connectivity, the selected tenant, the Foundry User role and the token audience (https://ai.azure.com). If the token expired, resume the session. Do not enable PNA to bypass the error. The bot deployment is denied. Check Microsoft.BotService registration, bot and deployment permissions, and any Azure Policy denial. The agent is missing from either client. Check the signed-in account, publication scope, admin approval and app policies. Refresh the store or sign out and back in; catalog caching can delay discovery. Activity returns 403 NetworkAccessDenied. Check that the Activity exception is enabled and test through Teams or Copilot. A public curl request from an arbitrary IP remains blocked by design. A user can open the app but receives an authorization error. Check that the user is signed in to the Foundry tenant and, for Shared, has Foundry Agent Consumer access. Do not switch to Tenant just to remove the error. The Teams sign-in card opens, but its redirect page does not load. Ask the network administrator to allow outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) to *.azureml.ms from the user's network, then retry sign-in. The agent replies, but tools or retrieval fail. Check runtime identity permissions, data authorization and outbound access. Trace the failing request through Teams or Copilot to verify identity propagation in that client. A conversation is stuck or returns no tool output found. In Teams, send /foundry_new_preview; in Copilot, start a new chat with the agent. Previous conversation context cannot be restored after a reset. Publication returns version already exists. Increase appVersion and submit the listing again. Do not change the runtime version to fix a listing-version error.

For other errors, use Foundry publishing troubleshooting and published-agent authorization.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
1. For a runtime-only regression, select the previous tested version using the active-version REST instructions. This affects every consumer of the stable endpoint. Repeat Validation before reopening access.
  2. To withdraw the newly introduced publication, disable the Activity exception using the block below, then ask the Microsoft 365 administrator to block or remove its listing from both catalogs. If other approved channel consumers already use this exception, coordinate withdrawal rather than interrupting their access.

To stop channel access from both clients, run the block below. It disables only the public Activity exception, leaving the other endpoint protocols and their private access unchanged. Keep Foundry PNA disabled.

Stop Teams and Copilot access

The commands read the current protocol configuration and change only the Activity exception:

$current = (Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers).Content | ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable
$protocols = $current.agent_endpoint.protocol_configuration
if (-not $protocols.activity) { throw "No Activity configuration found; review the endpoint." }
$protocols.activity.enable_m365_public_endpoint = $false
$disable = @{ agent_endpoint = @{ protocol_configuration = $protocols } } |
    ConvertTo-Json -Depth 100
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Patch -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/merge-patch+json" -Body $disable |
    Out-Null

After the update, confirm that new requests from Teams and Copilot no longer reach the agent. Ask the administrator to block or remove the app from the catalogs. Uninstalling the app alone does not revoke endpoint access. Do not delete shared Foundry resources or restore an old backup over later configuration changes.

For full pilot retirement, remove only the newly created bot and pilot-only agent-scoped grants after their owners confirm no other consumers depend on them. Retain the Foundry agent, its identity and data. If reverting listing metadata rather than withdrawing access, use the previous approved metadata with an increased appVersion; do not reuse an already published version.

docs.title: Resource naming
docs.text:
Infrastructure resource names are deployment inputs, not runtime settings. They are resolved before provisioning, including when the orchestrator is hosted in Foundry. Changing an input does not rename an existing Azure resource or move its data.

This page explains the naming model. The Deploy infra only and Deploy full stack runbooks provide the input and preview steps. Deployment settings describes other inputs; resource reuse is separate from naming.

The resource group destination inputs select where resources belong, not a naming mode. Select them before first provision; changing a group's input is not an existing-resource move or migration.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) naming is the default (RESOURCE_NAMING_MODE=caf). Generated names have the general shape type-workload-environment-region-instance, such as kv-chatapp-dev-eus2-001.

Deployment input Default when not supplied CAF_WORKLOAD_NAME First six characters of Bicep uniqueString(subscription().id, environmentName, location) CAF_ENVIRONMENT_NAME azd environment name (AZURE_ENV_NAME) CAF_REGION_NAME Deployment location (AZURE_LOCATION), mapped to a short code, such as eastus2 → eus2 CAF_INSTANCE 001

Tokens are lowercased. Region input also has spaces removed; unmapped regions use its first five characters. The naming region is based on the deployment location, not individual service-location overrides. CAF_REGION_NAME changes the name token, not where resources deploy. Overriding the CAF environment or region token does not change the inputs to the workload's deterministic six-character hash.

Storage and registry names omit hyphens. Generated names are truncated to service-specific lengths, so long tokens can lose distinguishing suffixes. Azure's resource naming rules and uniqueness scopes still apply, including global name availability where required.

docs.title: Naming inputs and explicit overrides
docs.text:
CAF defaults need no extra inputs. A readable CAF_WORKLOAD_NAME can express the workload name; the other tokens support organizational naming policies. The instance token distinguishes deliberately separate parallel copies, not successive updates to one deployment.

Explicit infrastructure parameters include keyVaultName, storageAccountName, searchServiceName and aiFoundryAccountName. They belong in the reviewed root main.parameters.json, not the generated infra/main.parameters.json. The root file does not map these examples to environment variables.

A nonempty explicit name normally takes precedence. The template can recognize an explicit value as a generated default and substitute the CAF name, so the deployment preview is the authority for the resolved result. Explicit names must satisfy each service's rules; CAF truncation does not sanitize them.

docs.title: Naming stability
docs.text:
Stable subscription, environment, location and naming inputs keep generated names stable. Changing a token or explicit resource name can create parallel resources or require replacement. Endpoints, identities, role assignments and private connections can change, while data remains in the original resources. Parallel resources can also incur duplicate costs.

The runbooks' preview allows comparison with existing names and resource IDs. It needs deployment permissions, not just Reader access, and can reveal naming collisions after truncation. Unexpected creates or deletes need review before any resource changes proceed.

Restoring earlier inputs does not move data or clean up resources already created under different names. Recovery requires dependency, data and access review before any cleanup. Operations covers ongoing deployment management.

docs.title: SharePoint
docs.text:
Foundry supports SharePoint through native knowledge sources and a native Foundry Agent Service tool. Custom ingestion is optional for SharePoint grounding.

This page explains content flow, permissions and accelerator readiness. Deployment procedures are in the Deploy full stack runbook.

docs.title: Native SharePoint options
docs.text:
Option Content flow Integration boundary Foundry IQ indexedSharePoint source (preview) Search copies and processes content into a managed index. Protected retrieval requires configured permission ingestion and query-time user authorization. Foundry IQ remoteSharePoint source (preview) Microsoft 365 is queried at retrieval time; no corpus copy is ingested into a landing-zone index. The knowledge base calls the Copilot Retrieval API under the user's permissions. Retrieved text still reaches the agent/model. Foundry Agent Service SharePoint tool (preview) A native agent tool uses Microsoft 365 retrieval without a custom landing-zone ingestion pipeline. Tool connection and user identity passthrough are configured in Foundry Agent Service, not as a knowledge-base source.

Microsoft's guides cover the indexed source, remote source and native agent tool. Preview features are available for evaluation under their documented terms; they have no preview SLA and are not recommended for production.

Remote SharePoint currently supports textual SharePoint content, not OneDrive, Copilot connector content or multimodal retrieval. It requires SharePoint and Azure in the same Entra tenant.

Each querying user needs a qualifying Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on license or enabled Retrieval API pay-as-you-go consumption. Pay-as-you-go requires administrator billing setup and at least one Microsoft 365 Copilot license in the tenant throughout use.

The native tool also requires eligible licensing or pay-as-you-go, Foundry User access to the project and Read access to the SharePoint site. Its calls require the user's delegated identity, not an application managed identity or service principal.

docs.title: What is wired into Agent Application
docs.text:
Native product support does not imply an end-to-end accelerator integration:

  • Indexed source: the template emits indexName, siteUrl and tenantId. The current documented source contract instead uses connectionString, containerName, query and ingestionParameters. Registration needs a reviewed template/API update plus source permissions and consent.
  • Remote source: the connector recognizes SHAREPOINT_REMOTE_ENABLED and SHAREPOINT_REMOTE_KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_NAME. The source must already exist and belong to the knowledge base. These keys do not create it or establish delegation.
  • Native tool: the service connection and identity-passthrough contract need an explicit application integration. The remote-source settings do not attach this tool.

The accelerator defaults to Search API 2026-05-01-preview. Current Microsoft source recipes use 2026-08-01-preview; a source extension needs compatible registration, retrieve requests and response handling, not a version edit alone. Platform provisioning can replace manual source references in its managed knowledge base.

Hosted delegated-user boundary

The shipped hosted entrypoint supplies empty user context to retrieval. The connector cannot forward the delegated user token required for protected SharePoint retrieval through that path. UI sign-in and a service managed identity do not fill this gap. The native service capability needs a reviewed trusted-user integration before hosted Agent Application can use it.

Remote knowledge-source retrieval uses x-ms-query-source-authorization for the Search-audience delegated user token, separately from service authentication. It preserves SharePoint permissions and supported Purview controls. Filters narrow the requested scope; they are not authorization. Invalid Keyword Query Language (KQL) filters can be ignored by the Retrieval API. Foundry IQ explains the shared integration boundary.

docs.title: Custom SharePoint ingestion
docs.text:
Agent App Ingestion provides a separate Graph-based connector with indexing and purge jobs. It copies content and permission metadata to Search. Permission changes need synchronization and allow/deny validation. It uses SHAREPOINT_* application credentials, not native remote-source settings; secrets belong in Key Vault.

This path is appropriate for required custom processing or connector behavior. Native indexed SharePoint also copies content, but its pipeline is managed by Search and does not need Agent App Ingestion. Neither approach removes the need to maintain permissions and enforce them during retrieval. Ingestion explains optional application selection.

docs.title: Permission synchronization
docs.text:
Each custom SharePoint indexing run reads current permissions independently of content modification timestamps. It compares the stored user and group ACLs on every indexed document for each selected item, including all document-library chunks and previously indexed file names. Changed ACLs are replaced, so revocations remove stale principals. A successful empty permission result clears the stored principal lists.

Equal ACL sets cause no writes; unchanged content is not downloaded, chunked or embedded. ACL-only merges change neither content, vectors nor content timestamps.

Custom target indexes need a filterable parent_id, sortable id, and retrievable ACL fields, as provided by the bundled index. Rebuild indexes that explicitly disable these attributes before running the connector.

The cadence is the ingestion application's CRON_RUN_SHAREPOINT_INDEX schedule, not real-time notification. An unset schedule performs no automatic refresh; the SharePoint index job can also be run manually.

Refresh applies only to configured collections and items returned by their source filters. A modification-time-only filter can omit permission-only changes: include every item whose access must be synchronized in the scheduled selection. Content retry blocking does not stop permission refresh for already indexed documents.

The supported representation is Graph-visible Entra user and group object IDs, with the connector's existing limit of 32 IDs in each ACL field.

Document libraries read effective drive-item sharing permissions, including inherited grants returned by Graph. Breaking or restoring inheritance replaces the stored ACL with the current effective result; the connector does not union parent grants into an item that has broken inheritance.

Generic lists use the permissions returned by the Graph list-item endpoint. This is not a complete SharePoint authorization-model replica: SharePoint-local group expansion, anonymous or organization-wide sharing-link semantics, and grants not exposed to the connector's application identity are not synthesized.

Configure application access so Graph can return the permissions required for the selected content, and validate both allowed and denied retrieval. Purview sensitivity label enforcement and document decryption are outside this connector's ACL synchronization.

Permission pages must all succeed before applying an item's ACL. A failed lookup is not treated as an empty ACL. Search must confirm every merge; a lookup or partial-update failure marks the item and job failed rather than reporting complete synchronization. Successful merges are not rolled back.

After restoring Graph/Search access, run the index job again: it compares current state and retries stale ACLs without reprocessing unchanged content.

Item logs use acl-updated for a successful permission-only change, and run summaries expose aclUpdatedItems and aclUpdatedDocuments for completed items. Keep restricted content unavailable until deny-path checks confirm revocations have reached every indexed copy.

docs.title: Acceptance and recovery
docs.text:
Acceptance uses a distinctive test document, an allowed user and a denied user. The allowed user receives grounded content and a citation that opens in SharePoint; the denied user's retrieved IDs, excerpts and citations exclude the document. Other sources must not expose an unprotected copy. Missing or expired user credentials must not fall back to service-only access.

Private Azure endpoints do not make Microsoft 365 a private-link source. Connectivity tests cover the actual calling service, Microsoft 365 and Entra. Recovery restores the previous application/settings and removes the pilot knowledge-base reference without deleting shared content or tenant objects. Permission revocation and retirement of indexed copies remain separate tasks.

docs.title: Sizing and capacity
docs.text:
Capacity depends on the workload, not only the number of people who can sign in. Concurrent agent requests, model calls, tool latency and document processing place different demands on the deployment.

The default is a Foundry hosted orchestrator using maf_lite, no panel and native Foundry IQ Blob ingestion. This reference explains its capacity constraints and optional components. Deployment choices covers resource selection; Cost planning covers spending. Execution steps belong to the Deploy infra only and Deploy full stack runbooks.

Validate defaults against your workload

Defaults are starting points, not benchmarked capacity profiles or throughput guarantees. Composed parameters and the deployed configuration determine the actual capacity, including for custom applications.

docs.title: Workload baseline
docs.text:
Capacity estimates need the following workload assumptions.

A token is a piece of text processed by a model. An embedding represents content as a numeric vector for similarity search. Host capacity is measured in CPU (processor capacity) and memory; Gi denotes gibibytes of memory. A service's SKU identifies its tier or capacity option, not measured usage.

Area Questions to answer Agent traffic How many requests run concurrently at peak? How long do turns take, and how many model or tool calls does each strategy make? Models Which deployments are required? What are the expected input/output token volumes, token-rate limits and target response times? Knowledge and ingestion How many documents and vectors (numeric content representations used for similarity search) are stored? What are their sizes, formats, update rate and ingestion completion targets? Will ingestion run alongside peak interactive traffic? Hosting Which strategies must run, on which host? What CPU, memory, concurrency and scaling behavior does representative execution require? Availability and operations What recovery targets, environment separation, telemetry retention and private-network requirements must the deployment meet?

Deployment settings and Agent hosting describe inputs and host constraints. The resource inventory describes resource families; the generated infra/main.parameters.json identifies the selected resources. Their count varies with topology and reuse.

docs.title: Models and quota
docs.text:
The root main.parameters.json selects a chat deployment of gpt-5-nano and a text-embedding deployment of text-embedding-3-large, each with sku.capacity=100. The token and request limits represented by this value depend on the model and deployment type. Limits and regional availability are listed in the model quota reference. modelDeploymentList in the root main.parameters.json controls that capacity.

Relevant demand includes input/output tokens per turn, model/tool calls, retries and peak turns per minute. Ingestion adds extracted tokens and embedding batches. Long contexts and multiple calls can exhaust quota even with few users. Application replicas do not increase model quota.

docs.title: Search capacity
docs.text:
Both newly created Search services start at Standard, one partition and one replica. The Agent Application Search service and the separate Foundry Agent Service Search service both count when both creation paths are enabled. They use AZURE_SEARCH_LOCATION, falling back to AZURE_LOCATION; quota must cover the complete enabled service count in that region.

  • Partitions: index/vector storage, document count and growth determine demand. A representative corpus reveals how splitting documents into passages expands the index; source-file size alone is not the index footprint.
  • Replicas: peak retrieval plus concurrent indexing affects latency and throttling. The current Search reliability and SLA requirements describe production availability requirements. The one-replica default is not a high-availability design.
  • Change path: the shipped infra/main.bicep declares SKU, partition and replica counts as literals for both services. There is no root SEARCH_REPLICA_COUNT or equivalent scaling input. Persistent sizing needs a reviewed infrastructure change; provisioning can reset portal-only changes. aiSearchResourceId does not reuse workload Search; it reuses Foundry's backing service.

Current Search service limits depend on tier, region and service creation date. Private native Blob ingestion also requires approved, ready shared private links; extra Search capacity does not bypass that gate.

docs.title: Application hosting
docs.text:
Host/resource Starting point Sizing considerations Foundry hosted orchestrator (default) The Agent Application's hosted-agent/azure.yaml declares 2 CPU and 4Gi memory. Memory peaks, streaming latency and concurrent turns determine demand. HOSTED_AGENT_CONTAINER_CPU / HOSTED_AGENT_CONTAINER_MEMORY affect provisioning but do not override the child's literal deployment fields. Resizing needs a compatible child definition, provisioned deployment metadata and a new agent version. Container Apps scaling does not control this host. Frontend Container App Root entry uses profile_name=main, min_replicas=1, max_replicas=1. With no explicit size, infrastructure placeholders use 0.5 CPU / 1.0Gi. Active revisions, CPU, memory, concurrent streams and startup latency show runtime demand. containerAppsList settings and child deployment behavior both matter; placeholder sizing is not a performance guarantee. Agent App Ingestion (optional, omitted by default) Root entry specifies 1.0 CPU / 3.0Gi and one minimum/maximum replica on main. Large files and expensive formats affect peak memory, backlog and embedding/Search throttling. Additional replicas require verified duplicate handling and concurrent writes to shared sources and indexes. Container Apps workload profiles Consumption plus main D4 with minimumCount=0, maximumCount=1. Aggregate CPU/memory placement and per-app limits both matter. Raising app replicas alone does not raise the profile's node ceiling. Minimum app replicas can keep a node allocated despite the zero-node profile minimum.

The root arrays/objects above belong in reviewed main.parameters.json; infra/main.parameters.json is generated. Deployed capacity can differ from placeholders after application deployment. Agent hosting describes strategy eligibility, immutable images and history limitations. Conversation continuity limits are not compute-sizing controls.

docs.title: Data, builds and observability
docs.text: Resource What to measure and decide Agent Application Cosmos DB hosted-no-panel does not deploy this account. Foundry Agent Service's backing Cosmos DB is separate and still needs its own capacity and retention review. Blob storage Original files, extracted images, enabled attachments, updates, retention, transaction rate and ingestion completion time all contribute. Omitting Agent App Ingestion does not omit native source processing. Registry and private build pool Image sizes, build duration and parallel build demand affect capacity. Isolated hosted preparation requires the private ACR Tasks pool and permitted package feeds; more runtime compute does not speed it up or connect the runner. Pool capacity depends on SKU and region. App Configuration and Key Vault Startup/restart bursts and service request limits matter. Secrets remain Key Vault references, not plain configuration values. Log Analytics and Application Insights Ingestion volume, investigation needs and compliance determine retention/sampling. Message-content capture is a privacy decision, not a required sizing test.

docs.title: Capacity validation
docs.text:
Useful acceptance targets include response time, error rate, ingestion delay and peak concurrency. Representative nonproduction tests cover configured tools, document sizes, native ingestion, authentication and document allow/deny behavior within regional service limits.

Service metrics and application traces distinguish model throttling, Search limits, tool latency and runtime CPU/memory pressure. Comparable tests before and after a capacity change show whether it addressed the actual bottleneck.

Scaling the application host does not increase model quota or Search capacity. Ingestion and interactive requests share those independent service limits.

docs.title: Capacity and cost
docs.text: The Agent-specific Cost planning reference covers region, enabled resources, measured usage and availability requirements. Shared infrastructure estimates are pricing examples, not workload capacity profiles. A recorded configuration, workload baseline and test evidence allow later capacity changes to be evaluated consistently.

docs.title: Terraform templates
docs.text:
The AI Landing Zone Terraform module provides Azure infrastructure modules and example deployments. Its deployment strategy is under review. It is not the standard deployment workflow for the Agent Application.

The Agent Landing Zone runbooks use Bicep for Azure infrastructure definitions and the Azure Developer CLI (azd) to coordinate deployment. They also configure services and prepare the hosted agent image. Terraform does not run this application lifecycle.

The Terraform infrastructure reference covers the module, examples and state management. The Deploy full stack runbook deploys the supplied Agent Application.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Find the first failing stage and its exact error, then use the matching section below. Deployment proceeds through resource provisioning, service configuration, image preparation and application deployment. Runtime checks confirm the application can authenticate and use its dependencies.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
Use this runbook after a provisioning, configuration, deployment or runtime failure. Diagnose the failing stage before retrying or changing inputs.

What you see Start here Multi-group setup reports a missing target or denied access Resource group destination checks azd down is blocked for split resource group destinations Split-group cleanup safety check Hosted deployment asks for preparation Hosted handoff Private endpoint or build-pool failure Private prerequisites, package installation Configuration stops after provisioning Post-provision diagnostics Deploy reports success but the application fails Revision health, startup authentication Chat, history or authorization fails Runtime diagnostics

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Run diagnostics from the platform repository root. Confirm the intended environment with azd env list and the Azure CLI subscription with az account show. Verify the identity used by azd separately from the CLI identity; each tool can use a different account.
  2. Record the failing command, time, stage, source revision and relevant non-secret settings, such as NETWORK_ISOLATION, BUILD_MODE and DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGY.
  3. For private environments, use a host with the required VPN/VNet connectivity. Inspect DNS, TLS and authorization separately.
  4. Preserve local work, data, environment bindings and security controls while investigating. Use the recovery steps below for the failed stage.

The default hosted-no-panel layout runs the orchestrator in Foundry, with maf_lite and Foundry IQ. Confirm the recorded layout before recovery. Do not switch runtimes or weaken authentication to diagnose a failure.

Share useful, redacted diagnostics

Hooks write to the terminal. Agent Application Container App component deployments also write child logs under <component>/.logs. Share the exact error and relevant log excerpt, not the full output of azd env get-values. Remove private environment names, user identifiers, document contents, signed URLs, tokens, cookies and credentials.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Capture the first error and match it to a diagnostic entry below.
  2. Check the named source, identity, endpoint and selected environment.
  3. Apply only the entry's scoped correction, then run its verification.
  4. Complete Validation before reopening access or promotion.

docs.title: Resource group destination checks
docs.text:
For Agent Bicep/azd deployments, compare the selected environment's AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP, AZURE_APP_RESOURCE_GROUP and AZURE_NETWORK_RESOURCE_GROUP with the approved destination mapping. New environments initialize separate application and network destinations; existing single-group environments retain their mapping.

With CREATE_RESOURCE_GROUPS=false, have the owner pre-create missing additional groups. Enabling creation instead requires explicit authorization and subscription-level Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups/write. An authorization failure is not evidence that the group is absent. Check the actual identity and denied action; do not grant subscription Owner or bypass the failure.

After partial creation, keep the same destinations, repair the cause and retry. Do not delete created/shared groups as rollback, change destinations to evade a binding check, or move existing resources through these inputs. Verify resource IDs and scoped permissions in every destination before continuing.

docs.title: Split-group cleanup safety check
docs.text:
The predown hook blocks azd down when the workload destinations span distinct resource groups. This is an intentional safety check, not a provisioning or permission failure. No automatic deletion or bypass option is provided; do not bypass the hook or change the destination mapping to make teardown proceed.

Inventory resources in every destination and identify shared dependencies, retained data, locks and ownership. Additional groups created by the feature do not receive the azd-env-name tag, so tag-based discovery is not a complete inventory. Arrange separately authorized, itemized manual removal with the owners. Confirm retained/shared resources remain intact afterward. The normal single-group azd down path is unchanged; its deletion review still applies.

docs.title: Hosted deployment is not prepared
docs.text:
Symptom: Deployment reports missing hosted foundation prerequisites or automatic image preparation fails.

Diagnose: Provision creates prerequisites and records HOSTED_AGENT_PREPARED=true. Deployment builds or reuses the immutable image, records its application handoff and creates the running agent version. A missing digest before deployment is normal; it does not require another provision.

Correct: Provision if the foundation is missing. Otherwise review the failed build, pinned source, registry access and private ACR Tasks pool, then retry azd deploy. A foundation project or registry binding mismatch must be resolved against the intended environment, not bypassed by editing output flags. Follow the Deploy full stack runbook. For an unchanged, compatible image, use the redeployment guidance. Let the workflow generate its output flags.

Verify: Deployment targets the intended digest and routed agent version. Then test authenticated task execution and the retrieval/authorization features you use.

docs.title: Hosted agent deployment returns an agent permission denial
docs.text:
Symptom: HTTP 403 names Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/AIServices/agents/read.

Diagnose: Compare the denied object ID with the actual deployment principal. Foundry data-plane permission is granted separately from ARM provisioning access.

Correct: Have an authorized administrator review the minimum project-scoped agent authoring role for that principal. A runner creating/updating agents needs Foundry User or the appropriate equivalent custom role. Azure AI Developer targets different hub/workspace scenarios. Allow role propagation before retrying, keeping grants scoped to the project.

Verify: The same principal can perform the previously denied operation. Test delegated-user/OBO access separately.

docs.title: Application definition does not match the environment
docs.text:
Symptom: Application definition binding check failed. No changes were made. with exit code 2. An invalid definition instead exits with code 1.

Diagnose: Compare the selected definition's application ID with the existing AGENTLZ_APP_ID binding. The application ID identifies the application selected for that environment; orchestrator topology is a separate choice.

Correct: Restore the matching definition. For a different application ID, use a separate environment and select the definition before first provision. Retain the original environment's binding and topology.

Verify: Definition validation and binding checks pass for the intended environment. See Custom applications.

docs.title: Custom hosted image pull fails
docs.text:
Symptom: A custom azure.ai.agent service cannot activate its private image, although Foundry project and registry outputs exist.

Diagnose: Check the Foundry project identity's registry pull grant and the exact image/registry. Custom hosted components require hosted foundation preparation regardless of where any other component runs.

Correct: Preserve the environment, definition and immutable image, then rerun the custom application workflow. Provisioning applies the declarative pull grant; refreshing outputs alone cannot. For an external registry, review its supported pull-role mode and resource scope separately.

Verify: Image activation succeeds and the actual runtime principal receives the declared capabilities. Check the routed version before testing the agent. Keep registry authentication identity-based, grants narrowly scoped and delegated-user/OBO authentication intact.

docs.title: Private deployment prerequisites failed
docs.text:
Symptom:

Private deployment prerequisites failed. Use a VPN/VNet-connected host; RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX is not a connectivity bypass.

Diagnose: With NETWORK_ISOLATION=true, the host cannot resolve or establish TLS to App Configuration, or to the Foundry project endpoint for hosted topologies. The gate allows up to 20 seconds per endpoint.

Correct: Move to the approved jumpbox, VPN or peered-VNet runner and inspect the private connectivity path. The RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX input requests a connectivity check from that host.

Verify: Resolve and reach each required endpoint from that runner, then retry the failed stage. If it returns an authorization error, check the requesting principal and its permissions next.

docs.title: ACR Task agent pool is missing
docs.text:
Symptom:

Run 'azd env set DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL true' and 'azd provision', or set BUILD_MODE=local on a VNet-connected host with Docker.

Diagnose: The private environment has no ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL output and BUILD_MODE is not local. This guard also applies to a custom service with a prebuilt digest.

Correct: Select the pool intentionally and run the foundation workflow:

azd env set DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL true
azd provision

For supported Container App builds, local Docker on a connected host is an alternative. The jumpbox does not include Docker by default. Automatic hosted image preparation and isolated custom source builds require the supported ACR Tasks path. See isolated image builds.

Verify: Confirm the selected environment has the provisioned pool output and that a build runs in it. Then resume the topology's deployment sequence; azd deploy resumes automatic hosted image preparation.

docs.title: Package installation fails inside the build pool
docs.text:
Symptom: An ACR run starts, but package installation fails. npm can report Exit handler never called!, followed by tsc: not found.

Diagnose: Retrieve the failed ACR run log from a connected host. Correlate timestamps and the build-agent source address with firewall deny logs. Check the pinned lockfile's resolved URLs, including redirect CDN destinations. Base-image registries and package feeds can require separate firewall allowances.

Correct: Confirm the pool and extendFirewallForAcrTaskBuilds are enabled and the shipped firewall changes are provisioned. The platform includes the orchestrator's Microsoft npm feeds, *.vsblob.vsassets.io and the existing packages.microsoft.com OS-package allowance. For additional verified dependencies, use application-specific package feeds. Keep exceptions limited to build-subnet HTTPS traffic.

Verify: Retry the same pinned source and confirm package installation and compilation both complete. Once dependencies are installed, diagnose the first remaining compilation error.

docs.title: Tokenizer initialization fails with an empty cache
docs.text:
Symptom: Orchestrator or ingestion startup fails while downloading a tiktoken encoding from openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net.

Diagnose: Check the failing HTTPS/443 destination and the actual workload subnet against firewall logs. A warm tokenizer cache can conceal this dependency; successful image builds do not verify runtime egress.

Correct: Review the selected components' runtime egress declarations. Both bundled tokenizer consumers declare this exact host. For a managed firewall, follow the normal provisioning sequence to save the declaration plan and reconcile its owned rules. For an external firewall, send the read-only resolved report to its policy owner. Keep the exception on the required workload subnet; do not allow all Blob Storage or Internet traffic.

Verify: From the actual workload network, initialize the configured tokenizer with a newly empty cache and confirm its asset download and startup complete. A local cold-cache test establishes the dependency, not traversal through the deployed firewall.

docs.title: Component egress reconciliation stops
docs.text:
Symptom: A hook reports a missing or stale egress plan, ownership collision, invalid source subnet or concurrent policy change.

Correct: Keep the same application binding. Review python -m config.deployment.egress --plan --environment <environment-name> and rerun the normal provisioning sequence after approved input changes. For collisions or changed policies, have the network owner inspect the reported group and current rules before retrying; do not delete unrelated entries, broaden sources or bypass the ownership checks.

Verify: The read-only --review report has the intended destinations and actual workload prefixes. Managed reconciliation completes without changing unrelated rules; external policies remain report-only.

docs.title: Stale component checkout
docs.text:
Symptom: Remove or relocate the stale sibling checkout.

Diagnose: An Agent Application component's sibling folder exists at a different commit from manifest.json. Check HEAD and local modifications before replacing it.

Correct: Inspect the named checkout, preserve local modifications and move it aside. Retry deployment to obtain the expected source. Delete it only after confirming it contains nothing needed; keep component development elsewhere.

Verify: The deployed source matches the manifest's tag and commit, and the intended application revision is healthy.

docs.title: A component deployment fails
docs.text:
Symptom: One or more components failed. See logs above.

Diagnose: Find the first failing component and its newest .logs file. Distinguish source checkout, image build/push, role and application-update failures.

Correct: Repair the dependency identified by that log. Use the private connectivity or build-pool entries above when appropriate.

Verify: Retry the failed workflow and inspect the actual image, intended revision and startup logs.

docs.title: Deploy succeeds but the UI or administrative panel does not start
docs.text:
Symptom: Child commands succeed, but the latest revision is unhealthy. Logs name OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_ID, OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_SECRET, OAUTH_AZURE_AD_TENANT_ID or missing panel OAuth settings.

Diagnose: Inspect the intended revision and image. A previous healthy placeholder can still serve HTTP 200 while the new revision fails.

Correct: Configure delegated authentication. Store the credential in Key Vault and publish its reference, not its value, under label agent-lz. Reload configuration through the supported lifecycle workflow.

Verify: Check revision health, the Entra login redirect, real user login, OBO and rejection of unauthenticated panel data requests. Keep panel authentication required throughout recovery.

docs.title: Search shared private links are not ready
docs.text:
Symptom: Private native azureBlob source configuration reports pending approval, denied Search reads or a readiness timeout.

Diagnose: Inspect the exact reported Search service, link name, target and group. Search uses its own outbound private links to storage and models, separately from the runner's network access. Each required source link must report both Approved and Succeeded.

Correct:

  • Pending: Have an authorized administrator investigate and approve only the exact target request using Microsoft's procedure.
  • ARM 401/403: Review the runner's Microsoft.Search/searchServices/sharedPrivateLinkResources/read permission. The runner needs this read permission in addition to target approval.
  • Approved but provisioning: Allow propagation and inspect the failed link's state. Readiness polling has a 600-second budget, 10-second intervals and requests bounded by 30 seconds and the remaining budget.
  • Missing link manifest: Re-provision the reviewed template through an authorized deployment to publish SEARCH_SHARED_PRIVATE_LINKS under agent-lz. Use the published link names to identify the matching requests.

Verify: Rerun post-provision from a connected host, then verify source processing and authorized retrieval. The gate runs before dependent Search mutation and source creation. Retain private access and the readiness gate; approve only the requests for the intended source targets. See Private native Blob ingestion.

docs.title: Ingestion selection does not match the source configuration
docs.text:
Symptom: A fresh environment has no ingestion Container App, a source combination fails validation, or attachment behavior differs from expectations.

Diagnose: Fresh Agent Application deployments default to DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP=false, independently of orchestrator hosting. Native source ingestion uses Search's service-managed pipeline. Conversation uploads and Agent App Ingestion features require separate selection. Existing environments and custom definitions retain their component selections.

Correct: Check the resolved component selection, retrieval backend, source kind and index bindings using Ingestion. To retain or restore Agent App Ingestion, select it explicitly and run the full workflow, not only azd deploy. An externally populated index must be named explicitly where required.

Verify: Confirm the effective agent-lz key and intended UI revision. With ingestion disabled, attachment controls must be hidden and direct/stale uploads rejected. Verify text chat and retrieval separately, including the protected-retrieval integration gate. Ingestion selection is not a source of delegated user or owner context.

If ingestion is selected, confirm the selection is true and test only eligible authenticated uploads. Processing success does not prove authorized conversation retrieval. Retire existing apps and permissions only as a separate authorized task, preserving documents and indexes.

docs.title: Shared-source permission options are rejected or unexpected
docs.text:
Symptom: Source configuration rejects FOUNDRY_IQ_INGESTION_PERMISSION_OPTIONS, or a source has unexpected permission metadata.

Diagnose: Omitted or null values retain ["rbacScope"]. For active native Blob ingestion, explicit [] selects shared access only for recognized non-ADLS azureBlob configuration. Unsupported or ambiguous active sources fail closed. In non-native ai_search or foundry_iq/searchIndex modes, accepted [] is unused metadata; the source's access policy remains unchanged.

Correct: Supply valid JSON for the intended source policy. For protected Blob ingestion, restore ["rbacScope"]. Nonempty non-ADLS Blob lists support only rbacScope and sensitivityLabels. Review the accepted permission values for source and pattern constraints.

Verify: Rerun source configuration, inspect permission metadata and test document allow/deny behavior. Select [] only for an intentionally shared corpus; resolve private-link, RBAC and authentication failures separately.

docs.title: Firewall DNS proxy is enabled but clients still resolve incorrectly
docs.text:
Symptom: Private names resolve incorrectly after enabling the DNS proxy.

Diagnose: ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY defaults to false; its opt-in applies only with firewall deployment and isolation enabled. VNet/VPN client DNS settings and build-feed egress are configured separately.

Correct: Inspect the affected client's DNS server, zone links and forwarding path. Make client DNS changes deliberately and separately from proxy enablement. See Firewall DNS proxy.

Verify: Resolve the required names and test private TLS from the actual client with public access still disabled.

docs.title: Hosted configuration TLS handshake stalls
docs.text:
Symptom: Hosted bootstrap stalls while loading App Configuration or Key Vault references.

Diagnose: Distinguish name resolution, routing, TLS and HTTP authorization errors at both endpoints. Confirm the actual runtime identity and identify which connection stage stalls before choosing a recovery action.

Correct: Only for the confirmed transport compatibility case, use the endpoint-scoped TLS profile. Supply the actual KEY_VAULT_URI, deliberately select APP_CONFIG_TLS_COMPATIBILITY=true and deploy a new agent version. To restore SDK defaults, use false and redeploy. Keep certificate verification, the minimum TLS version and scoped role assignments intact.

If bootstrap resolves a UI-only secret, inspect the actual label selectors: in the SDK, None selects all labels, while "\0" selects only unlabelled settings. Use the intended selector while retaining scoped vault permissions and labels.

Verify: The new version completes configuration using valid TLS and the intended identity. Test real application behavior separately.

docs.title: Search preflight region and quota
docs.text:
Symptom: Preflight checks AZURE_LOCATION despite AZURE_SEARCH_LOCATION, or counts only one service when two will be created.

Diagnose: An empty AZURE_SEARCH_LOCATION falls back to AZURE_LOCATION. Both workload and newly created Agent Service Search must be accounted for.

Correct: Check the effective region and selected resources using Search region and quota. Verify local hooks and repository-owned infrastructure match the intended coordinated source. Request quota or deliberately select a supported region; do not set PREFLIGHT_SKIP or AGENTLZ_REGIONAL_PREFLIGHT_SKIP.

Verify: Preflight checks the effective region and full creation count, then provisioning succeeds. Capacity remains subject to availability at provisioning time.

docs.title: Quota check rejects an unchanged existing deployment
docs.text:
Symptom: Re-provision reports insufficient remaining model quota for the same account, deployment and configured capacity.

Diagnose: Compare the requested capacity with the existing successful deployment and remaining regional quota. Reprovisioning must use the same reviewed account and model inputs. Hosted image preparation itself does not require reprovisioning.

Correct: Verify environment, account region, deployment, model/version and SKU. Preflight credits only verified successful matching capacity and aggregates quota pools. Fresh allocations and changed/unverified targets still need capacity. If a matching deployment is not credited, retain the gates and escalate with sanitized account, region, model and capacity evidence.

Verify: Both preflight gates evaluate the intended incremental request. Retain the existing deployment, intended capacity and preflight gates. Model availability checks still apply.

docs.title: Foundry rejects evaluation API-key creation
docs.text:
Symptom: Failed to list key. disableLocalAuth is set to be true.

Diagnose: The account requires Entra ID. Identify the caller still trying to obtain an API key.

Correct: Keep local authentication disabled and use Entra ID for evaluation. The supported configuration skips inapplicable key injection. Investigate unexpected key or Key Vault errors instead of enabling local authentication.

Verify: Post-provision reports the expected Entra-only path and evaluation works with the intended identity while local authentication remains disabled.

docs.title: Administrative panel cannot resolve its Cosmos database
docs.text:
Symptom: DEPLOY_ADMINISTRATIVE_PANEL is true but DATABASE_ACCOUNT_NAME is not set.

Diagnose: Identify the selected database account and name, then check process inputs and the settings published in App Configuration.

Correct: Confirm the two settings under agent-lz for the selected environment. Setup reads published settings when process inputs are absent. Resolve missing or conflicting values in their provisioning source.

Verify: Panel configuration resolves the actual account/database and preserves container-scoped grants. Compare the resolved names with the provisioned resources and keep permissions scoped to the required containers.

docs.title: Missing endpoint output
docs.text:
Symptom:

Missing <KEY>. Run provisioning and load the selected azd environment outputs before this stage.

Diagnose: The selected environment lacks a required output such as APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT, AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT or AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_ENDPOINT.

Correct: Confirm the environment first. If it is already provisioned and you moved machines, use azd env refresh. If provision is incomplete, follow the Deploy infra only runbook to generate the required outputs.

Verify: Confirm the outputs identify this environment's resources before retrying the failed stage.

docs.title: Private post-provision prerequisites failed
docs.text:
Symptom:

Private post-provision prerequisites failed. Connect through VPN/VNet and rerun postProvision; configuration has not started.

Diagnose: Provisioning completed, but the runner cannot reach private App Configuration, so configuration has not started.

Correct: Connect through an approved jumpbox, VPN or peered VNet. Follow Complete a deferred post-provision.

Verify: Complete the configuration hook from the connected host before resuming application deployment.

docs.title: Post-provision was deferred
docs.text:
Symptom:

Post-provision configuration explicitly deferred; application setup is incomplete.

Diagnose: An explicit deferral can exit successfully without configuring the application. In isolated mode, RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX=false (also 0, no, skip) or a truthy AZURE_SKIP_NETWORK_ISOLATION_WARNING without a truthy RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX selects deferral.

Correct: Complete the deferred step from a connected host. A truthy RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX requests connectivity checking from the runner's existing network path.

Verify: Post-provision logs show completed configuration rather than another deferral before resuming application deployment.

docs.title: NETWORK_ISOLATION is not a boolean
docs.text:
Symptom: A hook rejects the isolation value.

Diagnose: The selected environment contains a value other than literal true or false.

Correct: Restore the value required by the intended network design, for example azd env set NETWORK_ISOLATION true for an isolated environment. Use false only when the intended network design is non-isolated.

Verify: The effective value matches the intended network design and validation passes before any provisioning changes.

docs.title: Provisioning fails in Azure
docs.text:
Symptom: Preflight passes but Azure resource deployment fails.

Diagnose: Open Resource group > Deployments in the Azure portal and inspect the first failed operation, including its policy, quota, region or resource-name error.

Correct: Resolve that specific cause. Region/name changes can replace stateful resources, so review their impact before retrying the foundation workflow. For a name conflict, identify the existing resource and its owner before deciding whether to reuse it or choose another name.

Verify: The failed deployment and post-provision configuration both complete. Then deploy the application and run its authenticated task and access checks.

docs.title: Protected retrieval fails after hosted sign-in
docs.text:
Symptom: UI login and a greeting work, but protected Foundry IQ retrieval lacks delegated user context, is denied or omits documents.

Diagnose: Distinguish UI-to-Foundry OBO from downstream source authorization. The hosted gateway does not forward the caller's Authorization header. The shipped maf_lite direct connector does not complete the authenticated Toolbox integration needed for protected per-user retrieval.

Correct: Stop protected-data rollout and have a developer implement and validate the supported hosted identity integration. Follow the capability gate in the Deploy full stack runbook. Do not select another strategy as a workaround, invent identity headers, enable anonymous retrieval or replace the user with a service identity.

Verify: Use two users with different source permissions and confirm permitted retrieval and denial through the actual UI or channel. If that integration is absent, mark the capability blocked.

docs.title: The orchestrator returns HTTP 422
docs.text:
Symptom: The agent rejects a request with validation details.

Diagnose: The stateless Responses 2.0.0 adapter rejects non-null previous_response_id, empty asks and message arrays not ending with a user message. The adapter ignores top-level conversation. The UI's /invocations?api-version=v1 uses another request shape.

Correct: Use the returned validation detail and the correct request format. For stateless Responses, remove state selectors and supply complete, ordered context.

Verify: A request in the intended endpoint's format succeeds through that endpoint.

docs.title: Hosted chat works but history is unavailable
docs.text:
Symptom: A greeting works, but history is unavailable or panel history returns 503.

Diagnose: Hosted runtime is stateless. Without separately activated continuity, context is limited to the active UI session. Agent Application Cosmos DB in hosted-panel stores owner/index and feedback metadata, not transcripts. UI history requires continuity and the separately documented panel gates.

Correct: Review continuity activation, panel gates, owner binding and agent-scoped permissions in Hosted agents. Apply configuration changes through the full workflow using hosted continuity and owner-scoped permissions. Keep the hosted container's conversation access restricted; do not enable the panel merely to obtain persistence.

Verify: Open a saved conversation in a new session as its owner and confirm the transcript is available. Repeat as another user and confirm access is denied.

docs.title: The application starts but does not answer
docs.text:
Symptom: The application loads but an authenticated task fails.

Diagnose:

  1. Confirm the intended image and revision or routed hosted version using health checks.
  2. Read startup and request logs using correlated diagnostics.
  3. Inspect the effective configuration using the actual component selectors.
  4. Follow the first failing model, retrieval, tool or identity dependency.

Correct: Repair the identified dependency, then use the appropriate runtime-setting lifecycle or redeployment. Use provisioning for infrastructure changes and a new process or hosted version for startup settings, as specified in those workflows.

Verify: Repeat the same authenticated task and test document authorization when retrieval is involved. Keep credentials and content out of diagnostics.

docs.title: Access denied between services
docs.text:
Symptom: A dependency returns HTTP 401/403 or names a denied action.

Diagnose: Identify the caller's actual principal, target, denied action and scope. Project, deployment and hosted runtime principals each have their own grants. Check service authentication separately from delegated-user authorization.

Correct: Compare the deployed grants with capability profiles and the hosted runtime access model. Allow new assignments to propagate before requesting additional access. Use hosted recovery where required, keeping role assignments scoped to the required resources.

For application-component configuration failures, use this checklist of base capability permissions:

Role Intended resource scope Purpose App Configuration Data Reader Selected App Configuration store Read runtime settings AcrPull Selected container registry Pull images Key Vault Secrets User Selected Key Vault Resolve secret references

Additional grants depend on declared profiles, selected resources and topology. Hosted bootstrap, continuity and panel permissions are reconciled separately. Use the relevant workflow to grant only the roles required by the actual caller.

Verify: The same intended identity can perform the required operation while unauthorized users/documents remain denied.

docs.title: Check application health
docs.text:
List the latest and latest-ready Container Apps revisions:

az containerapp list -g "<resource-group>" --query "[].{name:name,state:properties.runningStatus,latest:properties.latestRevisionName,ready:properties.latestReadyRevisionName}" -o table
az containerapp revision list -g "<resource-group>" -n "<container-app-name>" --query "[].{name:name,active:properties.active,health:properties.healthState,image:properties.template.containers[].image}" -o json

Compare the intended image/revision with the ready revision and traffic routing. An older placeholder can return HTTP 200 while the intended application fails. Inspect system and startup logs for that exact revision.

For a Foundry hosted orchestrator, inspect its routed version, immutable image and Foundry runtime logs separately. Container Apps commands cover the UI, optional ingestion and Container App orchestration, not hosted agent compute.

docs.title: Stream logs from a container app
docs.text:
Select the failing revision explicitly:

az containerapp logs show -g "<resource-group>" -n "<container-app-name>" --revision "<revision-name>" --follow

If the revision has multiple replicas or containers, select the relevant ones using the command's --replica and --container options. Confirm the logs belong to the failed revision and image.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Use Application Insights > Transaction search to correlate a request with its dependencies and traces. Use Log Analytics for container output and platform events. Confirm diagnostic settings and the selected workspace if expected logs are absent.

Recent Container Apps errors:

ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Log_s has_any ("ERROR", "Exception", "Traceback")
| project TimeGenerated, ContainerAppName_s, Log_s
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Revision, scaling and startup events:

ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| project TimeGenerated, ContainerAppName_s, Reason_s, Log_s
| order by TimeGenerated desc

These queries depend on the configured Container Apps log destination and schema; they cover Container Apps rather than Foundry hosted runtime logs. If no rows match, check the time range, log destination and failing revision, then inspect application health directly.

UI records containing exception_type and failure_site intentionally omit dependency error payloads. Correlate the static operation, code location and request reference with dependency telemetry. Do not enable raw token, cookie, claim, signed-URL or document logging to fill that gap. A failed optional panel index write needs repair even when the chat continues. Confirm the expected owner-index record exists after retrying the write.

Telemetry content capture is off by default. Keep prompts and answers private; diagnose with request references and dependency status.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
1. Repeat the exact operation that failed, from the intended host and identity.
  2. Confirm the intended source commit, immutable image and routed hosted version or Container App revision. A placeholder response is not application health.
  3. Test user sign-in, the required tool or retrieval operation, and allowed and denied access to protected data. Keep unresolved runtime integration gates explicitly blocked.
  4. Record sanitized timestamps, request IDs, statuses and the scoped correction. Do not claim success from a green hook exit alone.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
1. Stop retries and promotion. Preserve the diagnostic record and known-good source, input and image records.
  2. Restore only the settings or grants changed during diagnosis, using the recorded values and exact assignment IDs. Preserve unrelated access.
  3. If an application or infrastructure redeployment is required, follow deployment rollback or infrastructure rollback.
