  4. Repeat Validation. Keep access closed if safe reversal or protected-data enforcement is not established. Arrange service-specific data recovery with the owner when necessary.

docs.title: User feedback
docs.text:
The default hosted-no-panel application has no supported feedback collection or feedback administration surface. Optional hosted-panel provides Cosmos-backed APIs, but the supplied chat controls do not call those APIs. Hosted feedback requires a custom UI control and validated conversation ownership. Foundry hosted agents provide the container runtime, not this feedback integration.

This page describes those boundaries. The Deploy full stack runbook covers deployment and redeployment, not a ready-made feedback customization.

docs.title: Available surfaces
docs.text:
Surface Supplied behavior hosted-no-panel Chat without application feedback storage. hosted-panel Metadata storage and gated APIs; selection alone does not activate feedback. ENABLE_USER_FEEDBACK Default false. Existing Chainlit thumbs call the non-hosted orchestrator backend, not the panel API. USER_FEEDBACK_RATING Default false. Changes those same controls to a rating/comment form; it does not connect them to hosted feedback.

Anonymous embedded sessions cannot use feedback actions. Keeping both control flags off avoids presenting a hosted feedback integration that is not supplied.

docs.title: Hosted-panel integration contract
docs.text:
User-facing history, feedback and deletion share the same gates.

Dependency Contract Panel deployment DEPLOY_ADMINISTRATIVE_PANEL reflects actual hosted-panel provisioning. Continuity Active owner-bound hosted continuity, not just HOSTED_CONTINUITY_ENABLED=true. User surfaces PANEL_HISTORY_ENABLED defaults to false. Token validation PANEL_CONVERSATIONS_TOKEN_AUDIENCE identifies the delegated token audience; tenant comes from PANEL_CONVERSATIONS_TENANT_ID or the OAuth tenant. Metadata Provisioned DATABASE_ACCOUNT_NAME, DATABASE_NAME and UI identity access to Cosmos. Enumeration PANEL_CONVERSATION_ENUMERATION_MODE=owner_index is the default. Delegated mode requires its own evidence gate.

The default containers are panel-conversation-owner-index and panel-feedback. HOSTED_CONVERSATION_OWNER_BINDING_VALIDATED gates delegated continuity; PANEL_HISTORY_OWNER_BINDING_VALIDATED independently gates delegated panel enumeration. Neither grants permissions. Provisioning resets owner-validation and operator-surface gates to false; they remain false until deployment-specific authorization evidence exists. Agent hosting describes the continuity protocol and permission requirements.

The custom control calls the UI service, not the hosted container:

UI endpoint Purpose GET /panel/conversations Lists the caller's conversation IDs. POST /panel/conversations/{conversation_id}/feedback Creates or upserts that owner's feedback. GET /panel/conversations/{conversation_id}/feedback Reads feedback after the same ownership check.

Every request requires a delegated user bearer with user_impersonation, valid tenant/audience and active gates. Listing is scoped to the caller; per-conversation operations require a Cosmos owner-index match. A conversation ID alone grants no access.

The body contains feedback_id and message_ref (1–128 characters each), optional integer rating from -5 to 5, category up to 64 characters and comment up to 2,000. Unknown fields are rejected. The feedback ID is unique across that owner's conversations; retrying it upserts the owner's record. Tokens are not body fields or URL parameters.

Runtime settings normally use App Configuration label agent-lz and load at UI startup. Deployment settings describes overrides; changes require a UI process reload. Source changes require a compatible application build. Neither enabling flags nor deploying the panel implements the missing control.

docs.title: Expected isolation and failures
docs.text:
An owner can submit and read back saved fields and timestamp. Another user receives 404, indistinguishable from a missing conversation. Missing active gates return 503; invalid identity returns 401/403; invalid input returns 422. Metadata or managed-conversation failures can return 502, not an empty successful feedback list.

PANEL_HISTORY_ENABLED=false disables user history, feedback and deletion after reload without deleting stored metadata or changing hosted chat routing.

docs.title: Administrative views
docs.text:
When the ingestion service is selected, its separate hosted-panel API exposes GET /api/panel/feedback and counts in GET /api/panel/overview. It validates an Entra bearer with the Admin app role and rejects missing tenant configuration. Its schema uses conversationId, messageId, rating: "up" | "down", comment and tags.

The UI schema instead uses message_ref and numeric ratings. There is no shipped adapter joining these schemas into an administrative view.

Operator overview/curation is separately gated by PANEL_OPERATOR_SURFACES_ENABLED, actual deployment, an explicit PANEL_OPERATOR_APP_ROLE or PANEL_OPERATOR_GROUP_ID, and the backend cursor-signing secret. Provisioning leaves it disabled pending authorization validation. The Admin role and user-history gate do not substitute for this operator contract.

docs.title: Privacy and retention
docs.text: Panel Cosmos stores ownership and feedback metadata, not chat transcripts or citations. Comments are still user-authored data and can contain sensitive content. Operator authorization and feedback retention need explicit policy separate from Foundry conversation retention. Cosmos DB time to live can expire configured metadata; this integration sets no automatic retention period. Conversation deletion attempts feedback cleanup, which can fail and needs result verification. Backups have their own retention boundary.

docs.title: Work IQ
docs.text:
Work IQ provides the signed-in user's Microsoft 365 context, including documents, email and meetings. As a Foundry IQ workIQ knowledge source, it queries that context at retrieval time, without Agent App Ingestion or a landing-zone index copy of the Microsoft 365 corpus.

This page explains the integration contract. Deployment procedures remain in the Deploy full stack runbook.

docs.title: Product support and application readiness
docs.text:
Microsoft supports a Work IQ knowledge source in preview. The source can participate in a Foundry IQ knowledge base called by Foundry Agent Service. Preview status does not require a custom ingestion pipeline.

The accelerator does not provide a configuration-only hosted integration. Its template emits a workIQ source without the app-authentication properties required by the current service contract. Its connector uses the generic source-authorization header, and its hosted entrypoint supplies no delegated user context. Source registration, token delivery and connector authentication need coordinated implementation before this path can work.

WORK_IQ_ENABLED and WORK_IQ_KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_NAME select the source in the shipped connector; they do not supply the missing integration. Foundry IQ explains the hosted identity integration gap.

docs.title: Tenant and governance requirements
docs.text:
The Work IQ tenant guide describes administrator enablement and billing. It requires a usage-based billing plan, its Azure subscription/resource group and assignment of querying users. Microsoft 365 Copilot licensing does not replace this billing setup.

Tenant enablement, delegated consent and retrieval-service access are separate requirements. The source administrator needs permission to manage knowledge objects; Microsoft recommends Search Service Contributor for keyless management. Network-isolated Azure resources still need the permitted paths to Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Entra services.

Preview scope

Microsoft warns that this source can invoke Work IQ capabilities that perform actions, not only retrieve information. A pilot needs trusted applications/users, reviewed permissions, billing and data-handling approval. Preview functionality has no SLA and is not recommended for production.

docs.title: Authentication contract
docs.text:
The accelerator defaults to Search API 2026-05-01-preview. Microsoft's current 2026-08-01-preview source contract requires workIQParameters.entraAppAuthentication, including the app's client ID and federated credential object ID. The tenant ID is required for a cross-tenant app registration. These are distinct Entra objects, not source names.

The customer-owned app exposes access_as_user and has the delegated WorkIQAgent.Ask permission with administrator consent. A federated credential allows the Search managed identity to authenticate as that app without storing a client secret in the source.

At query time, service authentication to Search is separate from the signed-in user's assertion:

  • The user assertion targets the customer-owned Work IQ app and includes access_as_user.
  • The current contract carries the raw assertion in x-ms-query-work-iq-source-authorization, not x-ms-query-source-authorization.
  • Search exchanges that assertion for delegated Work IQ access. A Search-audience user token or the agent's managed-identity token is not a substitute.

The official authentication procedure defines registration, federation and client consent. The shipped template and connector do not implement that complete contract. A reviewed custom application needs trusted per-user assertion delivery and matching registration/request changes, not runtime flags alone. Bearer tokens must stay out of prompts, history and logs.

docs.title: Acceptance and recovery
docs.text:
A pilot needs a known Microsoft 365 document and two accounts with different permissions. Acceptance includes the allowed user's grounded answer and source reference, exclusion of that document for the denied user, and rejection of missing or expired assertions. Concurrent sessions must not share tokens or retrieved content.

Provisioning can overwrite manual knowledge-base edits. Recovery restores the previous application/settings and removes the pilot source reference without deleting shared tenant objects. Revocation of pilot-only grants is a separate, authorized action.

The separate Work IQ MCP product exposes callable tools. It is not the workIQ knowledge source or a remedy for the hosted identity gap.

docs.title: Cost guide
docs.text:
Estimate the deployment you intend to run, not an all-services-enabled template. Begin with the resource inventory and scenario estimates, then build a regional estimate in the Azure Pricing Calculator. Use the sizing guide to identify the capacity assumptions you need to test.

Estimate dates and pricing evidence

The earlier version of this guide contained East US USD estimates dated November 5, 2025, linked to this saved calculator example. That example is not a current default deployment or a quote. The separate resource inventory identifies its own pricing date and assumptions. This guide's October 18, 2026 editorial review did not reprice Azure services. Recalculate for your region, agreement, currency and selected resources before approving spend.

docs.title: Build an estimate in five steps
docs.text:
1. Select the implementation and topology. Record whether you are estimating a foundation alone or the application too. For Agent Landing Zone, use its manifest.json, deployment definition and resolved configuration, not the standalone foundation's example defaults.
  2. Count the actual resources. Include separate Agent Service backing resources where created. Account for existing resources without counting their full shared cost twice.
  3. Separate allocation from usage. Estimate always-running capacity, variable consumption and one-time migration or indexing work separately.
  4. Price the region and tier. Use current calculator rates and your organization's applicable pricing. Record a date and shareable estimate.
  5. Validate after deployment. Compare the estimate with Cost Management, usage and performance. Revisit it after traffic, model, data or topology changes.

docs.title: What to include
docs.text:
The categories below are a costing checklist, not a statement that every resource is deployed by default. Check the selected template and effective parameters.

Category Include when selected or required Main cost drivers Models and Foundry Account/project, selected model deployments and agent/tool services Input/output tokens, model and deployment type, provisioned capacity, separately metered tools Search and ingestion Workload Search, Agent Service Search where created, native ingestion or the optional ingestion application Service count, SKU, replicas/partitions, semantic or agentic retrieval, indexing/enrichment and embedding usage Application hosting Selected Container Apps, Foundry hosted-agent compute, build services and Container Registry Active compute, minimum replicas, allocated workload-profile nodes, registry tier/storage and build-agent pool allocation Data Workload and Agent Service Storage/Cosmos DB as applicable Account count, throughput mode, requests, stored data, redundancy, backup and restore Configuration and secrets App Configuration and Key Vault Tier, requests and secret/key operations Observability Log Analytics, Application Insights and configured tests Ingested data, retention, queries and test execution; avoid double-counting workspace-based ingestion Private networking Private endpoints/DNS, firewall, NAT, peering, Bastion and connected-runner VMs where deployed Allocated hours, processed data, endpoint count, DNS queries, VM disks and data transfer Ingress and optional tools Application Gateway/WAF, API Management, Speech, Grounding with Bing or other selected services Tier and capacity, allocated hours, requests, tokens and data transfer

docs.title: Avoid common counting mistakes
docs.text:
• Agent backing resources are separate. Standard Agent Service setup can create its own Search, Storage and Cosmos DB resources in addition to workload resources. Count what is actually created or reused.
  • Application Cosmos DB depends on topology. Omitting the application's database does not imply that Agent Service has no backing database.
  • Ingestion is a separate choice. Omitting the optional ingestion app does not remove Search, source-processing, embedding or indexing charges.
  • Private networking is not a fixed package. Endpoint count and services depend on isolation, selected resources and existing platform integration. Count firewall, Bastion, NAT, VMs and disks only where present.
  • Optional does not mean free. Add API Management, public ingress and tools only when selected, with their own pricing assumptions.

docs.title: Record your sizing assumptions
docs.text:
Use measured or explicitly estimated inputs rather than a single unexplained monthly total:

Input What to record User and agent traffic Active users, turns per day, concurrency, peak rate and retries/tool calls per task Model usage Input/output tokens per task, context size, model choice and embedding volume Retrieval and ingestion Document count/size, update frequency, query volume and index growth Compute Hosting mode, instance size, minimum/maximum capacity and expected active hours Data protection Retention, backups, replication and recovery requirements Network and monitoring Outbound/cross-region data, private endpoint count, log volume and retention

Search's allocated capacity is only part of its cost: inspect separately billed features and usage. For Cosmos DB, distinguish provisioned or autoscale capacity from serverless request consumption. A stopped VM can still incur disk and network charges.

docs.title: Optimize without changing the security contract
docs.text:
Start with idle or oversized capacity, unnecessary duplicate resources and excessive telemetry. Validate each proposed saving against service limits and workload acceptance tests.

  • Schedule supported development VMs, while preserving the connected-runner access needed for private deployments.
  • Tune Container Apps minimum replicas and workload-profile allocation using measured startup and latency requirements. Consumption hosting is a design choice, not a drop-in instruction to replace the deployed application.
  • Choose Search capacity and replica counts according to index size, throughput and availability requirements, not price alone.
  • Evaluate commitments only after measuring sustained utilization.
  • Set intentional log retention and avoid unnecessary content capture without losing operational or compliance evidence.
  • Reuse shared networking only when ownership, routing and access requirements are satisfied. Do not disable firewall, authentication or private access to meet an arbitrary savings percentage.

Removing a component is not routine cost cleanup. Back up data, review dependencies and explicitly authorize retirement. For Agent Landing Zone, follow the full-stack lifecycle guidance rather than deleting individual resources behind the deployment's state.

docs.title: Monitor actual spend
docs.text:
Use Azure Cost Management to group spend by resource and environment, set budgets/alerts and investigate unexpected usage. Budgets are notifications, not an automatic cap on spending. Review both platform-shared and workload-specific charges with their owners.

Useful pricing references:

  • Azure Pricing Calculator
  • Azure OpenAI pricing
  • Azure AI Search pricing
  • Container Apps pricing
  • Azure Monitor pricing

docs.title: Design Checklist
docs.text: Use this checklist when designing an AI workload landing zone, before approving a deployment, and when reviewing a significant change. For each applicable row, record your decision, owner and how you will verify it. Use the deployment documentation to identify which controls the selected template configures and which your team needs to implement.

docs.title: Compute and cost
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References C-R1 Where will models, agents and application components run? Evaluate scaling, network and operational needs separately for models and application components, then choose compute for each. Standardize where their requirements align. Compute decision guide CO-R1 What is the workload's monthly cost and usage model? Estimate the selected resources, model tokens, indexing and observability before deployment. Include optional services and separate shared-platform costs. Cost guide, Foundry cost planning CO-R2 Is model traffic predictable enough for provisioned throughput? Compare measured utilization and commitment costs with pay-as-you-go to choose the lower-cost option for the workload. If using spillover, design gateway routing and test quota exhaustion. Provisioned throughput, Multi-backend gateway CO-R3 Which model deployment type meets residency, latency and cost requirements? Compare regional, data-zone and global options for the chosen model. Verify processing-location requirements before choosing a lower advertised token price. Deployment types CO-R4 Which nonproduction resources can stop outside working hours? Schedule shutdown only for supported resources that can tolerate downtime. Check disks, networking and other charges that continue while compute is stopped. VM auto-shutdown

docs.title: Data
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References D-R1 Where are agent state, uploaded files and application data stored? Identify the selected Agent Service setup and its backing resources. Record retention, access, backup and deletion requirements separately for each data store. Standard agent setup D-R2 Which resources may be shared across projects? Review supported resource-sharing constraints and choose explicit isolation boundaries. Separate application storage from Agent Service backing storage where required. Capability hosts and backing resources D-R3 Does the workload need data from Microsoft Fabric? Evaluate the Fabric data agent's supported access model, permissions and regional availability before selecting it as an agent tool. Fabric data agent tool

docs.title: Governance
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References G-R1 Which policies apply to the deployed services? Assign relevant built-in or custom policies at the appropriate scope. Review audit results and exemptions before enforcing deny effects. AI services policies, Search policies G-R2 Which regulatory and organizational obligations apply? Map each obligation to required controls and verification results. Use policy initiatives to assess supported Azure controls and document any additional reviews needed to demonstrate compliance. NIST AI RMF, Regulatory compliance initiatives G-R3 How will responsible AI risks be evaluated? Define evaluation datasets, human review, acceptance thresholds and escalation for the actual agent tasks. Select evaluation tools that support the models, inputs and outputs in use. Generative AI evaluation G-R4 What content safety controls are needed? Select supported filters and Content Safety APIs for the model and modalities in use. Test prompts, outputs and failure handling. Configure access to tools and documents separately through authorization controls. Content Safety overview G-R5 Which models may teams deploy? Review the applicable model-deployment policies. Start in audit mode, assess impact, then enforce approved restrictions and remediate existing noncompliant deployments separately. Model deployment policies

docs.title: Identity and access
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References I-R1 How do services authenticate to one another? Prefer managed identity where supported, with narrowly scoped roles for each runtime principal. Keep deployment, project and runtime identities distinct. Managed identities I-R2 How is privileged human access controlled? Require MFA and use just-in-time privileged access where available. Use a private administrative path when resources are isolated. MFA, Privileged Identity Management I-R3 Can clients use Microsoft Entra ID rather than static keys? Use identity-based authentication where supported. Where a key is necessary, store it securely, limit distribution and define rotation and recovery. AI services authentication I-R4 Which sign-in conditions should be enforced? Evaluate risk, device and location policies for human access. Configure service authorization for workload identities and test those identities separately from interactive sign-in. Conditional Access I-R5 What can each user and service read or modify? Grant minimal control-plane and data-plane permissions at the smallest supported scope. Test retrieval with allowed and denied users to verify document access. Foundry RBAC I-R6 Can local key authentication be disabled? Inventory dependent clients, migrate them to Entra ID and verify their workflows before disabling local authentication where supported. Azure OpenAI managed identity authentication

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References M-R1 What signals establish workload health? Define service-level objectives for availability, latency, task outcomes and data freshness. Monitor models, resources and data against those objectives. AI workload management M-R2 Which failures require an alert? Enable applicable baseline alerts, assign a response owner and document the response procedure. Tune thresholds and test alert delivery. Azure Monitor Baseline Alerts M-R3 Can one failed request be traced across dependencies? Correlate application, model and retrieval calls. Protect prompts, documents and user data; content capture must be a deliberate privacy decision. Foundry tracing M-R4 Which resource logs must be retained? Configure supported diagnostic categories and retention for key services. Confirm that logs reach the intended destination and restrict access to them. Diagnostic settings M-R5 How will quality changes be detected? Re-evaluate representative tasks after model, prompt, tool and data changes. Investigate regressions before deciding whether to change data, prompts or models. Evaluation metrics M-R6 Can private connectivity failures be diagnosed? Test DNS, routes, TLS and service authorization separately from the affected network. Use network diagnostics supported by the resource. Network Watcher

docs.title: Reliability and resource organization
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References R-R1 What are the recovery time and recovery point objectives? Plan backup, restore and regional recovery for each stateful dependency. For a secondary region, prepare the required services, data recovery and application routing, then test failover against the recovery objectives. Azure OpenAI continuity, Storage disaster recovery, Cosmos DB backup RO-R1 Are the required services and models available in the selected regions? Check the current service, model, deployment-type and feature availability references when choosing regions and again before deployment. Products by region, Model availability RO-R2 Is there enough quota for every resource to be created? Count all selected service instances, including separate Agent Service backing resources. Validate regional model capacity and request increases before deployment. Azure limits and quotas RO-R3 How will growth affect subscription and regional limits? Record capacity headroom, ownership and the process for requesting quota. Run preflight checks and confirm current service capacity when scheduling the deployment. Quota overview RO-R4 What are the account, project and billing boundaries? Align Foundry accounts and projects with access, network and operational requirements. Identify which isolation controls apply at account level and which apply at project level. Foundry architecture

docs.title: Security
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References S-R1 Which deployed AI risks can be monitored? Evaluate Defender for Cloud's supported AI posture and threat-protection features, coverage, prerequisites and cost for this workload. AI security posture S-R2 Which service security controls are required? Map applicable Azure security baselines and Well-Architected guidance to the services actually deployed. Security baselines, Service guides S-R3 How is sensitive data discovered and protected? Assess data classification, oversharing and insider-risk requirements. Evaluate Purview coverage and licensing, and configure retrieval permissions in the source and application authorization paths. Purview Insider Risk Management S-R4 Which AI-specific attack paths need testing? Threat-model tools, model calls, retrieved content and data access. Use established AI risk frameworks to define tests and mitigations. MITRE ATLAS, OWASP generative AI risks S-R5 How will prompt injection be handled? Evaluate Prompt Shields for supported inputs and test failures. Keep tool permissions and document authorization enforced independently of model output. Prompt Shields

docs.title: Networking
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References N-R1 Does public ingress need DDoS protection? Identify public endpoints and check the supported protection for each resource type. Reuse platform DDoS protection for eligible public IP resources. DDoS Protection overview N-R2 How will operators reach private resources? Use an approved VPN, connected runner or jumpbox. Reuse central Bastion and administrative access where available, keeping VM administration on an approved private path. Azure Bastion N-R3 Which services require private endpoints? Design private ingress and service-managed outbound links separately. Select networking controls for the Foundry resource type in use: account/project or hub-based. Verify DNS and the intended private path before disabling public access. Foundry private networking N-R4 Where should NSGs enforce traffic policy? Apply supported NSG rules to subnets or network interfaces. Preserve service-specific subnet and platform connectivity requirements. Network security groups N-R5 Is a regional or global web application firewall needed? Select Application Gateway or Front Door according to ingress requirements. Verify routing, authentication and backend access as well as WAF rules. Azure WAF N-R6 Does the workload need an AI gateway? Evaluate API Management for routing, token controls and authentication. Confirm tier support and configure policies explicitly. Avoid logging raw prompts or responses by default. AI gateway capabilities N-R7 Which outbound traffic must traverse a firewall? Reuse a platform firewall where appropriate. Verify routes, supported service paths and required destinations before enforcing egress restrictions. Azure Firewall N-R8 How will private service names resolve from every client network? Plan zone links, conditional forwarding and connected-network resolution. Configure routes and service permissions alongside DNS so clients can reach and use the resolved endpoints. Private endpoint DNS integration N-R9 What outbound destinations are allowed? Restrict egress to verified service and build dependencies where supported. Review exceptions and test recovery without opening unrestricted internet access as a troubleshooting shortcut. AI services data-loss prevention

docs.title: How do Azure Landing Zones and AI Landing Zones relate?
docs.text:
Azure Landing Zones distinguish between a platform landing zone, which provides shared services and governance, and workload landing zones, which contain the resources for individual workloads.

An AI Landing Zone is a workload landing zone designed for AI services and applications. It can integrate with an existing platform landing zone or provide a standalone foundation when shared platform services are not available.

docs.title: Should I integrate with a platform landing zone or deploy standalone?
docs.text:
Use platform integration when your organization already provides shared connectivity, DNS, firewall and administrative access. This keeps those services centrally managed while AI-specific resources remain in the workload landing zone.

A standalone deployment is useful when no shared platform exists or the workload needs a separately managed foundation. Its team must then operate the required networking and governance services. Standalone does not, by itself, guarantee network isolation or remove the need for security controls.

See the Azure Landing Zones guidance and design checklist before choosing a deployment model.

docs.title: Customize the incorporated foundation
docs.text: The maintained Bicep foundation lives in Azure/agent-landing-zone under infra/. It is regular repository-owned source, not a Git submodule or a separate checkout to initialize. Foundation changes are reviewed and released with the platform.

docs.title: Application and infrastructure boundaries
docs.text: For a different application, use the application-definition contract. Keep application images and runtime configuration outside foundation modules. Use Deploy infrastructure only when the foundation is needed before application deployment, or Deploy the full stack for both.

docs.title: Parameters and lifecycle
docs.text:
Keep azure.yaml, manifest.json, the root main.parameters.json, infra/, config/, contracts/ and scripts/ together at the reviewed platform revision. Run azd from the platform root.

The platform hooks validate the selected application and immutable environment binding, compose the root parameters into infra/main.parameters.json, and run foundation preflight. Do not edit the generated parameter copy or replace the hooks with submodule initialization scripts. See How it works and Deployment settings.

Use azd env set for documented environment variables that take one value, such as NETWORK_ISOLATION. Settings containing lists ([...]) or groups of named fields ({...}) belong in the reviewed root main.parameters.json file. Parameters without a documented environment-variable equivalent also go in that file.

Keep the JSON value types shown in the parameter examples: for instance, use true for a boolean, not the text "true", and keep lists and objects in their original JSON format. Follow the parameter reference rather than copying legacy hook starters.

docs.title: Changes and upgrades
docs.text:
Review changes to the incorporated Bicep source with their compatible platform parameters, hooks and contracts. manifest.json infra.source records where the foundation was incorporated from; it does not select a separate infrastructure checkout at deployment time.

Upgrade through a coordinated platform release and preserve the previous compatible revision and approved inputs for rollback. Follow the upgrade and rollback runbook rather than fetching a foundation tag into infra/.

docs.title: Deployed Resources & Cost Estimates
docs.text:
This page answers the two questions operators always ask before approving an AI Landing Zone deployment:

  1. What does this template actually deploy? — every resource, broken down by always-on baseline, default-on (toggleable), BYO-capable, and opt-in add-on.
  2. What will it cost? — an order-of-magnitude monthly estimate for three common scenarios, with the variable (token / call / data) drivers called out separately.

Foundation scope

This inventory describes native Bicep foundation building blocks under Agent Landing Zone's infra/, not the Agent application footprint. Agent Landing Zone composes its own services, topology and component selection. Foundry backing resources are separate from application stores, and conditional creation/reuse applies across all resource families.

Check the selected source's current parameters, deployment preview and Agent choices. Cost scenarios below are dated example configurations, not current defaults or full Agent deployment quotes.

Cost figures are estimates, not a quote

All numbers here are USD/month, East US 2 PAYG retail pricing, as of 2026-05-29, with empty data and a quiet workload (~1 user). Your bill will vary with region, currency, EA/MCA discounts, reserved capacity, autoscale behavior, data volumes, model token consumption, AI Search index size, and Application Gateway capacity units. Always validate with the Azure Pricing Calculator before committing.

docs.title: The "Standard Agent Setup" gotcha — read this first
docs.text:
By default the landing zone deploys AI Foundry with the Standard Agent Setup (deployAiFoundry=true + deployAfProject=true + deployAAfAgentSvc=true). The Agent Service requires its own data plane, so when this combination is on the template provisions a second, dedicated set of supporting resources just for Foundry:

Resource family Default count when Agent Service is enabled Why Azure AI Search 2 — one for Foundry agents, one for the workload Agent Service stores agent state, thread embeddings, and tool indices in its own Search service so workload index churn never affects agents Storage account 2 — one for Foundry artifacts, one for workload blobs Agent files, run outputs, and Foundry connections live in the Foundry-owned account Cosmos DB account 2 — one for Foundry agent threads/state, one for workload documents Foundry-owned account holds thread/run/message documents Key Vault 1 workload vault, plus an optional VM vault deployVmKeyVault=false by default; a VM vault requires explicit selection and applicable resource conditions

How to opt out of the duplicate Foundry data plane

  • Bring your own — set aiSearchResourceId, aiFoundryStorageAccountResourceId, and aiFoundryCosmosDBAccountResourceId to existing resource IDs of a dedicated Foundry-only trio that belongs exclusively to this Foundry instance. Don't share the Agent Service data plane with the workload or with other Foundry instances — only use BYO to reattach a trio already provisioned out-of-band for this same Foundry.
  • Disable the Agent Service — set deployAAfAgentSvc=false (and optionally deployAfProject=false). The Foundry account stays, but the second Search / Storage / Cosmos are not created. Use this when you only need model deployments and don't use Foundry agents.
  • Foundry AI Search defaults to 1 partition × 1 replica — scale it up to 3 replicas in-place if you need Azure AI Search's read/write SLA.

docs.title: Estimated monthly cost — by scenario
docs.text:
The three scenarios correspond to the most common shapes operators ask about. Each shows:

  • Fixed monthly cost — what you pay even with zero traffic and empty data (the resource exists and is billed by allocation).
  • Variable driver — what makes the line grow over the fixed floor.

Quick mental model

Most of the fixed cost comes from a small number of allocation-based resources: the two AI Search services, Application Gateway (if any), Azure Firewall (if any), Bastion, ACR Premium, App Configuration, and any pinned D4 workload-profile node. Everything else is essentially zero at idle but scales fast with use.

docs.title: Scenario 1 — Basic deployment (public, no network isolation)
docs.text:
This cost example is for an approved, short-lived sandbox, demonstration or development/test evaluation using synthetic or non-sensitive data. It is not the recommended production setup: service endpoints remain public, even when authentication is required.

networkIsolation        = false
deployAzureFirewall     = false   (auto-suppressed when NI is off)
deployJumpbox / Bastion / NatGateway = false (defaults to NI; no VNet)
publicIngress.enabled   = false
deployAAfAgentSvc       = true    (default — Standard Agent Setup)
deployAcrTaskAgentPool  = false   (private pool is not created in this public scenario)
deployGroundingWithBing = true    (explicit scenario choice; native foundation default is false)
Resource Fixed monthly Variable driver AI Foundry account + project $0 Per-token model usage Model: gpt-5-nano (GlobalStandard, cap 40) $0 ~$0.05 / 1M input tokens, ~$0.40 / 1M output tokens — pay-as-you-go Model: text-embedding-3-large (Standard, cap 10) $0 ~$0.13 / 1M tokens Grounding with Bing (S1) $0 ~$3 per 1,000 transactions Foundry AI Search (Standard, 1p × 1r) ~$245 Index storage; queries scale with QPS. Scale to 3r for read/write SLA (~$735/mo) Foundry Storage (Standard_LRS, Hot) ~$1 ~$0.018 / GB + ~$0.005 / 10K ops Foundry Cosmos DB (autoscale) ~$24 Min 400 RU/s autoscale floor + storage Workload AI Search (Standard, 1p × 1r) ~$245 Index storage; queries scale with QPS Workload Storage (Standard_LRS, Hot) ~$1 ~$0.018 / GB + ~$0.005 / 10K ops Workload Cosmos DB (serverless) $0 ~$0.25 / 1M RU + ~$0.25 / GB-month Workload Key Vault (Standard) $0 ~$0.03 / 10K operations Container Apps Environment — D4 workload-profile node (pinned by orchestrator min_replicas=1) ~$290 Additional D4 instances when scaled up Container Apps Environment — Consumption profile $0 vCPU-s + GiB-s per request Container Registry (Premium) ~$50 Storage above 500 GB + geo-replication if enabled ACR build-agent pool (S1, on-demand) $0 ~$0.50 / build-hour App Configuration (Standard) ~$36 Per-request above the included quota Log Analytics workspace $0 ~$2.30 / GB ingested Application Insights $0 (Bundled into Log Analytics billing) Subtotal — Basic ~$892 / month + token / data / request usage

docs.title: Scenario 2 — Zero Trust (private, internal users only)
docs.text:
networkIsolation        = true
deployAzureFirewall     = true     (default when NI; share hub FW to skip)
deployJumpbox           = true     (default = NI)
deployBastion           = true     (default = NI && deployJumpbox)
deployNatGateway        = true     (default = NI && deployJumpbox)
deployVmKeyVault        = true     (explicit scenario choice; current default is false)
publicIngress.enabled   = false

Best for: production internal workloads — users reach the app over ExpressRoute / VPN / Bastion; no public ingress.

Adds, on top of Scenario 1:

Resource Fixed monthly Variable driver VNet + subnets + NSGs + Private DNS zones (×15) ~$8 $0.50 / DNS zone / mo Private endpoints (~13–15) ~$105 ~$7.30 each + ~$0.01 / GB processed Azure Firewall (Standard) ~$912 + ~$0.016 / GB processed Public IP (firewall) ~$4 — Azure Bastion (Standard) ~$140 + ~$0.09 / GB outbound Jumpbox VM (Standard_D2s_v3 + 128 GB P10) ~$87 (~$70 VM + ~$17 disk) — VM Key Vault (Standard) $0 ~$0.03 / 10K operations NAT Gateway ~$32 + ~$0.045 / GB processed Public IP (NAT) ~$4 — Zero Trust additions subtotal ~$1,292 / month + per-GB processing Subtotal — ZTA (Basic + ZT) ~$2,184 / month + token / data / request usage

Where Zero Trust cost actually goes

Roughly 70 % of the ZT-only surcharge is Azure Firewall (~$912). If your platform team already operates a hub Firewall, set deployAzureFirewall=false and configure hubIntegrationEgressNextHopIp=<hub-firewall-private-IP>. The spoke then reuses the hub's firewall and the ZT delta drops to ~$380/month. See Hub-and-Spoke Topology.

docs.title: Scenario 3 — Zero Trust + Application Gateway (external users)
docs.text:
(everything from Scenario 2, plus)
publicIngress.enabled   = true   # exposes a private Container App via App Gateway WAF v2

Best for: production workloads that need to serve external users over the public internet while keeping the workload itself private (the frontend Container App is reachable only through the gateway).

Adds, on top of Scenario 2:

Resource Fixed monthly Variable driver Application Gateway WAF v2 (1 instance, minimum) ~$250 + ~$0.0072 / capacity-unit-hour; scales with throughput, TLS, and WAF rules Public IP (App Gateway) ~$4 — WAF policy $0 — App Gateway additions subtotal ~$254 / month + capacity-unit consumption Subtotal — ZTA + App Gateway (Basic + ZT + AppGW) ~$2,438 / month + token / data / request usage

See Public Ingress with Application Gateway for the topology and parameters.

docs.title: Cost comparison at a glance
docs.text:
Scenario Fixed monthly floor Best for 1. Basic ~$892 Sandbox, demo, dev/test, public evaluation 2. Zero Trust (internal) ~$2,184 Production for internal users (VPN / ExpressRoute / Bastion) 3. Zero Trust + App Gateway ~$2,438 Production for external users with WAF-protected public ingress

Variable model / data / processing cost applies to all three and depends entirely on traffic.

Concrete levers to lower the floor

Lever Savings (approx.) Trade-off deployAAfAgentSvc=false — turn off Standard Agent Setup if you don't use Foundry agents ~$270/mo (drops Foundry Search + Cosmos) No Agent Service; you keep models, projects, and your own workload Search aiSearchResourceId=<existing> — reattach Foundry to a dedicated Search service it already exclusively owns (e.g. one provisioned out-of-band for this same Foundry instance) ~$245/mo Only valid when the Search service is exclusively dedicated to this Foundry account; do not share it with the workload or with other Foundry instances Drop the D4 workload profile (use Consumption-only) and remove min_replicas=1 from orchestrator ~$290/mo Cold-start latency on first request deployAzureFirewall=false + hubIntegrationEgressNextHopIp=… (share hub FW) ~$912/mo (ZT scenarios only) Requires a hub firewall already operated by the platform team BYO Log Analytics / App Insights (existingLogAnalyticsWorkspaceResourceId, existingApplicationInsightsResourceId) Avoids duplicate workspaces Workspace governed centrally BYO Private DNS zones (any of the 15 existingPrivateDnsZone*ResourceId params) $0.50/zone/mo + admin time Zones owned by the platform team deployGroundingWithBing=false if you don't use Bing-grounded answers $0 fixed; saves variable Bing query cost No Bing grounding Deallocate the Jumpbox VM when idle ~$70/mo (compute only; disk continues) Manual stop/start

Disabling unused Agent Service backing resources and moving the placeholder runtime off D4 gives the illustrative reduction from ~$892 to ~$332/month. Do not count Foundry Search reuse as an additional saving after already removing Agent Service. Shared resources still incur costs in their owning scope.

docs.title: Methodology and caveats
docs.text:
• Pricing snapshot: Azure retail PAYG, East US 2, 2026-05-29.
  • Currency: USD; convert at your contract rate.
  • Discounts not applied: EA, MCA, CSP, reservations, savings plans, Azure Hybrid Benefit, dev/test rates — all of these can materially lower the floor.
  • Empty-data assumption: Storage, Log Analytics, and Cosmos data charges are shown as ~$0 fixed because the resource itself is free at zero bytes; they grow linearly with data.
  • Quiet workload assumption: variable token / call / processing line items are listed without a number because they depend entirely on your traffic — model the load you actually expect in the Pricing Calculator.
  • Foundry Cosmos floor reflects the minimum autoscale band (400 RU/s) commonly used by the AVM Foundry module; the exact number depends on the Foundry CapabilityHost configuration.
  • Container Apps: the D4 workload-profile baseline assumes 1 node remains active because the default orchestrator app pins min_replicas=1 on profile_name: "main". With Consumption-only deployments the baseline drops to $0.
  • Region matters: AI Search, Azure Firewall, and Application Gateway can vary by ±20 % across regions.
  • Page is a snapshot, not a contract: when in doubt, the Azure Pricing Calculator is the source of truth.

docs.title: Hub-and-spoke network reference
docs.text:
A private spoke can reuse an existing hub's controlled egress, operator access, DNS and monitoring rather than recreate them. This page defines the ownership and inputs for that design. It does not deploy a hub or provide a separate landing-zone deployment recipe.

Apply these choices in Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack. For a network without shared hub dependencies, use the standalone reference.

docs.title: Agree ownership and permissions
docs.text:
Owner Contract before deployment Workload team Dedicated spoke scope, nonoverlapping addresses, workload resources, private endpoints and identities Hub/network team Hub VNet, firewall policy, forward/return routes, both peering directions, Bastion/VPN and shared route tables DNS team Zone inventory, zone groups/records, links or resolver forwarding, cross-scope permissions and conflict prevention Monitoring team Shared workspace/component access, retention and any central Azure Monitor Private Link Scope (AMPLS)

Contributor and role-assignment authority on the workload do not automatically authorize hub operations. Peering needs permissions at both VNet scopes, including remote peer/action. Shared-zone operations need zone join access; link creation needs zone/link write and VNet join permissions. Authorize monitoring access separately. Cross-subscription resources require appropriate provider registration and scoped access.

The deployment host needs private DNS resolution and network/data-plane access. An ACR Tasks pool is not a connected deployment host. Bastion is interactive VM access, not a VPN for a workstation.

Test fixtures are not shared-platform deployments

Foundation infra/tests/hub/ and infra/tests/scripts/ simulate a hub. Do not deploy them into an operational connectivity subscription or copy their empty route, disabled Search, skipped bootstrap or skipped preflight settings.

docs.title: Address and subnet contract
docs.text:
Review the complete address plan against hub, spokes, VPN/on-premises and future networks. A VNet prefix alone does not update its default subnets. Store the approved native parameters in the selected source's root parameter file.

For an existing VNet, preserve externally owned subnets, NSGs and delegations. With USE_EXISTING_VNET=true, the template does not create forward peering; the network team owns both directions. Do not update isolated existing subnets with native root deployNsgs=false: retain managed NSGs or set DEPLOY_SUBNETS=false and have the network owner prepare the complete configuration.

docs.title: Hub integration inputs
docs.text:
DEPLOYMENT_MODE=ailz-integrated records intent. The explicit inputs below select resources and behavior; the preset alone does not enable isolation or wire a hub.

Environment input Intended value or role NETWORK_ISOLATION true DEPLOY_AZURE_FIREWALL false when using hub egress DEPLOY_BASTION, DEPLOY_NAT_GATEWAY false when not deploying local counterparts DEPLOY_JUMPBOX Explicit choice; true creates a workload jumpbox EXISTING_BASTION_RESOURCE_ID Exact approved hub Bastion ID HUB_INTEGRATION_HUB_VNET_RESOURCE_ID Exact hub VNet ID HUB_INTEGRATION_CREATE_HUB_PEERING true creates spoke→hub for a new isolated VNet; false leaves it externally managed HUB_INTEGRATION_EGRESS_NEXT_HOP_IP Hub firewall/NVA private IP for the workload default route HUB_INTEGRATION_EXISTING_ROUTE_TABLE_RESOURCE_ID Alternative approved route table; mutually exclusive with next-hop IP EXISTING_LOG_ANALYTICS_WORKSPACE_RESOURCE_ID Approved shared workspace, if reused EXISTING_APPLICATION_INSIGHTS_RESOURCE_ID Optional reused component; also supply its protected EXISTING_APPLICATION_INSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING

With a next-hop IP, the template creates a spoke route table with 0.0.0.0/0 to the hub appliance. A supplied route table is reused, not rewritten. Neither input being set does not enforce hub egress. Confirm region, association permissions and routes before choosing a shared table.

Allow required spoke source CIDRs and destinations before bootstrap, image pulls and data-plane configuration. Review the foundation firewall source and the Agent platform's build-egress requirements. Check return paths, DNS transport, NSGs and forwarded traffic rather than opening unrestricted Internet access. Peering is not transitive.

Reusing a central workspace does not automatically create local AMPLS. Local private monitoring has its own conditions; the central monitoring owner must provide private ingestion/query connectivity when needed. Confirm a reused Application Insights component belongs to the selected workspace. Do not enable mixed workspaces just to suppress validation.

docs.title: Private DNS ownership
docs.text:
Choose one ownership model:

Model Responsibility Locally managed Template creates applicable zones and links Per-zone BYO Exact existing zone IDs suppress local creation and automatic VNet links; owners supply links/resolution Azure Policy-managed POLICY_MANAGED_PRIVATE_DNS=true suppresses template DNS zones/zone groups; clear BYO overrides and agree the Policy-owned records/groups/links

Peering does not propagate DNS zone links. Every client VNet needs a direct link or explicit DNS resolver/forwarding path to a linked network. With custom DNS, a zone link alone does not reconfigure clients. Avoid duplicate authoritative zones that hide records.

Use actual approved zone IDs, not guessed names or synthesized cross-scope IDs. The following suffixes complete EXISTING_PRIVATE_DNS_ZONE_<SUFFIX>_RESOURCE_ID for Azure public cloud:

Suffix Zone COGSVCS privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com OPENAI privatelink.openai.azure.com AISERVICES privatelink.services.ai.azure.com SEARCH privatelink.search.windows.net COSMOS privatelink.documents.azure.com BLOB privatelink.blob.core.windows.net KEYVAULT privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net APPCONFIG privatelink.azconfig.io CONTAINERAPPS privatelink.<region>.azurecontainerapps.io — must match the deployment region ACR privatelink.azurecr.io AZUREMONITOR privatelink.monitor.azure.com OMSOPSINSIGHTS privatelink.oms.opinsights.azure.com ODSOPSINSIGHTS privatelink.ods.opinsights.azure.com AZUREAUTOMATION privatelink.agentsvc.azure.automation.net APPINSIGHTS privatelink.applicationinsights.io

Monitoring overrides apply only when the corresponding local private-monitoring resources are created; they do not configure a central AMPLS. Provide only applicable zones. See the full parameter reference. Use unique link names where multiple spokes share zones; DNS_ZONE_LINK_SUFFIX only affects links the template itself creates.

docs.title: Peering and bootstrap ordering
docs.text:
A fresh spoke can require the network operator during the first provision. As soon as the VNet exists, complete the authorized reverse peering and DNS links so bootstrap and private configuration can resolve and reach dependencies. Waiting for those stages to finish first can cause a recoverable failure.

The template creates spoke→hub only, for a new isolated VNet when enabled. The hub owner creates the matching hub→spoke peering with forwarded traffic and VNet access. If peering is externally managed or the VNet is BYO, the network owner creates both. Record exact spoke-specific names for retirement.

Gateway transit is a separate design choice. To consume the hub's gateway, the hub side allows gateway transit and the spoke uses remote gateways (HUB_INTEGRATION_PEERING_USE_REMOTE_GATEWAYS=true for template-managed peering). Do not set the spoke's ALLOW_GATEWAY_TRANSIT to consume a hub gateway; that is the opposite direction.

docs.title: Verify the network contract
docs.text:
Use exact selected names and IDs:

az network vnet peering list -g <hub-resource-group> --vnet-name <hub-vnet> \
  --subscription <hub-subscription-id> -o table
az network vnet peering list -g <spoke-resource-group> --vnet-name <spoke-vnet> \
  --subscription <spoke-subscription-id> -o table
az network private-dns link vnet list -g <dns-resource-group> \
  --zone-name <private-zone-name> --subscription <dns-subscription-id> -o table

Expect both peerings Connected with the approved forwarded-traffic/gateway settings, and required DNS links Completed. Inspect effective routes on a running workload/jumpbox NIC and route-table associations on managed subnets:

az network nic show-effective-route-table --ids <running-jumpbox-nic-id> -o table
az network vnet subnet list -g <spoke-resource-group> --vnet-name <spoke-vnet> \
  --query "[].{name:name,prefix:addressPrefix,routeTable:routeTable.id}" -o table

Expect the intended hub VirtualAppliance default route or approved shared route policy. Confirm the actual deployment host's private DNS/TCP/TLS path with the standalone connectivity checks. Check service authorization and a new test trace in the intended workspace. Connected alone proves none of those data-plane results.

For interactive access, use the hub's Bastion or approved VPN, not a local Bastion that this design disabled. Native RDP requires supported client/SKU and tunneling. An authorized portal password reset is safer than placing credentials in shell history or adding a public VM IP.

docs.title: Recovery and spoke retirement
docs.text:
Symptom Inspect before retry Peering not connected Both IDs, overlap, remote-scope permissions and reverse peering Public/NXDOMAIN answers inside the network Zone IDs, groups/records, links for the actual client VNet and resolver forwarding Bootstrap, pull or package timeout Effective UDR/NSG, reverse peering and firewall denies for the actual source subnet/destination Missing central telemetry Workspace/component permissions and association, AMPLS, DNS and ingestion/query paths Quota, Policy or expired token Failed deployment operations and the specific approved capacity, policy or authentication repair

Retry with the same approved revision, parameters and environment after repair; do not disable Search, open endpoints or skip checks for a green result. Use foundation reconfiguration.

For safe removal, obtain workload/data-retention approval and inventory dependencies first. Retire only recorded reverse peering and DNS links dedicated to this spoke with their owners. Preserve shared zones, hub VNet, Bastion, firewall, route tables, workspace and Application Insights. Confirm other spokes remain healthy.

docs.title: Bicep documentation
docs.text: This page is no longer part of the Bicep documentation flow. Continue with How to Deploy.

docs.title: Bicep foundation overview
docs.text: The AI Landing Zone Bicep foundation is maintained in Azure/agent-landing-zone under infra/. It is repository-owned source, reviewed and released with Agent Landing Zone, alongside application composition, service configuration and deployment hooks. Run the lifecycle from the Agent Landing Zone repository root, not infra/.

docs.title: Deployment modes
docs.text:
The network design is distinct from the Agent application's orchestrator topology. deploymentMode records intent; explicit flags and resource IDs determine the actual resources, routing and reuse.

For production or sensitive data, set NETWORK_ISOLATION=true explicitly, whether you manage a standalone network or use an existing hub. The template currently defaults to false, leaving service endpoints public. Reserve that option for approved, short-lived evaluations without sensitive data.

Foundation shape Intent Reference Self-contained standalone; use NETWORK_ISOLATION=true for the recommended private network Standalone network Existing hub integration ailz-integrated; explicit private networking, hub routing, peering, DNS and shared-service inputs Hub-and-spoke network

The hub test fixture is not a third production topology. Neither preset automatically supplies an operational hub, DNS resolver or connected deployment host.

docs.title: What gets deployed
docs.text:
Enabled parameters select Foundry/model services, workload data services, container runtimes, configuration/secrets, observability, network resources and optional add-ons. Service-specific conditions and existing-resource inputs determine which are created, reused or omitted.

Infrastructure-only provisioning can leave selected Container Apps running placeholder images; these are not the deployed Agent Application. Foundry Agent Service backing resources are distinct from workload data stores. Review the resource inventory and cost scenarios for foundation scope and the parameter reference for supported inputs. Do not infer the selected application footprint from native Bicep defaults alone.

docs.title: Access and validation
docs.text:
Managed identities and scoped role assignments provide service-to-service access; Permissions describes the foundation's default assignments. Effective application grants depend on the selected definition, capabilities and topology.

The preprovision hook checks inputs, BYO resource references, network constraints and regional readiness. A passing check is not proof of regional capacity, private DNS resolution, data-plane authorization or application readiness. Resolve findings instead of skipping the checks.

docs.title: Use the canonical runbooks
docs.text:
• Deploy infrastructure only — provision the incorporated foundation without application image deployment.
  • Deploy the full stack — deploy the Agent foundation and selected application.

For implementation details, see Bicep deployment considerations, parameterization and Application Gateway ingress.

docs.title: Parameterization
docs.text:
This reference describes native parameters of the Bicep foundation maintained in Agent Landing Zone's infra/. The platform's root main.parameters.json supplies reviewed values and ${VARIABLE_NAME} substitutions. Use azd env set only for substitutions actually present in that file; native arrays and objects need reviewed file changes.

Agent Landing Zone composes its own root parameter file and regenerates infra/main.parameters.json. Its definition and topology can override foundation choices. See Agent configuration rather than assuming every foundation deploy toggle is an Agent environment variable. Execute changes through the infrastructure or full-stack runbook.

# Example: set a parameter via azd
azd env set NETWORK_ISOLATION true

Tip

Parameters set via azd env set are stored locally in the azd environment and override the defaults in main.parameters.json at provisioning time. This only works for parameters whose default value uses the ${...} syntax.

docs.title: Solution Storage controls
docs.text:
These three inputs apply only to the solution Storage account controlled by deployStorageAccount, not auxiliary AI Foundry Storage, VM storage, or other services. The Storage AVM dependency remains br/public:avm/res/storage/storage-account:0.26.2.

Parameter Bicep type Default Description storageAccountNetworkAclsBypass String-literal union 'AzureServices' Value passed to the solution account's networkAcls.bypass. Only the exact strings listed below are accepted. storageAccountResourceAccessRules Array of sealed objects with required resourceId: string and tenantId: string fields [] Complete desired list of resource-instance network rules passed to networkAcls.resourceAccessRules. Additional object properties are not accepted. storageAccountAllowSharedKeyAccess bool true Value passed to allowSharedKeyAccess. Disabling Shared Key authorization is an explicit, compatibility-sensitive opt-in.

The bypass union accepts exactly these eight values, with the spelling, comma-space separators, and ordering shown:

  • 'None'
  • 'AzureServices'
  • 'Logging'
  • 'Metrics'
  • 'AzureServices, Logging'
  • 'AzureServices, Metrics'
  • 'AzureServices, Logging, Metrics'
  • 'Logging, Metrics'

Do not combine None with another value or use a differently ordered or unspaced string.

docs.title: Native parameter values and defaults
docs.text:
These inputs use native JSON values in main.parameters.json: a string, an array of objects, and a boolean. They do not introduce environment-variable substitutions, environment-variable names, or JSON-string aliases. In particular, do not quote booleans or serialize the rules array into a string.

Top-level null selects defaults

Bicep 0.42.1 treats an explicit top-level null for these defaulted parameters as omission/default selection: AzureServices, [], and true, respectively. This is compiler behavior, not a new runtime fallback or a change to product defaults. For the stricter profile, explicitly set bypass to None and Shared Key access to false, not null; use [] when no resource-instance exceptions are desired.

This top-level behavior does not permit malformed nested rule fields. Each rule still requires non-empty string resourceId and tenantId fields; missing fields, nested null, wrong types, empty strings, and extra properties are invalid. Wrong bypass enum values and other wrong parameter types remain invalid.

Omitting all three inputs from a compatible parameter file uses the defaults. The equivalent explicit defaults are shown below as a fragment of the file's parameters object, not as a complete deployment parameter file:

{
  "storageAccountNetworkAclsBypass": {
    "value": "AzureServices"
  },
  "storageAccountResourceAccessRules": {
    "value": []
  },
  "storageAccountAllowSharedKeyAccess": {
    "value": true
  }
}

Keep customizations in the platform's reviewed, version-controlled root main.parameters.json. The platform hooks compose infra/main.parameters.json; do not patch that generated copy or change the pinned AVM to apply these settings. See foundation customization and the deployment and migration guidance.

docs.title: Network rules are desired state, not discovered exceptions
docs.text:
storageAccountResourceAccessRules declares the entire desired rules list. A redeployment removes resource-instance rules not included in it, including undesired or manually added exceptions. An empty array, including the omitted-input default, does not preserve rules that exist on the live account. There is no live-state merge or automatic discovery of Defender scanner exceptions.

Each entry must use the exact, approved, existing Azure resource's full ARM resource ID and its tenant ID. Do not use wildcards, tenant/subscription/resource-group-wide scopes, or a synthesized scanner ID. Resource instances must belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant as the Storage account, although their subscriptions can differ.

A sealed object validates the input shape, not the resource's existence, supported type, tenant eligibility, or permissions; those remain Azure-side checks.

A resource-instance network rule provides network eligibility, not data permissions. The resource's managed identity still needs the appropriate data-plane authorization, managed separately.

These inputs do not change the existing networkIsolation, public network access (PNA), allowedIpRanges, defaultAction, or private-endpoint behavior. Bypass None alone does not make an account private. Conversely, PNA Disabled does not make trusted-service or resource-instance exceptions irrelevant: previously configured exceptions can remain effective. Review them explicitly using the Storage firewall limitations and network access rules.

An approved existing Defender scanner can be included explicitly in the rules list when needed. These inputs do not enable a Defender plan or create a scanner, its managed identity, or role assignments. Defender's own configuration is a separate prerequisite; see resources deployed by malware scanning.

docs.title: Shared Key compatibility boundary
docs.text:
Before opting into storageAccountAllowSharedKeyAccess=false, inventory and migrate all account-key clients, key-based connection strings, service SAS and account SAS consumers, and Azure Files clients and tools. Validate each required protocol and workflow before rollout.

Microsoft Entra authorization and Blob user delegation SAS are distinct from key-signed service/account SAS; disabling Shared Key does not disable the former, but they still require suitable network access and data permissions. See prevent Shared Key authorization.

This is a data-plane authorization control, not a promise of a key-free management-plane deployment. AVM 0.26.2 retains secure outputs that use listKeys; setting this input to false does not remove those outputs or their management-plane requirements.

docs.title: Deploy toggles
docs.text:
Each toggle controls whether a specific service is provisioned. Set to true to deploy or false to skip.

Parameter Default Description deployAiFoundry true AI Foundry account and project deployAiFoundrySubnet true Foundry Agent Service subnet association; deployAgentSubnet independently controls subnet creation deployAppConfig true Azure App Configuration store deployAppInsights true Application Insights instance deployCosmosDb true Azure Cosmos DB account and database deployContainerApps true Container Apps (based on containerAppsList) deployContainerRegistry true Azure Container Registry deployContainerEnv true Container Apps Environment deployNsgs true Network Security Groups deployMcp true MCP (Model Context Protocol) server deployGroundingWithBing false Bing Grounding service deployKeyVault true Azure Key Vault deployVmKeyVault — Separate Key Vault for VM secrets (DEPLOY_VM_KEY_VAULT) deployLogAnalytics true Log Analytics workspace deploySearchService true Azure AI Search service deployStorageAccount true Azure Storage account deployJumpbox null (inherits from preset) Jumpbox VM deployBastion null (inherits from preset) Azure Bastion host deployNatGateway null (inherits from preset) NAT Gateway for outbound traffic deploySoftware true Pre-install development tools on the Jumpbox VM

Jumpbox, Bastion, and NAT Gateway

These components are controlled independently with deployJumpbox, deployBastion, and deployNatGateway, so each topology can choose only the pieces it needs.

docs.title: Resource naming
docs.text:
By default, generated resource names follow the Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) pattern type-workload-environment-region-instance, for example kv-a1b2c3-dev-eus2-001. You do not have to set anything: every CAF token has a safe default, so a plain azd provision produces valid, readable names.

Parameter Env variable Default Description resourceNamingMode RESOURCE_NAMING_MODE caf Naming strategy: caf (default) or legacy (older resourceToken-based names). cafWorkloadName CAF_WORKLOAD_NAME short deterministic hash Workload token. When empty, derived from subscription, environment, and location. Override with a meaningful name such as contosoai. cafEnvironmentName CAF_ENVIRONMENT_NAME azd environment name Environment token, for example dev or prod. cafRegionName CAF_REGION_NAME mapped from AZURE_LOCATION Region token. eastus2 becomes eus2. cafInstance CAF_INSTANCE 001 Instance token. Increment only for a second parallel copy of the same workload in the same environment and region.

Names are length-bounded automatically so they stay within Azure limits (storage 24, Key Vault 24, Container Apps environment 32, and so on). Because the tokens are deterministic, redeploying the same environment produces the same names, so naming stays idempotent.

Override a single token

azd env set CAF_WORKLOAD_NAME contosoai

Upgrading an existing deployment

CAF is now the default. To keep the older resourceToken-based names and avoid renaming existing resources, pin the legacy mode before provisioning: 

azd env set RESOURCE_NAMING_MODE legacy

docs.text:

docs.title: Existing resource IDs (BYO)
docs.text:
All of the parameters below are optional. Leave them empty to let the template create the resource; set any of them to a resource ID to reuse an existing resource instead. Cross-resource-group and cross-subscription IDs are supported throughout.

Use these for hub-and-spoke and workload landing zone designs where a platform team owns shared services. Resource reuse needs explicit scoped permissions and connectivity; a resource ID alone does not supply them.

docs.title: Workload data services
docs.text: Parameter Env variable Description aiSearchResourceId — (native string) Reattach a dedicated Foundry backing Search service; this is not the workload Search reuse input. aiFoundryStorageAccountResourceId — (native string) Reuse dedicated Foundry backing Storage. aiFoundryCosmosDBAccountResourceId — (native string) Reuse dedicated Foundry backing Cosmos DB. keyVaultResourceId — (native string; add to reviewed root file if needed) Existing workload Key Vault ID. Review its deployment and access conditions.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Parameter Env variable Description existingLogAnalyticsWorkspaceResourceId EXISTING_LOG_ANALYTICS_WORKSPACE_RESOURCE_ID Reuse a central Log Analytics workspace. All diagnostic settings, AMPLS linkage, and the App Configuration entries point at this workspace. existingApplicationInsightsResourceId EXISTING_APPLICATION_INSIGHTS_RESOURCE_ID Reuse an existing Application Insights component. Pair with existingApplicationInsightsConnectionString so downstream consumers (Container Apps Environment, App Configuration) receive a working connection string without needing access to the AppInsights resource. existingApplicationInsightsConnectionString EXISTING_APPLICATION_INSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING Connection string for the reused AppInsights component (az monitor app-insights component show -g <rg> -a <name> --query connectionString -o tsv). Marked @secure().

docs.title: Networking
docs.text: Parameter Env variable Description existingVnetResourceId EXISTING_VNET_RESOURCE_ID Existing VNet to deploy the workload subnets into. Used together with useExistingVNet=true. hubIntegrationHubVnetResourceId HUB_INTEGRATION_HUB_VNET_RESOURCE_ID Resource ID of the hub VNet to peer with. When set and hubIntegrationCreateHubPeering=true, the deployment creates the spoke→hub peering automatically (the reverse hub→spoke direction is the operator's responsibility — see tests/scripts/Add-HubSpokePeering.ps1). hubIntegrationExistingRouteTableResourceId HUB_INTEGRATION_EXISTING_ROUTE_TABLE_RESOURCE_ID Existing Route Table to attach to the spoke workload subnets. When set, the deployment skips local RT creation and assumes the RT is already configured with the correct default route.

docs.title: Hub jumpbox / Bastion / NAT
docs.text:
An existing ID influences the matching nullable deploy* default; an explicit deploy flag wins. Review the effective flags together rather than assuming the ID alone suppresses every local resource.

Parameter Env variable Description existingBastionResourceId EXISTING_BASTION_RESOURCE_ID Hub-managed Bastion host that has line-of-sight to the spoke jumpbox via peering. existingNatGatewayResourceId EXISTING_NAT_GATEWAY_RESOURCE_ID Hub-managed NAT Gateway to associate with the spoke subnets for outbound egress. existingJumpboxResourceId EXISTING_JUMPBOX_RESOURCE_ID Reference to a hub-managed jumpbox VM. Informational — surfaced to runbooks and post-provision scripts.

docs.title: Private DNS zones
docs.text:
Each applicable zone can be brought from a central platform subscription. An existing zone ID suppresses its local creation and automatic spoke link. Every client VNet needs a zone link or explicit DNS forwarding path to a linked network; peering alone does not propagate DNS zone links. With policyManagedPrivateDns=true, use the Policy-owned DNS model instead of BYO overrides and agree who creates zone groups, records and links.

docs.title: Hub integration
docs.text:
For deploymentMode=ailz-integrated or hybrid hub-and-spoke designs. See the hub-and-spoke reference for ownership, DNS and peering.

Parameter Default Description hubIntegrationCreateHubPeering true When true and hubIntegrationHubVnetResourceId is set, the deployment creates the spoke→hub peering inline. Set to false to defer peering creation to the platform team. hubIntegrationEgressNextHopIp null Private IP of the hub Azure Firewall / NVA. When set, the spoke UDR for 0.0.0.0/0 points here. Effective only when deployAzureFirewall=false and networkIsolation=true. hubIntegrationPeeringAllowGatewayTransit false allowGatewayTransit flag on the spoke→hub peering. Set to true only when the spoke owns a VPN / ExpressRoute gateway. hubIntegrationPeeringUseRemoteGateways false useRemoteGateways flag on the spoke→hub peering. Set to true to route on-premises traffic through a hub-owned gateway.

The BYO IDs that drive this section (hubIntegrationHubVnetResourceId, hubIntegrationExistingRouteTableResourceId) are listed in the Networking BYO table above.

docs.title: DNS zone link suffix
docs.text: Parameter Default Env variable Description dnsZoneLinkSuffix '' DNS_ZONE_LINK_SUFFIX Suffix appended to VNet-link names when multiple spokes share the same hub Private DNS zones, so the per-spoke link names don't collide. Typical values: spoke01, spoke02, …

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
Parameter Default Env variable Description useExistingVNet false USE_EXISTING_VNET Use an existing VNet instead of creating a new one. Pair with existingVnetResourceId. deploySubnets true DEPLOY_SUBNETS Global creation switch for all twelve subnets, in both new and existing VNets. Effective creation also requires networkIsolation and the individual subnet flag. vnetAddressPrefixes ["192.168.0.0/21"] — (explicit root array) Address space for a new VNet. A reused VNet's actual address space is authoritative and is not resized. sideBySideDeploy false SIDE_BY_SIDE Allow a second AI LZ to be deployed side-by-side in the same existing VNet without disturbing the first one's subnets / NSGs.

See subnet creation and addressing for all twelve creation flags (each defaults to true), root name/prefix parameters and their exact environment bindings. A false creation flag does not disable a consumer: its valid subnet must already exist in the selected VNet, or the consumer must be explicitly disabled. Application private endpoints use their configured subnet without falling back to the Foundry PE subnet. The default allocation table lists names, CIDRs and delegations.

docs.text:
The modelDeploymentList parameter defines which AI models to deploy in the Foundry account.

      "model": {
        "format": "OpenAI",
        "name": "gpt-5-nano",
        "version": "2025-08-07"
      },
      "sku": {
        "name": "GlobalStandard",
        "capacity": 40
      },
      "canonical_name": "CHAT_DEPLOYMENT_NAME",
      "apiVersion": "2025-12-01-preview"
    },
    {
      "name": "text-embedding",
      "model": {
        "format": "OpenAI",
        "name": "text-embedding-3-large",
        "version": "1"
      },

docs.text:
The containerAppsList parameter defines the container apps to deploy and their RBAC roles.

"containerAppsList": {
  "value": [
    {
      "name": null,
      "external": true,
      "target_port": 8080,
      "service_name": "orchestrator",
      "profile_name": "main",
      "min_replicas": 1,
      "max_replicas": 1,
      "canonical_name": "ORCHESTRATOR_APP",
      "dapr": {
        "enabled": true,
        "appId": "orchestrator",
        "appPort": 8080
      },
      "roles": [
        "AppConfigurationDataReader",
        "CognitiveServicesUser",
        "CognitiveServicesOpenAIUser",
        "AcrPull",
        "CosmosDBBuiltInDataContributor",
        "SearchIndexDataReader",
